We start with a bar that we turn about its axis, like a screw with a screwdriver. In chapter 5 we named such a moment as an internal quantity of the space frame, in chapter 12 we built it into the frame element, and in chapter 13 into the model of the shaft. Everywhere it was a formula taken from a source and not proved. Now we derive it from the equations of elasticity of chapter 11.

The word torsion (torzija) means twisting. When a moment turns a bar about its axis, the bar does not turn as a whole. Each cross section turns about the axis by a slightly different angle than its neighbour, so the bar is twisted, as a wrung cloth is. The name is therefore an honest picture of what happens: not the rotation of a body, but the twisting of its parts against one another.

Why does it matter? A shaft in a gearbox carries moment from the motor to the wheel. It must withstand the stress the moment causes and must not turn too far. A frame made of profiles is often loaded so that it is twisted, and then the shape of the section decides its stiffness. A tube twists much less than a tube of the same sheet with a slit along its wall, although both hold the same amount of metal.

The chapter promises four things. First, for the circle we will compute the twist and the stresses exactly, because there every step can be checked. Second, for any section we will find how the points of the section move along the axis when it is twisted, and write the stresses with a single function on the section. This also solves the rectangle that chapter 12 needs. Third, we will show why thin open sections and hollow sections behave so differently from solid ones, and through which point a transverse force must pass so that the section does not turn under it. Fourth, we will estimate how close an approximate calculation is to the true one, also with the finite element calculation of chapter 15. What we cannot prove from the book we will state with a source and say that it is stated.

First the circle, because it is the simplest.

16.1 Torsion of the circle (torzija kroga)

A steel shaft with a diameter of \(40\) mm and a length of \(1\) m is clamped into a wall at its left end, and at its right end we turn it with a moment of \(50\) N m about its axis, like a bolt with a wrench. How far does the right end turn? Where in the shaft is the material loaded most? And how would we find the answer for a shaft that has a rectangle instead of a circle? This phenomenon is called torsion (torzija, in Slovenian also zvijanje), from the Latin torquere, to twist. We begin the chapter with the circle, because there the ideas of elementary strength of materials are exact and every step can be tested. Then we change the cross section and see what breaks.

From history

Coulomb measured the twisting of a wire. Chapter 1 said that from the oscillation of a metal cylinder on a wire he determined how the wire resists twisting. Let us now add what he derived from it. For the oscillation he assumed that the moment with which the twisted wire resists is proportional to the angle of rotation \(\varphi\), and he obtained the period of oscillation. The experiment showed that the period does not depend on the angle if the angle is not too large, and from this he concluded that the proportionality of the moment to the angle is correct (TIMO, PDF p. 60). The reason is that a cylinder with moment of inertia \(J_{\mathrm{v}}\) on a wire that gives the moment \(c\,\varphi\) obeys \(J_{\mathrm{v}}\,\ddot\varphi = -c\,\varphi\), and its period does not depend on the amplitude, as we saw for torsional oscillation in chapter 9. Then he took wires of the same metal but of different lengths and diameters, and obtained the equation for the moment

\[M = \frac{\mu\,d^4}{l}\,\varphi , \tag{16.1}\]

where \(l\) is the length of the wire, \(d\) its diameter and \(\mu\) a constant of the material (TIMO, PDF p. 61, equation (i), printed page 53). The diameter thus stands in the fourth power: a wire with twice the diameter is \(2^4 = 16\) times stiffer at the same angle and length, and a wire twice as long is twice as soft.

Equation (16.1) is the law that this section explains: it hides the fourth power of the diameter and the constant \(\mu\), which we shall express by the shear modulus of the material. Before we start, let us say precisely what we compute.

Definition 16.1 Torsion of a prism (torzija prizme)

A prism (prizma) is a body obtained when a cross section \(S\), a figure in a plane with an area (definition 4.27), is moved by a length \(L\) perpendicular to itself. The axis \(x\) runs along the prism, in the cross section we measure the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) as in chapter 5, with the origin \(O\) in the cross section. The material is homogeneous, isotropic and linearly elastic with shear modulus \(G\) (definition 3.9), there is no body force, and the lateral surface is free, that is, without forces. On the two end sections only surface forces act (stress vector, definition 2.20) that have zero resultant and the moment \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\): the moment about the axis \(x\) is \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), the moments about the axes \(y\) and \(z\) are zero. The moment \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the moment of the forces on the section with outward normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), with respect to the direction \(+x\), and on the opposite section its moment is \(-M_{\mathrm{x}}\).

The torsion is uniform (enakomerna torzija) if the displacement in the plane of the section at every \(x\) agrees with a rigid rotation of the section about the point \(O\) by a small angle \(\varphi(x)\),

\[u_{\mathrm{y}} = -\varphi(x)\,z , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = \varphi(x)\,y , \qquad \varphi(x) = \alpha\,x , \tag{16.2}\]

with a constant number \(\alpha\), which we call the twist per unit length (zasuk na enoto dolžine), unit rad/m. The displacement along the axis, \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), is not prescribed: in this section we test \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), in the following ones we shall look for it.

Source: SADD section 9.3 (PDF p. 246) prescribes the same displacement in the plane and an unknown function for \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), with the axis \(z\) along the bar, the cross section in the plane \(x\), \(y\) and the twist per unit length \(\alpha\). Here the axes are moved to ours (axis \(x\) along the bar). The definition is not from the source.

The words each have a reason. A prism is a body with a constant cross section, as bars and shafts have. The twist per unit length is called so because \(\alpha = \varphi(x)/x\) is the angle by which the section turns for every metre of length. Let us watch the letters: \(\varphi\) is here the rotation of the section as in chapter 13, not the Airy function of chapter 11. The letter \(\alpha\) in this chapter is not the thermal expansion coefficient of chapter 3, which we shall not use. We write the moment about the axis \(x\) as \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) as in chapters 5 and 13, because the letter \(T\) would be taken by temperature.

The assumptions are idealizations and each has its meaning. Linear elasticity holds as long as the stress does not reach the yield limit, which we shall test. A free lateral surface means that nothing slides along the shaft. Loading the end with an exactly given distribution of forces is an idealization: the real load is a bolt or a gear. Saint-Venant's principle (section 11.11) says that another distribution with the same moment differs only near the end, which we state here and do not prove. The twisting that develops equally in every section is the one required by the constant twist \(\alpha\). For nonuniform torsion (neenakomerna torzija), which is hindered by the clamping and which we do not treat here, see COOK (PDF pp. 42 and 43) and ONATE2 section 4.10 (PDF pp. 227 to 246).

Why do we expect a constant \(\alpha\)? Let us draw the shaft and think.

The hatched line is the wall into which the shaft is clamped. From it along the axis \(x\) extends the shaft, a cylinder of length \(L\), measured from the wall. At the right end we turn it with the moment \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) about the axis. Before we load it, we draw a straight thread on the surface along the shaft. Let us cut off in thought the right part of the shaft, from the section at \(x\) to the end. Only the moment \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) at the end and the moment of the forces of the left part across the section act on this part, the lateral surface is free. The moment about the axis \(x\) must be in equilibrium, therefore the moment across every section equals \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\). Every piece of the shaft with the same length and cross section thus has the same moment and therefore turns by the same angle. If the cross section is the same everywhere, the rotation of the section \(\varphi(x)\) therefore grows from \(\varphi(0) = 0\) at the wall with the same rate \(\alpha\) along the shaft, and after loading the thread bends into a helix. The height of the orange line at the right end is \(R\sin\varphi(L)\), which shows the rotation of the end.

Let us enlarge the view. On the surface of the shaft take a window with a square of side \(h\), enlarged on the right. Before loading its edges are perpendicular. One runs along the axis, the other along the circumference. After loading, the section at \(x\) and the section at \(x + h\) are turned with respect to the wall by \(\alpha x\) and \(\alpha(x + h)\), therefore with respect to each other by \(\alpha h\). A point on the surface that is \(R\) from the axis is thereby shifted along the circumference by \(R\alpha h\), this is the shift. The edge in the direction of the axis therefore tilts by the angle \(\gamma\) with respect to the original direction, the sheared square is no longer rectangular, and

\[\tan\gamma = \frac{R\alpha h}{h} = R\alpha , \qquad \gamma \approx R\alpha , \tag{16.3}\]

for a small angle. The change of the right angle between two edges is the shear strain (chapter 1, definition 1.115), in the engineering form \(\gamma = 2\varepsilon\) as in definition 3.9. With it the stress on the surface is \(\tau = G\gamma = G R\alpha\), which is the first estimate that the theorem below will prove and extend to every radius.

So we arrived at the displacement (16.2) with \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\). Can this really be a solution? The displacement was obtained by guessing, and this is exactly the semi-inverse method (definition 11.11): we choose a field, check the field equations and the boundary conditions, and then theorem 11.4 guarantees that there is no other solution. For the computation we first need the polar second moment of the circle, which chapter 5 took from a source. The circle is not a figure made of rectangles, so there is no computation by rectangles, and the integral requires polar coordinates.

Let us first draw the coordinate axes of the section and the circle of radius \(R\) about the origin. A point of the circle is written with the distance \(r\) from the centre and the angle \(\theta\) from the axis \(y\), \(y = r\cos\theta\), \(z = r\sin\theta\). The angle \(\theta\) and the distance \(r\) are thus coordinates of the point, and every pair \((r, \theta)\) from the rectangle on the right gives a point of the circle. This assignment, \(\Phi(r, \theta) = (r\cos\theta,\ r\sin\theta)\), is shown by the arrows between the two pictures: \(\Phi\) takes the rectangle onto the circle, the inverse map \(\Phi^{-1}\) takes a point of the circle back into the rectangle. If the angle \(\theta\) runs from \(0\) to \(2\pi\), the point comes back to the same place: the side \(\theta = 0\) and the side \(\theta = 2\pi\) of the rectangle are mapped onto the same segment, the radius on the axis \(y\), which we therefore cut out of the circle. Let us choose a piece of the circle between the radii \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) and between the angles \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\). Its preimage in the rectangle has area \((r_2 - r_1)(\theta_2 - \theta_1)\), and the piece itself has the area of the difference of two circular sectors, \(\tfrac12(\theta_2 - \theta_1)(r_2^2 - r_1^2)\). Since \(r_2^2 - r_1^2 = (r_2 - r_1)(r_2 + r_1)\), this is \(\bar r\,(r_2 - r_1)(\theta_2 - \theta_1)\) with the mean radius \(\bar r\). The piece is therefore \(\bar r\) times larger than its preimage: the larger, the farther from the centre it lies. This factor, equal to \(r\) at the point \((r, \theta)\), is the Jacobian determinant of the map \(\Phi\). Its matrix of derivatives and determinant are

\[\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta & -r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta\end{pmatrix} , \qquad J_\Phi = r\cos^2\theta + r\sin^2\theta = r ,\]

as in lemma 11.15, item 1, only without the coordinate \(z\). Theorem 4.59 on the change of variables uses this factor exactly.

Lemma 16.2 Second moments of a disc and an annulus (vztrajnostni momenti kroga in kolobarja)

Let \(K\) be a disc of radius \(R\) with centre at the origin of the plane \(y\), \(z\), and \(K_{\mathrm{i}}\) a disc of radius \(R_{\mathrm{i}} < R\) with the same centre. Both are sets with an area (definition 4.27), since they are closed, bounded and their boundary is a circle. Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} y\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{K}} z\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 , \qquad I_{\mathrm{z}} = \int_{\mathrm{K}} y^2\,\mathrm{d}A = I_{\mathrm{y}} = \int_{\mathrm{K}} z^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \frac{\pi R^4}{4} , \tag{16.4}\]

the polar second moment of area (polarni vztrajnostni moment) \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = \int_{\mathrm{K}} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A = I_{\mathrm{y}} + I_{\mathrm{z}}\) is

\[I_{\mathrm{p}} = \frac{\pi R^4}{2} , \tag{16.5}\]

and for the annulus \(K \setminus K_{\mathrm{i}}\) it is

\[I_{\mathrm{p}} = \frac{\pi}{2}\,\big(R^4 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^4\big) . \tag{16.6}\]
Proof

We must show that the integral of \(r^2\) over the disc can be computed with radii and angles, and the other relations follow by reflection. We cut the disc into a piece with an exact computation and a remainder whose area is arbitrarily small.

  1. Let \(0 < \rho < R\) and \(0 < \delta < \pi/2\) be numbers. Let \(\Phi(r, \theta) = (r\cos\theta,\ r\sin\theta)\) on the open set \(D = (\rho/2, 2R) \times (0, 2\pi)\). The map \(\Phi\) is continuously differentiable and has, as computed at figure 16.2, the Jacobian determinant \(J_\Phi = r > 0\). The map is injective: from \(r\cos\theta = r'\cos\theta'\) and \(r\sin\theta = r'\sin\theta'\) it follows that \(r^2 = r'^2\), so \(r = r'\), and then \(\cos\theta = \cos\theta'\), \(\sin\theta = \sin\theta'\), which in \((0, 2\pi)\) gives \(\theta = \theta'\).
  2. The rectangle \(W = [\rho, R] \times [\delta, 2\pi - \delta]\) lies in \(D\) and is a set with an area, its image \(\Phi(W)\) is the disc without the small disc of radius \(\rho\) and without the sector with angle \(2\delta\) around the radius \(\theta = 0\). By theorem 4.59 on the change of variables, for the function \(f(y, z) = y^2 + z^2 = r^2\),
    \[\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{W}} r^2\cdot r\,\mathrm{d}A = (2\pi - 2\delta)\int_\rho^R r^3\,\mathrm{d}r = (\pi - \delta)\,\frac{R^4 - \rho^4}{2} ,\]
    since the integral over a rectangle is the product of two integrals (theorem 4.9) and \(r^4/4\) is an indefinite integral of \(r^3\) (fundamental theorem of calculus, 3.40).
  3. Let \(N\) be the closure of the set \(K \setminus \Phi(W)\). A point of \(N\) is at most \(\rho\) from the origin or has the polar angle in \([-\delta, \delta]\). The former lie in the square \([-\rho, \rho]^2\) with area \(4\rho^2\). The latter have \(0 \le y \le R\) and \(|z| = r|\sin\theta| \le R\sin\delta \le R\delta\) and lie in a rectangle with area \(2R^2\delta\). So the area of the set \(N\) is at most \(4\rho^2 + 2R^2\delta\) (monotonicity and additivity, lemma 4.32, items 2 and 4).
  4. The sets \(\Phi(W)\) and \(N\) have union \(K\) and no interior point of one lies in the other. By additivity (lemma 4.32, item 4) and by the bound (item 3, \(|f| \le R^2\) on \(K\)),
    \[\Big|\int_{\mathrm{K}} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A - \int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A\Big| = \Big|\int_{\mathrm{N}} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A\Big| \le R^2\,\big(4\rho^2 + 2R^2\delta\big) .\]
  5. Let \(\rho \to 0\) and \(\delta \to 0\). The right-hand side of step 4 tends to zero, and the integral of step 2 tends to \(\pi R^4/2\). So \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = \pi R^4/2\). For \(R = 20\) mm, \(\rho = 0{,}01\) mm and \(\delta = 0{,}01\) rad the integral of step 2 equals \(250\,527\) mm\(^4\), it differs from the exact value \(251\,327\) mm\(^4\) by \(800\) mm\(^4\), and the estimate of step 4 is \(3200\) mm\(^4\).
  6. The map \((y, z) \mapsto (z, y)\) is linear with \(|J| = 1\) and maps \(K\) onto itself. By theorem 4.59, \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} y^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{K}} z^2\,\mathrm{d}A\), so \(I_{\mathrm{y}} = I_{\mathrm{z}} = I_{\mathrm{p}}/2 = \pi R^4/4\). The map \((y, z) \mapsto (-y, z)\) has \(|J| = 1\) and maps \(K\) onto itself, therefore \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} y\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{K}} (-y)\,\mathrm{d}A\) and this integral is zero. The same holds for \(z\).
  7. The annulus \(K \setminus K_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(K_{\mathrm{i}}\) have union \(K\) and no interior point of one lies in the other. By additivity \(I_{\mathrm{p}}(K \setminus K_{\mathrm{i}}) = I_{\mathrm{p}}(K) - I_{\mathrm{p}}(K_{\mathrm{i}}) = \tfrac{\pi}{2}(R^4 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^4)\).

Source: The value \(I = \pi R^4/4\) is in ONATE2 (Fig. 1.3, PDF p. 35) and SADD (D.2, PDF p. 573) for the polar moment \(J = \pi c^4/2\) with radius \(c\). The computation with polar coordinates and with reflection is not from the sources.

Chapter 5 took \(I = \pi R^4/4\) for a circle of diameter \(d = 32\) mm: \(\pi \cdot 16^4/4 = 51\,472\) mm\(^4\). Now it is proved. The polar moment of a shaft with \(d = 40\) mm is \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = \pi \cdot 20^4/2 = 251\,327\) mm\(^4\), and of a hollow shaft with \(d_{\mathrm{o}} = 40\) mm and \(d_{\mathrm{i}} = 32\) mm it is \(\pi(20^4 - 16^4)/2 = 148\,384\) mm\(^4\).

Now the theorem. The guess is the displacement (16.2) with \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), we omit nothing.

Theorem 16.3 Torsion of a circle and an annulus (torzija kroga in kolobarja)

Let the prism of definition 16.1 be uniformly twisted, with a cross section that is a disc of radius \(R\) or an annulus with radii \(R_{\mathrm{i}} < R\) and centre at \(O\), of a material as required by theorems 11.6 and 11.4 (ideally elastic with positive strain energy density). Let \(r = \sqrt{y^2 + z^2}\) be the distance from the axis. The displacement field

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0 , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = -\alpha\,x\,z , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = \alpha\,x\,y \tag{16.7}\]

has the following properties.

  1. It satisfies the Navier-Lamé equations (11.3) with zero body force.
  2. The stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -G\alpha\,z\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\alpha\,y\) and all other components are zero. The shear vector \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) is perpendicular to the radius, tangential, with magnitude \(\tau = G\alpha\,r\).
  3. The lateral surface is free: the stress vector on the outer and, for the annulus, the inner circle is zero.
  4. On an end section with normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) the resultant force and the moments about the axes \(y\) and \(z\) are zero, and the moment about the axis \(x\) is
    \[M_{\mathrm{x}} = G\,I_{\mathrm{p}}\,\alpha . \tag{16.8}\]
  5. This field is, up to a small rigid motion, the only one that has such stresses and such forces on the end sections. At the clamping, where \(u = 0\) at \(x = 0\), it is the only solution and its displacement is exactly (16.7).
Idea

We check everything that the boundary value problem demands: the field equations, the condition on the lateral surface and the distribution of forces at the ends. The lateral surface is the key: the vector \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) is perpendicular to the radius, and the normal of the circle is parallel to the radius, so their product is zero. This is why the circle works.

Proof
  1. By definition 1.115 the strains of the field (16.7) are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = 0\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = 0\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = 0\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial y) = \tfrac12(-\alpha x + \alpha x) = 0\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x) = -\alpha z/2\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x) = \alpha y/2\). The trace of the strain is zero.
  2. By Hooke's law (theorem 3.11, \(\ten\sigma = \lambda\,(\tr\ten\varepsilon)\,\mat I + 2G\,\ten\varepsilon\)), because of step 1, \(\ten\sigma = 2G\,\ten\varepsilon\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -G\alpha z\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\alpha y\) and the other components are zero. With the coordinates \(y = r\cos\theta\), \(z = r\sin\theta\) we have \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}) = G\alpha r\,(-\sin\theta, \cos\theta)\), a vector of length \(G\alpha r\) perpendicular to the radius. This is item 2.
  3. Every component of the field (16.7) is a product of \(x\) and \(y\) or \(z\), so the second derivatives \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x^2\), \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y^2\) and \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial z^2\) are zero, so \(\nabla^2\vek u = \vek 0\). At the same time \(\operatorname{div}\vek u = 0 + 0 + 0\). The left-hand side of equation (11.3) is therefore zero, the body force is zero (theorem 11.6). This is item 1.
  4. Let \(\rho\) be the radius of one circle of the lateral surface, \(\rho = R\) or \(\rho = R_{\mathrm{i}}\). A point \((y, z)\) of the circle has the normal \(\vek n = \pm(0, y, z)/\rho\), so \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\). By Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.24), \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}} = \pm(-G\alpha z\,y + G\alpha y\,z)/\rho = 0\), \(t_{\mathrm{y}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and \(t_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), because \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\). This is item 3.
  5. On the section with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) the stress vector is \(\vek t = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}) = (0, -G\alpha z, G\alpha y)\) by step 2 and the symmetry of stress (theorem 2.36). The resultant is \(\int \vek t\,\mathrm{d}A = (0, -G\alpha\int z\,\mathrm{d}A, G\alpha\int y\,\mathrm{d}A) = \vek 0\) by lemma 16.2, equation (16.4). For the annulus the integral is a difference of integrals over \(K\) and \(K_{\mathrm{i}}\) and is again zero.
  6. The moment about the axis \(x\) of these forces is \(\int (y\,t_{\mathrm{z}} - z\,t_{\mathrm{y}})\,\mathrm{d}A = G\alpha\int (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A = G\alpha\,I_{\mathrm{p}}\). The moments about the axes \(y\) and \(z\) are \(\int (z\,t_{\mathrm{x}} - x\,t_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}A\) and \(\int (x\,t_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,t_{\mathrm{x}})\,\mathrm{d}A\). Since \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) and \(x\) is constant on the section, they equal \(-x\int t_{\mathrm{z}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) and \(x\int t_{\mathrm{y}}\,\mathrm{d}A\), so by step 5 they are zero. At \(x = 0\) the normal is \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and the forces and the moment are opposite. This is item 4.
  7. The forces on the lateral surface and on the end sections are thereby given, the body force is zero. By theorem 11.4, item 1, the stresses and strains of every solution with the same forces equal ours, the difference of the displacements is a small rigid motion (item 2 of the theorem), that is \(\vek a + \mat W\vek r\) with an antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\). At the clamping, displacement \(u = 0\) at \(x = 0\), our displacement is of this kind, since at \(x = 0\) also \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) are zero. Item 3 of the theorem further requires that the only small rigid motion that is zero on the clamped section \(x = 0\) is zero. For two points \(\vek r\), \(\vek r'\) of this section, \(\vek a + \mat W\vek r = \vek a + \mat W\vek r' = \vek 0\), so \(\mat W(\vek r - \vek r') = \vek 0\), and since \(\vek r - \vek r'\) can point in the direction \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) or \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(\mat W\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \mat W\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek 0\). Then \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = W_{\mathrm{zy}} = W_{\mathrm{xz}} = W_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\) and by antisymmetry \(\mat W = 0\), and then \(\vek a = \vek 0\). By item 3 of the theorem our solution is therefore the only one. This is item 5.
Explanation

The sections do not warp (\(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\)) and radial lines stay straight and radial: the point \((y, z)\) of the section at \(x\) moves under the field to \((y - \varphi z,\ z + \varphi y)\) with small \(\varphi = \alpha x\). Up to terms of order \(\varphi^2\) this is the point \(r(\cos(\theta + \varphi), \sin(\theta + \varphi))\), the original point \(r(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\) rotated by \(\varphi\). The map is linear, so it takes a segment from the centre to a segment from the centre, and radial lines stay straight and radial. So the assumptions of elementary strength of materials from chapter 13 (axis straight, sections plane, radial lines straight) are here a result of the computation. The moment (16.8) proves for the circle equation (12.16) of chapter 12, with the torsion constant \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}}\), and equation (13.14) of chapter 13 for uniform torsion, when the twist per unit length \(\partial\varphi/\partial x = \alpha\) is constant. When \(\partial\varphi/\partial x\) varies along the shaft or in time, as in vibration, equation (13.14) remains a model that this theorem supports but does not prove.

Source: SADD section D.2 (PDF pp. 573 and 574) has the field (16.7) from the assumption that the points of the section move tangentially in proportion to the distance from the centre, and from equilibrium obtains \(\tau = T\rho/J\) and equation (D.4). SADD example 5.3 (PDF p. 117) checks this field by the semi-inverse method. The proof with the Navier-Lamé equations, the boundary condition and uniqueness is ours, not from the sources.

Let us look at the result on the section.

We draw the section of the solid shaft and its axes. The stress at a point of the section is the shear vector \(G\alpha r\) with direction perpendicular to the radius. On the radius on the axis \(y\) the arrows grow from zero at the centre to \(G\alpha R = 3{,}98\) MPa at the edge, which is a straight line in \(r\). On the circumference the arrow at every point has the same length and points in the direction of circulation, as the vector \((-\sin\theta, \cos\theta)\) shows. On the right is the tube with outer radius \(R\) and inner radius \(R_{\mathrm{i}}\), on the inner and outer circle the stresses are \(5{,}39\) and \(6{,}74\) MPa (at the same moment it is larger because the \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) of the tube is smaller). The distance \(R_{\mathrm{i}}\) is a cavity where there is no material and no stress.

Corollary 16.4 Angle, stiffness and largest stress of a circular shaft (zasuk, togost in največja napetost krožne gredi)

Let a shaft of length \(L\) with a solid circular or annular cross section, as in theorem 16.3, be loaded by the moment \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) at the end. Then

\[\alpha = \frac{M_{\mathrm{x}}}{G\,I_{\mathrm{p}}} , \qquad \varphi(L) = \frac{M_{\mathrm{x}}\,L}{G\,I_{\mathrm{p}}} , \qquad k_{\mathrm{t}} = \frac{M_{\mathrm{x}}}{\varphi(L)} = \frac{G\,I_{\mathrm{p}}}{L} , \tag{16.9}\]

the shear stress at radius \(r\) is \(\tau(r) = M_{\mathrm{x}}\,r/I_{\mathrm{p}}\) and the largest is at the outer edge,

\[\tau_{\max} = \frac{M_{\mathrm{x}}\,R}{I_{\mathrm{p}}} , \qquad \gamma_{\max} = R\,\alpha .\]
Proof

From equation (16.8), \(\alpha = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(G I_{\mathrm{p}})\) and from equation (16.2) \(\varphi(L) = \alpha L\). From item 2 of theorem 16.3, \(\tau(r) = G\alpha r = M_{\mathrm{x}} r/I_{\mathrm{p}}\). The function \(r \mapsto r\) is increasing, so the maximum is at \(r = R\). The shear strain \(\gamma = \tau/G = \alpha r\) has its largest value \(R\alpha\), which agrees with equation (16.3).

Source: SADD (D.3) and (D.4) (PDF pp. 573 and 574), CK (12.10) (PDF p. 389). The equation for \(k_{\mathrm{t}}\) is taken in chapters 9 and 13 as a model. Here it is proved for a shaft at rest in uniform torsion. In the vibrating shaft of chapter 13 the twist per unit length varies along the shaft and in time, and there the equation remains a model.

Now let us answer the questions from the beginning.

Example 16.5 Steel shaft (jeklena gred)

The shaft has \(d = 40\) mm, \(L = 1\) m, steel \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\), so \(G = E/(2(1 + \nu)) = 75{,}38\) GPa. The polar moment is \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 251\,327\) mm\(^4\), the torsional stiffness \(G I_{\mathrm{p}} = 18\,946\) N m\(^2\) and \(k_{\mathrm{t}} = 18\,946\) N m/rad. Results by equations (16.9):

\(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) \(\alpha\) \(\varphi(L)\) \(\tau_{\max}\) \(\gamma_{\max}\)
\(50\) N m \(0{,}00264\) rad/m \(0{,}151^\circ\) \(3{,}98\) MPa \(5{,}28 \cdot 10^{-5}\)
\(500\) N m \(0{,}02639\) rad/m \(1{,}512^\circ\) \(39{,}79\) MPa \(5{,}28 \cdot 10^{-4}\)

At \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 500\) N m the stress at radius \(10\) mm is half of that on the surface, \(19{,}89\) MPa.

When does the shaft begin to yield? On the surface the state is pure shear with stress \(\tau\) and principal stresses \(\tau\), \(0\), \(-\tau\). By theorem 2.70 the largest shear stress is \((\tau - (-\tau))/2 = \tau\), and at the yield limit \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa the first yielding by the criterion of the largest shear is at \(\tau = 110\) MPa, that is at \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = \tau\,I_{\mathrm{p}}/R = 1382\) N m. By von Mises (definition 2.76) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{3J_2} = \sqrt3\,\tau\), because the deviator of pure shear equals the stress and \(J_2 = \tau^2\), so \(\tau = 220/\sqrt3 = 127{,}0\) MPa and \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 1596\) N m. At \(500\) N m the shaft is therefore still elastic.

Is the rotation really small? At \(500\) N m we have \(\varphi(L) = 0{,}02639\) rad and a point on the surface moves by \(R\sin\varphi = 0{,}528\) mm. The field (16.2) moves the point along the circumference by \(R\varphi\) instead of \(R\sin\varphi\), and the difference \(R(\varphi - \sin\varphi)\) is \(6 \cdot 10^{-5}\) mm. The displacement towards the axis that the exact rotation has, \(R(1 - \cos\varphi) = 0{,}00696\) mm, the field does not have. The ratio of this displacement to the displacement along the circumference is \((1 - \cos\varphi)/\sin\varphi = \tan(\varphi/2)\), which is \(1{,}32\,\%\), and at \(50\) N m it is \(0{,}13\,\%\).

The tube \(d_{\mathrm{o}} = 40\) mm, \(d_{\mathrm{i}} = 32\) mm has \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 148\,384\) mm\(^4\), which is \(0{,}590\) of the solid shaft, but only \(0{,}360\) of its mass. At \(50\) N m, \(\alpha = 0{,}00447\) rad/m, \(\tau(R) = 6{,}74\) MPa and \(\tau(R_{\mathrm{i}}) = 5{,}39\) MPa. The reason for the ratio \(0{,}590\) against \(0{,}360\): in the integral \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = \int (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A\) the area at radius \(r\) counts with the weight \(r^2\), because there it has the stress \(G\alpha r\) and the lever arm \(r\). The tube removes the disc of radius \(R_{\mathrm{i}} = 0{,}8\,R\). This is \(0{,}8^2 = 0{,}64\) of the area and the mass, but only \(0{,}8^4 = 0{,}41\) of the polar moment (equation (16.5) with radius \(0{,}8\,R\)), because the removed material lies close to the axis. So \(1 - 0{,}41 = 0{,}59\) of the stiffness remains at \(1 - 0{,}64 = 0{,}36\) of the mass.

For the circle the twist \(\alpha\) of all points of the section is equal and the section does not warp. Is this true for every section? A section of another shape is the first test, and the story of how it was tested follows.

From history

Coulomb's law was also tested by experiments on shafts with other cross sections. Duleau tried iron bars, first round shafts, for which, with the assumption that the sections stay plane and the radii in them straight, he obtained an equation for the rotation that agreed with Coulomb's, and the same for tubes (TIMO, PDF pp. 90 and 91). For rectangular bars he found that these assumptions no longer hold: until then the stresses had been taken as proportional to the distance from the axis, but Duleau's experiments showed that this is not true (TIMO, PDF p. 91). At the same time, the practical handbooks of the first half of the 19th century used for the torsion of every cross section Coulomb's result with the second moment of the section (LOVE, PDF p. 36). Why this result fails for the rectangle is shown by the test below.

Chapter 5 has already introduced Duleau as a person. Let us return to the section \(20 \times 40\) mm of chapter 12 with half sides \(a = 10\) mm along \(y\) and \(b = 20\) mm along \(z\), loaded with \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m. Let us try the same field (16.7) and the same \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 4ab(a^2 + b^2)/3 = 133\,333\) mm\(^4\) (with the expression of lemma 5.27 for \(I_{\mathrm{y}} + I_{\mathrm{z}}\)).

Lemma 16.6 The guess of the circle fails on a rectangle (ugibanje kroga na pravokotniku odpove)

Let the cross section be the rectangle \([-a, a] \times [-b, b]\) with \(a, b > 0\) and let \(\alpha \ne 0\). For the field (16.7) the same field equations and stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -G\alpha z\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\alpha y\) hold as in items 1 and 2 of theorem 16.3, but on the lateral face \(y = a\) the stress vector has the component

\[t_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -G\alpha\,z ,\]

which is zero only at \(z = 0\), and on the face \(z = b\) the component \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = G\alpha y\), which is zero only at \(y = 0\). The field is therefore not a solution of the problem with a free lateral surface.

Proof

We must show that the requirement of a free lateral surface fails, although the field equations hold by the same computation as in the proof of the theorem.

  1. The field equations and stresses are computed in steps 1 to 3 of the proof of theorem 16.3, which say nothing about the shape of the section.
  2. On the face \(y = a\) the outward normal is \(\vek n = (0, 1, 0)\). By Cauchy's formula \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} = -G\alpha z\).
  3. On the face \(z = b\) we have \(\vek n = (0, 0, 1)\) and \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}} = G\alpha y\).
  4. For \(\alpha \ne 0\) and \(G > 0\) the expressions are zero only at \(z = 0\) and \(y = 0\) respectively. On most of the edge the stress vector is therefore different from zero.
Explanation

Numbers for our section: at \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m, \(G = 75\,385\) MPa and the torsion constant \(J\) of chapter 12 taken as \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}}\) we have \(\alpha = 4{,}97 \cdot 10^{-6}\) rad/mm and \(G\alpha = 0{,}375\) MPa/mm. On the face \(y = a\) the corner \(z = b\) has the component \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = -G\alpha b = -7{,}50\) MPa, on the face \(z = b\) it is \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = 3{,}75\) MPa. The stress vector at the corner has length \(G\alpha\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = 8{,}39\) MPa, although at the corner where two free faces meet all the shear stress must be zero. At the middle of the long face the given value is \(3{,}75\) MPa, and the true one is \(12{,}71\) MPa, which we compute in the following sections. The rotation with \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}}\) is also wrong: \(\alpha = 0{,}00497\) rad/m, while the true value with \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\) from chapter 12 is \(0{,}00906\) rad/m. The ratio is \(J/I_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}549\), so the rotation is \(45\,\%\) too small. The same difference was found by the frame in chapter 12, where the twisting with \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) gave \(4{,}97\) mm instead of \(9{,}06\) mm. What to do instead is shown by the following sections.

Source: The test is ours. The value \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\) is taken from SADD (9.5.12) in chapter 12, in the following sections it is derived.

Figure 16.4 shows what happens. Drawn is the section \(20 \times 40\) mm with the axes. Through the corner runs a circle about the origin: the shear vector of the circle is tangential to it. On the edge we draw the vector \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) at four points of the right face and two points of the upper one. A free face cannot carry a force, so its component along the normal is a stress on the face. For the circle this component is zero everywhere, because the normal is parallel to the radius and the vector perpendicular to it. For the rectangle the normal of the face \(y = a\) is parallel to the axis \(y\), and the vector \(G\alpha(-z, y)\) has there the component \(-G\alpha z\). The corner with two components is the extreme case: the stress vector has length \(8{,}39\) MPa, at the place where all the shear stress must be zero.

So what Duleau noticed shows up. For the circle the shear vector at the edge is along the edge, for the rectangle it must be so too, and at the corner even zero, and the field of the circle cannot do this. The assumptions of elementary strength of materials are therefore not slightly inexact for the rectangle, they fail the boundary condition. The next section therefore extends the displacement: we add to it a displacement along the axis, \(u_{\mathrm{x}} \ne 0\), which makes the sections bulge, and look for the \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) that satisfies the boundary condition.

16.2 Warping function (funkcija zvitja)

The previous section showed that the field of the circle fails on the \(20 \times 40\) mm strip: on the free long face it leaves a stress of \(7{,}50\) MPa, and at the corner a stress of \(8{,}39\) MPa where it must be zero (lemma 16.6). The field assumed that the section stays plane, that is, that all its points move only in the plane of the section. If this is not true, then besides turning about the axis a point of the section must also move along the axis. How much, and how to compute it for every section, not only for a rectangle, is the question of this section.

From history

That the sections of a twisted bar do not stay plane was first noticed by Cauchy. Applying the general equations of elasticity to rectangular bars, he found a satisfactory solution for a narrow rectangle and showed that the sections of a twisted bar in general do not stay plane but bulge (TIMO, PDF p. 118). LOVE says that his result was not correct, but that it is historically important because he recognized that the normal sections do not remain plane (LOVE, PDF p. 36). No year for Cauchy's work is given on these pages. Attempts to use the assumption of plane sections for shafts of other shapes did not agree with experiments (TIMO, PDF p. 207). For this reason Saint-Venant assumed only a rotation of the section in its own plane and added the warping as an unknown that the equations of elasticity determine (TIMO, PDF p. 207). This is the semi-inverse method (definition 11.11), which chapter 11 presented together with Saint-Venant's treatise. This section carries it through to the end.

The semi-inverse method is a proposal, and the field equations tell whether the proposal holds. We propose that every section at \(x\) rotates about the origin \(O\) by the angle \(\alpha x\), as in equation (16.2), and that at the same time its points move along the axis by a length that depends only on the place \((y, z)\) in the section and not on \(x\). Why not on \(x\)? Every piece of the prism with the same section and length carries the same moment (section 16.1) and therefore deforms in the same way. Why proportional to \(\alpha\)? The problem is linear and \(\alpha\) is the only parameter of the load, so every displacement is a multiple of it.

Let us draw what we propose (figure 16.5). On the left is the section \(20 \times 40\) mm viewed along the axis \(x\), with the coordinate axes \(y\) and \(z\) and the origin \(O\). The point \(P\) is the corner with the coordinates \(y = a = 10\) mm and \(z = b = 20\) mm. As before, \(P\) moves in the plane of the section by the vector \(\vek d\), perpendicular to \(OP\). On the right is the view from the side, with the axes \(x\) and \(z\). The grey vertical line is the section before loading, drawn at one place \(x\). After loading the points of the face \(y = a\) move along the axis: at \(z = 0\) not at all, above in the direction \(+x\), below in the direction \(-x\), at the corner \(z = b\) by \(0{,}832\) \(\mu\)m and at most \(0{,}953\) \(\mu\)m at \(z = 16{,}6\) mm, at \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m. The points of the face \(y = -a\) move in the opposite direction, so the section does not rotate as a rigid body but bulges like a saddle. The length of the arrow between the grey line and the curve at \(z = 15\) mm is the displacement \(\alpha\psi\) of that point, \(0{,}934\) \(\mu\)m. The displacements are drawn \(12\,600\) times larger than in reality, and the curves are computed with the series of section 16.5 and serve here only as a view of what we are looking for.

The word warping translates the Slovenian zvitje. Let us write the proposal as a definition.

Definition 16.7 Warping function (funkcija zvitja)

Let a prism with section \(S\) be uniformly twisted (definition 16.1) with the twist per unit length \(\alpha \ne 0\). The displacement of the point \((x, y, z)\) has the form

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha\,\psi(y, z) , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = -\alpha\,x\,z , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = \alpha\,x\,y , \tag{16.10}\]

where \(\psi : S \to \mathbb{R}\) is a twice continuously differentiable function on an open set that contains \(S\). We call the function \(\psi\) the warping function (funkcija zvitja), and measure its values in mm\(^2\).

Explanation

The unit is such that \(\alpha\psi\) is a length: \(\alpha\) is in rad/mm (rad is a number without a unit) and \(\psi\) in mm\(^2\). The value \(\alpha\psi(y, z)\) is the displacement of the point of the section along the axis, which the arrow \(\alpha\psi\) on the right half of figure 16.5 shows. For the circle \(\psi = 0\) (section 16.1). The letter \(\psi\) has several meanings in the book: a trial function in chapter 6 and a shape function in chapter 7. In this chapter it means only the warping function.

Source: SADD section 9.3 (PDF pp. 246 and 247): the in-plane displacement is a rigid rotation about the center of twist \(O\), where \(u = v = 0\), the rotation is a linear function of the axial coordinate, and the displacement along the axis, which SADD calls \(w\), is an unknown function of the coordinates in the section only (SADD (9.3.3)). SADD has the axis \(z\) along the bar, we have the axis \(x\), its \(w(x, y)\) is our \(\alpha\psi(y, z)\) and its \(\alpha\) is our \(\alpha\). The name warping function with the symbol \(\psi\) and the definition are ours.

What does the displacement (16.10) do to the strains? The first part, \((0, -\alpha xz, \alpha xy)\), is the rotation of the section about \(O\) by the angle \(\alpha x\) that we already know, and the second part, \((\alpha\psi, 0, 0)\), is a displacement that has only a component along the axis and depends only on the place in the section. Chapter 11 called this form, with a component along the axis, the antiplane state and announced it as the setting of torsion. Let us compute the strains of both parts together.

Lemma 16.8 Strains in torsion (deformacije pri torziji)

Let the displacement have the form (16.10). Then at every point of the prism

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0 , \qquad \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z) , \qquad \gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y) , \tag{16.11}\]

where \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}}\) mean \(\partial\psi/\partial y\) and \(\partial\psi/\partial z\). The strains depend only on \((y, z)\) and not on \(x\). By Hooke's law (theorem 3.11) the only nonzero stresses are

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = G\alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z) , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y) . \tag{16.12}\]
Idea

Every term is a derivative of a product in which one factor is \(x\) or does not depend on the variable we differentiate by.

Proof
  1. By definition 1.115, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = \alpha\,\partial\psi/\partial x = 0\), because \(\psi\) does not depend on \(x\). Similarly \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = -\alpha x\,\partial z/\partial y = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = 0\).
  2. \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial y) = \tfrac12(-\alpha x + \alpha x) = 0\).
  3. \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x) = \tfrac12\alpha(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z)\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x) = \tfrac12\alpha(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y)\). The shear strains are by convention twice these.
  4. The trace of the strain is zero by step 1, so by Hooke's law \(\ten\sigma = 2G\,\ten\varepsilon\). Only the components with the indices \(xy\) and \(xz\) are nonzero (and the symmetric \(yx\), \(zx\) by theorem 2.36).

Source: SADD section 9.3.1, equations (9.3.4) and (9.3.5) (PDF p. 247): from the displacement (9.3.3) it obtains the same two shear strains. The split into rotation and antiplane part is ours.

Let us see what this means for our strip, the right half of figure 16.5. At the middle of the long face, at the point \((a, 0)\), the rotation alone gives the stress \(G\alpha\,(-z, y) = (0,\ G\alpha a)\), that is \(6{,}83\) MPa at \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m and the true \(\alpha = 9{,}064 \cdot 10^{-6}\) rad/mm, which section 16.5 computes for the strip. Section 16.1 computed \(\alpha\) with the polar moment \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\), got a smaller \(\alpha\) and therefore only \(3{,}75\) MPa there. The true stress \(12{,}71\) MPa, which section 16.5 computes, we obtain only with the warping: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 1{,}686 \cdot 10^{-4}\). The stress there is tangent to the face \(y = a\), as the free face demands, and almost twice as large as the rotation alone would give.

Did we overlook something in the rotation? The field (16.10) is the linear form of the true rotation and neglects \(R(1 - \cos\varphi)\) (section 16.1). For the strip \(20 \times 40\) mm and the length \(1\) m the corner is \(22{,}36\) mm from the axis. The ratio \((1 - \cos\varphi)/\sin\varphi = \tan(\varphi/2)\) tells by what fraction of its displacement the corner at the end lies off compared with the true rotation. At \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m, \(\varphi(L) = 0{,}00906\) rad, this is \(0{,}453\,\%\), and at \(500\) N m, \(\varphi(L) = 0{,}0906\) rad, it is \(4{,}53\,\%\). This error concerns the position of the points, not the stresses. The stresses depend on the strains, which at \(50\) N m are at most \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 1{,}686 \cdot 10^{-4}\). At \(500\) N m, however, the model fails earlier because of the material: the largest shear stress of the strip is \(127{,}1\) MPa, above the shear yield stress \(110\) MPa by the Tresca condition (section 16.5), and the strip is no longer linearly elastic there. For this reason we took \(50\) N m for the strip.

Now we look for \(\psi\). There are three demands: the field equations in the body, the free lateral surface, and the forces at the ends. Let us begin with the boundary.

Let us draw the free lateral surface on a section that we can test (figure 16.6). For the boundary take an ellipse with the semi-axes \(10\) mm along \(y\) and \(20\) mm along \(z\), drawn with the axes and the origin \(O\), and on it the point \(B\) with the coordinates \(y = 8{,}660\) mm and \(z = 10{,}000\) mm. There the outward normal \(\vek n\) has the components \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = 0{,}9608\) and \(n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0{,}2774\), and the tangent is perpendicular to it. We divide the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) by \(G\alpha\) to get a vector in mm, and write it as \(\vek s = (\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z,\ \psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y)\). It is the sum of two parts: the rotation vector \(\vek q = (-z, y)\) with the components \(-10{,}000\) mm and \(8{,}660\) mm, which is perpendicular to \(OB\), and the gradient \(\nabla\psi = (\psi_{\mathrm{y}}, \psi_{\mathrm{z}})\). For \(\psi = 0{,}6\,yz\), a function that section 16.3 finds for the ellipse, \(\nabla\psi\) has the components \(6{,}000\) mm and \(5{,}196\) mm. Their sum is the stress vector \(\vek s\) with the components \(-4{,}000\) mm and \(13{,}856\) mm. The free face cannot carry a force, so \(\vek s\) must be tangent to the boundary, that is perpendicular to \(\vek n\): indeed \(\vek q \cdot \vek n = -7{,}206\) and \(\nabla\psi \cdot \vek n = 7{,}206\), and the sum \(\vek s \cdot \vek n\) is zero. With \(\psi = 0\) the sum would be \(\vek q\) alone and \(\vek s \cdot \vek n = -7{,}206 \ne 0\). So the condition becomes an equation for the normal derivative of \(\psi\) on the boundary.

For the theorem we also need the divergence theorem in the plane, which we obtain from the theorem for the prism.

Lemma 16.9 Divergence theorem in the section (izrek o divergenci v prerezu)

Let \(S\) be a section for which the prism \(S \times [0, \ell]\) is a body from corollary 4.68, cut so that every outer piece of the lateral surface is described by \((t, x) \mapsto (x, \gamma(t))\) for \(t \in [t_0, t_1]\) and \(x \in [0, \ell]\). Here \(\gamma = (\gamma_{\mathrm{y}}, \gamma_{\mathrm{z}})\) is an arc of the boundary \(\partial S\), continuously differentiable with \(\gamma'(t) \ne \vek 0\). This holds for all sections in this chapter: the circle, the annulus (for example four curved boxes in cylindrical coordinates, definition 4.65), the ellipse, the triangle, the rectangle. The boundary \(\partial S\) has the outward normal \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\). Let \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) be a field continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\). Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{S}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint_{\partial \mathrm{S}} \big( v_{\mathrm{y}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}s , \tag{16.13}\]

where the integral of a function \(f\) over the boundary is the sum of the integrals over its arcs,

\[\oint_{\partial \mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}s = \sum_{\gamma} \int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^{t_1} f\big(\gamma(t)\big)\,|\gamma'(t)|\,\mathrm{d}t .\]

For \(f = 1\) this is the length of the boundary by definition 8.4, so we call \(s\) the arc length of the boundary.

Proof
  1. The field \((0, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) does not depend on \(x\) and is continuously differentiable. Its divergence is the sum in the expression on the left.
  2. By corollary 4.68 the integral of the divergence over the prism equals the flux through its surface. The integral over the prism is \(\ell\) times the integral over the section, because the function does not depend on \(x\).
  3. On both end faces the normal is \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), so \((0, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\cdot\vek n = 0\). A piece of the lateral surface described by \(\vek r(t, x) = (x, \gamma_{\mathrm{y}}(t), \gamma_{\mathrm{z}}(t))\) has the derivatives \(\partial\vek r/\partial t = (0, \gamma_{\mathrm{y}}', \gamma_{\mathrm{z}}')\) and \(\partial\vek r/\partial x = (1, 0, 0)\), so its surface vector is \(\pm(0, \gamma_{\mathrm{z}}', -\gamma_{\mathrm{y}}')\), of length \(|\gamma'(t)|\). It points outward, so it equals \(|\gamma'(t)|\,(0, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\). The field does not depend on \(x\), so by definition 4.65 the flux through this piece is \(\int_0^\ell\!\int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^{t_1}(v_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}})\,|\gamma'(t)|\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}x = \ell\int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^{t_1}(v_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}})\,|\gamma'(t)|\,\mathrm{d}t\). The sum over all pieces of the lateral surface is \(\ell\oint(v_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  4. Cancel \(\ell\).

Source: The plane form of the divergence theorem is in SADD (1.8.11) (PDF p. 28), which it uses in (9.3.15) and (9.3.17) (PDF p. 250). The derivation from corollary 4.68 with a prism is not from the source.

Now we have everything for the theorem. It joins three demands: the field equation for \(\psi\), the condition on the boundary, and the forces at the ends.

Theorem 16.10 Saint-Venant torsion (Saint-Venantova torzija)

Let \(S\) be a bounded section for which lemma 16.9 holds and whose interior is connected. Let \(\psi\) be twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\) (for a rectangle this fails at the corners, section 16.5), and let \(\alpha \ne 0\). Let the material be as in theorems 11.6 and 11.4. Let us write two conditions for \(\psi\):

\[\nabla^2\psi = \frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial z^2} = 0 \quad \text{in } S , \qquad \frac{\partial\psi}{\partial n} = \psi_{\mathrm{y}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \psi_{\mathrm{z}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} = z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,n_{\mathrm{z}} \quad \text{on } \partial S . \tag{16.14}\]

For the displacement (16.10) the following holds:

  1. It satisfies the Navier-Lamé equations (theorem 11.6) with zero body force exactly when the first equation \(\nabla^2\psi = 0\) holds.
  2. The lateral surface is free exactly when the second condition holds, the boundary condition for \(\partial\psi/\partial n\).
  3. If both conditions hold, the resultant force on every end section is zero, and the moment about the axis \(x\) is
    \[M_{\mathrm{x}} = G\,J\,\alpha , \qquad J = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \big( y^2 + z^2 + y\,\psi_{\mathrm{z}} - z\,\psi_{\mathrm{y}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{16.15}\]
  4. This field is, up to a small rigid displacement, the only one with such surface forces on the whole surface of the prism. The number \(J\) is called the torsion constant (torzijska konstanta), \(GJ\) the torsional rigidity (torzijska togost), \(J\) in mm\(^4\).
Idea

We check everything that the boundary value problem demands, as for the circle. The free surface brings a condition on the boundary, and the resultant and the moment we get with the divergence theorem in the plane. Uniqueness is a theorem of chapter 11.

Proof
  1. From equation (16.10), \(\nabla^2u_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha(\psi_{\mathrm{yy}} + \psi_{\mathrm{zz}})\), \(\nabla^2u_{\mathrm{y}} = \nabla^2u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) (the components are linear in every variable), and \(\operatorname{div}\vek u = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = 0 + 0 + 0\). By theorem 11.6 and \(\mu = G\) (definition 3.10) the left side of equation (11.3) equals \((G\alpha\,\nabla^2\psi,\ 0,\ 0)\), so the equation holds exactly when \(\nabla^2\psi = 0\). This is point 1.
  2. On the lateral surface the normal is \(\vek n = (0, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\). By Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.24), \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(t_{\mathrm{y}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}n_{\mathrm{z}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\) and \(t_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), because by lemma 16.8 all other stresses are zero. The component \(t_{\mathrm{x}}\) is zero exactly when \(G\alpha(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \psi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}} - zn_{\mathrm{y}} + yn_{\mathrm{z}}) = 0\), and since \(G\alpha \ne 0\) this is \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \psi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}} = zn_{\mathrm{y}} - yn_{\mathrm{z}}\). This is point 2.
  3. Let (16.14) hold. On the end section at \(x = L\) with the normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) the stress vector is \(\vek t = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}) = (0, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) by theorem 2.36. By equation (16.12), \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial y + \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/\partial z = G\alpha\,\nabla^2\psi = 0\).
  4. The field \(\vek v = (y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}},\ y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) is continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\) and has the divergence \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} + y\,(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial y + \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/\partial z) = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) by step 3. By lemma 16.9, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint y\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\), since the expression in the parentheses is zero on the boundary (step 2). Likewise with the field \((z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}},\ z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) for \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\). The force in the direction \(x\) is zero because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\). So the resultant is zero.
  5. Because of \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) and the zero resultant, the moments about the axes \(y\) and \(z\), \(\int(z\,t_{\mathrm{x}} - L\,t_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}A = -L\int\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\) and \(\int(L\,t_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,t_{\mathrm{x}})\,\mathrm{d}A = L\int\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), are zero. The moment about the axis \(x\) is \(\int(y\,t_{\mathrm{z}} - z\,t_{\mathrm{y}})\,\mathrm{d}A = \int(y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} - z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\,\mathrm{d}A = G\alpha\int(y\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y^2 - z\psi_{\mathrm{y}} + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A = G\alpha J\). At \(x = 0\) the normal is \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and the resultant and the moment are opposite. This is point 3.
  6. The forces on the whole surface are thus given and there is no body force. Let \(\tilde{\vek u}\) be another field with the same surface forces. By theorem 11.4, point 2, the difference \(\tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) is a small rigid displacement. This is point 4.
Explanation

The torsion constant \(J\) replaces the polar moment \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) of the circle. Example: for the rectangle \(20 \times 40\) mm, \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\) and \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 133\,333\) mm\(^4\) (section 16.5). The product \(GJ\) is what chapter 12 took as a model in equation (12.16), and chapter 13 took \(GI_{\mathrm{p}}\) for the circle in equation (13.14). The theorem proves the equation for every section for which the function \(\psi\) that solves the conditions (16.14) is twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\): for the circle and the annulus (\(\psi = 0\)) and for the ellipse (\(\psi = 0{,}6\,yz\) for the semi-axes \(10\) and \(20\) mm, section 16.3). The rectangle has corners where \(\psi\) does not meet this condition (section 16.5). The proof would need cutting out small squares around the corners and a limit, which we do not carry out here, so for the rectangle the theorem is not proved here. The numbers for the strip in this section are computed with the series of section 16.5. The ends are loaded only with the distribution \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) of equation (16.12). A different loading of the end with the same moment differs, by Saint-Venant's principle (section 11.11, stated there and not proved), only near the end. The solution is thus exact for this loading, and for others it holds far from the ends.

Source: SADD section 9.3.2, equations (9.3.19) to (9.3.24) (PDF p. 251): \(\nabla^2 w = 0\) in the section, the condition on the normal derivative on the boundary, \(T = \alpha\mu J\) with \(J\) defined as an integral over the section. The proof with the Navier-Lamé equations, the divergence theorem and uniqueness is ours. SADD's \(T\) is our \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), its \(J\) is our \(GJ\).

We wrote the boundary so that the derivative of the function \(\psi\) along the normal is known and the value is not. Such problems have an unusual property: they cannot be solved for every right-hand side.

Let us draw this (figure 16.7). On the left is the circle with the radius \(20\) mm, and on its boundary we would like \(\partial\psi/\partial n = 10\) mm everywhere, which the orange arrows with the datum \(g = 10\) show, all outward. Since \(\nabla^2\psi = 0\), the field \(\nabla\psi\) has neither a source nor a sink in the interior, so as much as flows out would also have to flow in. The total outflow through the boundary would be \(2\pi \cdot 20 \cdot 10 = 1256{,}6\) mm\(^2\), and there is no inflow anywhere. Such a \(\psi\) does not exist. On the right is the rectangle \(20 \times 40\) mm and the arrows on its boundary show the right-hand side of the torsion condition, \(g = z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\). Where \(g > 0\), an orange arrow points out, where \(g < 0\), a blue one points in. On the face \(y = a\) we have \(g = z\): for \(z > 0\) the arrows point out, for \(z < 0\) in, and the sum over this face is zero. On the face \(z = b\) we have \(g = -y\), and so on for all four faces. Outflow and inflow balance.

Lemma 16.11 Solvability condition and uniqueness (pogoj rešljivosti in enoličnost)

Let \(S\) be a section as in theorem 16.10 and let \(g\) be a continuous function on the boundary \(\partial S\). Then:

  1. If \(\psi\) is a harmonic function, twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\), with \(\partial\psi/\partial n = g\) on the boundary, then \(\oint_{\partial \mathrm{S}}g\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\).
  2. Two such functions differ by a constant.
  3. The torsion datum \(g = z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\) satisfies \(\oint_{\partial \mathrm{S}}g\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\) for every section.
Idea

The flux of the field \(\nabla\psi\) through the boundary is the integral of its divergence, which is \(\nabla^2\psi = 0\). For uniqueness we use energy, as for the uniqueness of the boundary value problem.

Proof
  1. The field \(\vek v = \nabla\psi = (\psi_{\mathrm{y}}, \psi_{\mathrm{z}})\) is continuously differentiable and has the divergence \(\nabla^2\psi = 0\). By lemma 16.9, \(0 = \oint(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \psi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = \oint g\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  2. Let \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_2\) be two such functions and \(w = \psi_1 - \psi_2\). Then \(\nabla^2w = 0\) and \(\partial w/\partial n = 0\) on the boundary. The field \(w\nabla w\) has the divergence \(|\nabla w|^2 + w\nabla^2w = |\nabla w|^2\), and by lemma 16.9, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint w\,\partial w/\partial n\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\). The function \(|\nabla w|^2\) is continuous and nonnegative, so it is zero everywhere. Indeed, if it were equal to \(h > 0\) at an interior point \(P\), then by continuity it would be at least \(h/2\) on a small square \(Q\) around \(P\) that lies in \(S\), and by monotonicity (lemma 4.32, points 2 and 6) the integral would be at least \(h/2\) times the area of the square \(Q\), so greater than zero. On the boundary it is zero by continuity. So \(\nabla w = 0\). The function \((x, y, z) \mapsto w(y, z)\) then has zero partial derivatives on the prism \((0, \ell) \times\) interior of \(S\). This is a connected open set (definition 1.130), since a broken line in the connected interior of \(S\) is completed with a segment along the axis \(x\). By lemma 1.133, \(w\) is constant on the interior of \(S\), and by continuity on all of \(S\).
  3. The field \(\vek v = (z, -y)\) has the divergence \(\partial z/\partial y + \partial(-y)/\partial z = 0\), and by lemma 16.9, \(0 = \oint(z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s\).
Explanation

Point 3 says that the condition demanded by point 1 always holds in torsion, and so there is no contradiction. The condition is necessary. That it is also sufficient, that is, that a solution exists for every such section, we do not prove here. SADD places such problems in potential theory (section 9.3.2, PDF p. 252). For the sections of this chapter we find the solution: the circle (\(\psi = 0\)), the ellipse (section 16.3) and the rectangle with a series (section 16.5). The constant that point 2 leaves is the displacement along the axis \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha c\) of all points of the section together, a rigid displacement.

Example for the condition: for a circle with the radius \(20\) mm and the datum \(g = 10\) mm, \(\oint g\,\mathrm{d}s = 1256{,}6\) mm\(^2 \ne 0\), so there is no solution. The rectangle \(20 \times 40\) mm gives four faces with \(\int g\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\) each: \(\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}z\,\mathrm{d}z = 0\) on \(y = \pm a\) and \(\int_{-\mathrm{a}}^{a}y\,\mathrm{d}y = 0\) on \(z = \pm b\). At a corner \(g\) has two values, \(z = 20\) mm on the face \(y = a\) and \(-y = -10\) mm on the face \(z = b\), because there are two normals there. The datum is thus not continuous at the corners, and the rectangle demands more care (section 16.5).

Example for guessing: for the strip, \(\psi = 0\) gives \(\partial\psi/\partial n = 0\), and on the face \(y = a\) the amount \(z\) is missing, that is \(20\) mm at the corner, \(10\) mm at \(z = 10\) mm and \(0\) at \(z = 0\). The function \(\psi = 0{,}6\,yz\) of the ellipse gives \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = 0{,}6z\) and \(0{,}4z\) is missing, that is \(8{,}0\) mm at the corner. Neither of them is thus the solution for the rectangle.

Source: The proof by the divergence lemma is ours, not from the source. SADD section 9.3.2 (PDF p. 252) states that such boundary problems belong to potential theory (Kellogg 1969). The numbers are ours (num-02.py).

What does the warping do to the torsion constant? The expression (16.15) has the terms \(y\psi_{\mathrm{z}} - z\psi_{\mathrm{y}}\) of unknown sign, so we do not know whether \(J\) is larger or smaller than \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) and whether it is positive at all. The answer is one equation.

Lemma 16.12 The torsion constant is smaller than the polar moment (torzijska konstanta je manjša od polarnega momenta)

Let \(\psi\) be the warping function of the section \(S\) as in theorem 16.10, satisfying (16.14). Let \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = \int_{\mathrm{S}} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A\) be the polar second moment of area of the section about \(O\), as in lemma 16.2. Then:

  1. \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}} - \int_{\mathrm{S}} |\nabla\psi|^2\,\mathrm{d}A\), so \(J \le I_{\mathrm{p}}\).
  2. \(J = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \big( (\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z)^2 + (\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y)^2 \big)\,\mathrm{d}A > 0\).
  3. \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}}\) exactly when \(\psi\) is constant.
Idea

The term with \(\psi\) in \(J\) we turn with the divergence theorem in the plane into an integral over the boundary, where the boundary condition links it to the energy \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2\).

Proof
  1. The field \(\vek v = (-z\,\psi,\ y\,\psi)\) has the divergence \(-z\psi_{\mathrm{y}} + y\psi_{\mathrm{z}}\). By lemma 16.9, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}(y\psi_{\mathrm{z}} - z\psi_{\mathrm{y}})\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint\psi\,(-z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + y\,n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = -\oint\psi\,\partial\psi/\partial n\,\mathrm{d}s\) by the boundary condition.
  2. The field \(\psi\nabla\psi\) has the divergence \(|\nabla\psi|^2 + \psi\nabla^2\psi = |\nabla\psi|^2\), so \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla\psi|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint\psi\,\partial\psi/\partial n\,\mathrm{d}s\). From step 1, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}(y\psi_{\mathrm{z}} - z\psi_{\mathrm{y}})\,\mathrm{d}A = -\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla\psi|^2\,\mathrm{d}A\), and in the expression for \(J\) from equation (16.15) point 1 follows.
  3. Expand the squares: \((\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z)^2 + (\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y)^2 = |\nabla\psi|^2 + y^2 + z^2 + 2\,(y\psi_{\mathrm{z}} - z\psi_{\mathrm{y}})\). By step 2 the integral is \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2 + I_{\mathrm{p}} - 2\int|\nabla\psi|^2 = I_{\mathrm{p}} - \int|\nabla\psi|^2 = J\), which is the equality of point 2.
  4. Positivity in point 2: if \(J = 0\), the continuous nonnegative function under the integral would be zero everywhere (as in step 2 of the proof of lemma 16.11), so \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = z\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = -y\). The mixed derivatives would be \(\psi_{\mathrm{yz}} = 1\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{zy}} = -1\), which by theorem 1.125 is not possible for a twice continuously differentiable \(\psi\). So \(J > 0\).
  5. Point 3: by point 1, \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}}\) exactly when \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2 = 0\). As in step 2 of the proof of lemma 16.11, then \(\nabla\psi = 0\) and \(\psi\) is constant on the interior of \(S\), and by continuity on all of \(S\). Conversely, for constant \(\psi\) the integral is zero.
Explanation

Result 2 says that \(J\) is the integral of a sum of squares of shear strains, \((\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 + \gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}^2)/\alpha^2\) by lemma 16.8. This sum, multiplied by \(G/2\), is the strain energy density (definition 3.44 with Hooke's law \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = G\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\)), so \(J\) cannot be negative. Result 1 says that warping subtracts \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2 \ge 0\) from \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\). Warping thus always reduces the stiffness: plane sections (\(\psi = 0\)) give \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}}\) and therefore always overestimate the stiffness. For the strip \(20 \times 40\) mm, \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2 = 60\,155\) mm\(^4\), which is \(0{,}4512\) of \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 133\,333\) mm\(^4\), and \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\), the ratio \(J/I_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}5488\). For the square \(20 \times 20\) mm, \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2 = 4174\) mm\(^4\), \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 26\,667\) mm\(^4\) and \(J = 22\,492\) mm\(^4\), the ratio \(0{,}8435\): the square bulges less than the strip. The strip and the square have corners, so the lemma is not proved for them here (explanation of theorem 16.10). The numbers confirm it all the same: we computed \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2\) directly from the series for \(\psi\), and \(J\) with the series for \(J\) of section 16.5, and the difference \(I_{\mathrm{p}} - J\) agrees with \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2\) to the last digit given, \(60\,155\) and \(4174\) mm\(^4\) (num-02.py). For the ellipse with the semi-axes \(10\) and \(20\) mm, \(\psi = k\,yz\) with \(k = 0{,}6\), and \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2 = k^2\int(y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A = k^2I_{\mathrm{p}}\), so \(J = (1 - k^2)I_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}640\,I_{\mathrm{p}} = 50\,265\) mm\(^4\) (derived in section 16.3).

The origin \(O\) does not matter. Let us move it by \((y_0, z_0)\) and denote the coordinates from the new origin by \(\bar y = y - y_0\), \(\bar z = z - z_0\). The function \(\bar\psi = \psi - z_0\,y + y_0\,z\) is harmonic, because the added function is linear, its normal derivative is \(\partial\psi/\partial n - z_0n_{\mathrm{y}} + y_0n_{\mathrm{z}} = \bar z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - \bar y\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\), which is the boundary condition for the new coordinates. At the same time \(\bar\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - \bar z = \psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z\) and \(\bar\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + \bar y = \psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y\), so the stresses are the same, and by point 2 so is \(J\). For the strip moved by \(3\) mm and \(-4\) mm, at the point \((5, 7)\) mm the ratio \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/(G\alpha) = -1{,}3228\) mm before and after the move, \(J\) is \(73\,178\) mm\(^4\) in both cases, and the polar moment about a point \(5\) mm from the centroid is \(153\,333\) mm\(^4\) instead of \(133\,333\) mm\(^4\), which is \(I_{\mathrm{p}} + A\,d^2\). The number \(J\) thus does not change, and \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) depends on the center. The warping function is thus determined up to an added linear function (a shift of the center of twist) and a constant (lemma 16.11, a rigid displacement along the axis).

Source: We do not find the equation \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}} - \int|\nabla\psi|^2\) and the positivity in SADD (9.3.24), where \(J\) is given only as an integral. The proof by energy is ours. The numbers are from num-02.py.

When is the warping zero? The answer is given by point 3 of the lemma and by a conclusion that chapter 13 used without proof.

Corollary 16.13 Sections stay plane exactly for circles and annuli (ravni prerezi natanko pri krogu in kolobarju)

Let \(S\) be a section as in theorem 16.10. Then:

  1. The warping function is constant exactly when every connected part of the boundary is a circle with the center at \(O\).
  2. The warping function is affine, \(\psi = c + p\,y + q\,z\) with constants \(c\), \(p\), \(q\), exactly when every connected part of the boundary is a circle with the same center. Then the displacement along the axis \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha\psi\) is an affine function of the place in the section, and the section stays plane, it only tilts.

So the sections stay plane for the circle and for the annulus bounded by two circles with the same center, and for no other boundary. If the center is at \(O\), then \(\psi = 0\).

Proof
  1. Let \(\psi\) be constant. Then \(\partial\psi/\partial n = 0\) and the boundary condition (16.14) gives \(z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) on the boundary. The tangent of the boundary is \(\vek t = (-n_{\mathrm{z}}, n_{\mathrm{y}})\) and the derivative of \(r^2 = y^2 + z^2\) along it is \(2\,(y\,t_{\mathrm{y}} + z\,t_{\mathrm{z}}) = 2\,(-y\,n_{\mathrm{z}} + z\,n_{\mathrm{y}}) = 0\). The distance \(r\) from \(O\) is thus constant along every connected smooth curve of the boundary.
  2. Smooth arcs of the boundary that meet have the same \(r\) at the junction, so they lie on the same circle about \(O\). A closed curve that lies on a circle is the whole circle. Every connected part of the boundary is thus a circle about \(O\).
  3. Conversely, let the boundary be made of circles about \(O\). The normal there is parallel to the position vector \((y, z)\), so \(z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), and the function \(\psi = 0\) satisfies \(\nabla^2\psi = 0\) and the boundary condition. By lemma 16.11, point 2, it is the only solution up to a constant. Steps 1 to 3 prove point 1.
  4. For point 2 we move the center of twist to the point \((y_0, z_0)\). The function \(\bar\psi = \psi - z_0\,y + y_0\,z\) is harmonic and satisfies the boundary condition (16.14) for the coordinates \(\bar y = y - y_0\), \(\bar z = z - z_0\) (computed in the explanation of lemma 16.12). Let \(\psi = c + p\,y + q\,z\). With \(z_0 = p\) and \(y_0 = -q\), \(\bar\psi = c\) is constant, and by point 1 for the new center every connected part of the boundary is a circle with the center \((-q, p)\).
  5. Conversely, let every connected part of the boundary be a circle with the center \((y_0, z_0)\). By point 1 for this center, \(\bar\psi\) is constant, \(\bar\psi = c\). Then \(\psi = c + z_0\,y - y_0\,z\) is a warping function for \(O\) that is affine, and by lemma 16.11, point 2, every other one differs from it only by a constant.
Explanation

The circle and the annulus thus do not bulge because for them the right-hand side of the boundary condition for \(\partial\psi/\partial n\) is zero. This is the proof of the claim of chapter 13 that the circle does not warp because of axial symmetry: there the symmetry was the argument, here it is a conclusion from the equation. For every other boundary, for example the strip of section 16.1, \(\psi\) is not affine and the section bulges: for \(20 \times 40\) mm the largest displacement along the axis is only \(0{,}953\) \(\mu\)m at \(50\) N m, but the warping nevertheless reduces the stiffness to \(J = 0{,}549\,I_{\mathrm{p}}\).

Source: The proof is ours. SADD section 9.3 (PDF p. 246) says that circular sections stay plane because of symmetry, and the same conclusion for every section with a different boundary makes the warping unavoidable.

The task is thus: find a harmonic function \(\psi\) with a known normal derivative on the boundary and from it compute \(J\) and the stresses. For the circle the solution is \(\psi = 0\). For other shapes the form with a normal derivative is awkward: the boundary condition is not a value of the function but its derivative. The next section therefore looks for another function, one that is constant on the boundary and from which we read the stresses directly.

16.3 Prandtl's function

In section 16.2 we led the twisting of a prism to the warping function \(\psi(y, z)\), harmonic in the cross section \(S\) with a boundary condition on its derivative (theorem 16.10). What interests us above all is where in the section the stresses are large and how large a moment it carries. Is there a function from which the stresses can be read directly, and which has a simpler condition on the boundary than \(\psi\)? Such a condition would be the value of the function on the boundary, not its derivative. We shall call this function Prandtl's and use it in this section to solve the ellipse, the equilateral triangle and, once more, the circle.

We take the stresses from section 16.2. For small twists and Hooke's law (theorem 3.11), by lemma 16.8 only two shear stresses are nonzero. They are expressed with the shear modulus \(G\) (definition 3.9), the twist per unit length \(\alpha\) and the warping function:

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = G\alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z) , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y) , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0 . \tag{16.16}\]

Here \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}}\) mean the partial derivatives \(\partial\psi/\partial y\) and \(\partial\psi/\partial z\). No stress depends on \(x\), so the equilibrium equation in the direction \(x\) (theorem 2.28, without body force) remains the only one:

\[\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial z} = 0 . \tag{16.17}\]

This equation connects only two stresses. We shall find one function that carries both of them, as in section 4.7.8 we looked for a function from its derivatives. But first let us see what the free lateral surface demands of the stresses.

Take the section \(S\) and draw it together with the axes \(y\) and \(z\) [figure 16.8]. The outline of the section is the curve that bounds it, and we call it the boundary. On the boundary we choose a point \(P\). In it the outward normal \(\vek n\) is the unit vector \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\) that points out of the section and is perpendicular to the boundary, and the tangent is the line that touches the boundary at \(P\). Next to the point \(P\) a small piece of material lies on the lateral surface of the prism. The surface carries no load, since it is free (definition 16.1), so the stress vector on it is zero. By Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.24) the component of this vector in the direction of the bar's axis, for the normal \((0, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\) of the lateral surface, equals \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}}\), and therefore

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 \quad \text{on the boundary.} \tag{16.18}\]

This is the scalar product of the pair \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) with the normal \(\vek n\). The shear stress \(\boldsymbol\tau\) is this pair, drawn as an arrow in the plane of the section. If the scalar product is zero, it is perpendicular to \(\vek n\), so it lies along the tangent. An oblique arrow would have a component along the normal, and the force in the direction of the bar's axis would then have to be carried by a lateral surface that holds nothing. Such stresses do not exist on a free boundary: the shear stress on the boundary is always tangent to the boundary.
