The equilibrium equation (16.17) and the boundary condition (16.18) speak of both stresses together. Let \(\Phi\) be a function whose derivatives are the stresses. If \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}\), the left side of equation (16.17) equals \(\Phi_{\mathrm{zy}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{yz}}\), which is zero because the mixed derivatives of a smooth function are equal. Equilibrium is then satisfied by itself, and the boundary condition becomes simple: the tangent to the boundary has the direction \(\vek t = (-n_{\mathrm{z}}, n_{\mathrm{y}})\) (the normal turned by a right angle counterclockwise), so the derivative of \(\Phi\) along the boundary is \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} t_{\mathrm{y}} + \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} t_{\mathrm{z}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} n_{\mathrm{y}}\), which by equation (16.18) is zero. The function \(\Phi\) does not change its value along the boundary.

Definition 16.14 Prandtl stress function (Prandtlova funkcija)

Let \(S\) be the section of a prism in Saint-Venant torsion (definition 16.1) with the stresses (16.16). A function \(\Phi : S \to \mathbb{R}\) with values in N/mm, twice continuously differentiable in the interior of the section, is the Prandtl stress function (Prandtlova funkcija) of the torsion if at every point of the section

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial y} . \tag{16.19}\]

The function assigns one number to every point of the section. Its values are a stress multiplied by a length, so we measure them in N/mm.

Explanation

It is named after Prandtl, who in 1903 showed that the same equations hold for it as for a membrane under pressure (section 16.4). It is called a stress function because the stresses are obtained by differentiation. The letter \(\Phi\) has several meanings in the book: \(\varphi\) is the rotation of a section (chapter 13) and Airy's function (chapter 11), and the capital \(\Phi\) is a local name for a mapping in the proofs of chapter 4 and in section 16.1. SADD writes \(\phi\) for Prandtl's function. From here on, \(\Phi\) in this chapter means only this function.

Source: SADD section 9.3.1, equation (9.3.8) (PDF p. 248), the name after Prandtl and the year 1903 in section 9.3.4 (PDF p. 254). SADD has the bar's axis \(z\), the section in the plane \(x, y\) and the twist \(\alpha\), we have the axis \(x\) and the section in the plane \(y, z\): SADD's \((x, y)\) is our \((y, z)\) and its \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\) is our \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) with the sign according to our axes.

Does such a function exist at all for the stresses (16.16)? From equilibrium it follows that it does. The theorem on a field from partial derivatives (theorem 4.114) is exactly this step: if the mixed derivatives of a pair of functions agree and the region is simply connected (definition 1.136), the pair comes from one function. A section with a hole, such as a tube, does not guarantee this. So in this section we restrict ourselves to sections without holes and leave tubes for section 16.8.

Lemma 16.15 Existence of the Prandtl function (obstoj Prandtlove funkcije)

Let \(S\) be a bounded section whose interior is connected and simply connected (definition 1.136) and whose boundary is one closed curve with a piecewise continuously differentiable tangent, let the warping function \(\psi\) of theorem 16.10 be twice continuously differentiable on an open set \(E\) that contains \(S\) and is connected (definition 1.130) and simply connected (for the circle, the ellipse and the triangle \(\psi\) is a polynomial and \(E\) is the whole plane, for the rectangle see section 16.5), and let \(G\alpha \ne 0\). Then:

  1. A Prandtl function \(\Phi\) of the section exists (definition 16.14), twice continuously differentiable on \(E\).
  2. The function \(\Phi\) is determined up to an added constant, and it has a constant value on the boundary.
  3. Since the stresses contain only derivatives, we can choose \(\Phi = 0\) on the boundary.
Idea

We show that the field \((0, -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\) satisfies the condition of the theorem on a field from derivatives, because that condition is equilibrium (16.17). Constancy on the boundary is an expression of the boundary condition (16.18).

Proof
  1. Let \(D = E \times \mathbb{R}\) be the cylinder over the set \(E\). It is an open and connected set. It is also simply connected: a loop in \(D\) is contracted by contracting its projection into \(E\) by definition 1.136 and at the same time pulling the coordinate \(x\) to a constant value.
  2. The field \(\vek w = (0, -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\), since the stresses (16.16) have continuous first derivatives (\(\psi\) has continuous second ones). Because it does not depend on \(x\), the derivatives with respect to \(x\) are zero. The condition of theorem 4.114 is the equality of mixed derivatives, \(\partial w_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial z = \partial w_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial y\), and the other pairs are zero. The first two are \(-\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/\partial z\) and \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial y\) and they are equal exactly by equation (16.17). By the theorem a continuously differentiable function \(\varphi\) exists on \(D\) with \(\partial\varphi/\partial y = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\partial\varphi/\partial z = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\partial\varphi/\partial x = 0\).
  3. The derivative with respect to \(x\) is zero on every segment along the axis \(x\) in \(D\), so by corollary 1.85 \(\varphi\) is constant along it and is a function of \((y, z)\) only. We call it \(\Phi\). Since the first derivatives \(-\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are continuously differentiable on \(E\), \(\Phi\) is twice continuously differentiable on \(E\), and so also at the points of the boundary of the section. Equation (16.19) holds.
  4. If \(\tilde\Phi\) is another such function on \(E\), the difference \(\tilde\Phi - \Phi\) has both derivatives zero on the connected set \(E\), so it is constant.
  5. On the boundary, by what was written before the definition, \(\Phi\) has the derivative along the tangent \(\vek t\) equal to \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} t_{\mathrm{y}} + \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} t_{\mathrm{z}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) by equation (16.18). The boundary is one connected curve, and a function with zero derivative along it is constant. Point 3 follows, because \(\Phi - \Phi_{\text{boundary}}\) gives the same stresses.

Source: SADD section 9.3.1 (PDF p. 248-249): at (9.3.8) and (9.3.12) it says that the function is constant on the boundary and that the constant is chosen to be zero. The proof of existence with the theorem on a field from derivatives is not from the source. The existence of the warping function for a general section is stated by SADD and we do not prove it (section 16.2).

What equation does \(\Phi\) satisfy in the interior? Equilibrium is already used up. What remains is a requirement that the warping function satisfies by itself, but \(\Phi\) must be given it: the shear strains must come from one displacement. From equations (16.16),

\[\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial z} = G\alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{zy}} + 1 - \psi_{\mathrm{yz}} + 1) = 2G\alpha , \tag{16.20}\]

since the mixed derivatives of \(\psi\) are equal. The left side does not contain \(\psi\), so this is a condition on the stresses themselves. We call it the compatibility condition (pogoj kompatibilnosti) of torsion, since like the compatibility equations (theorem 1.127) it ensures that the strains come from one displacement. Written with \(\Phi\) it is the equation of the theorem that follows.

How do we compute from \(\Phi\) the moment that the section carries? The moment is the sum of the moments of the shear forces of the section about the axis \(x\). The force \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) at the point \((y, z)\) has the arm \(y\) and the force \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) the arm \(z\) with the opposite sign, so

\[M_{\mathrm{x}} = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \big( y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} - z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}A = -\int_{\mathrm{S}} \big( y\,\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + z\,\Phi_{\mathrm{z}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{16.21}\]

The expression \(y\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + z\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) is the scalar product of the position vector \((y, z)\) with the gradient \(\nabla\Phi = (\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\). This product is a part of the divergence of the field \(\Phi\,(y, z)\). The divergence theorem (theorem 4.14, section 4.2.5) turns the divergence into an integral over the boundary, where \(\Phi = 0\). Since the section is a figure in the plane, we need the theorem in the plane, lemma 16.9, which we proved in section 16.2.

Now we have everything for the theorem. It contains three claims: the equation for \(\Phi\), the moment, and a converse which says that every solution of the equation really is a torsion.

Theorem 16.16 Prandtl's equation (Prandtlova enačba)

Let \(S\) be a section as in lemma 16.15, and let \(\Phi\) be the Prandtl function of the section with the value zero on the boundary, twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\) (for a rectangle this does not happen at the corners, section 16.5).

  1. We have
    \[\nabla^2\Phi = \frac{\partial^2\Phi}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2\Phi}{\partial z^2} = -2G\alpha \quad \text{in } S , \qquad \Phi = 0 \quad \text{on } \partial S . \tag{16.22}\]
  2. The resultant of the forces of the section is zero, and its moment about the axis \(x\) is
    \[M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}} \Phi\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{16.23}\]
    So \(J = (2/G\alpha)\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A\) is the torsion constant of theorem 16.10, \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = GJ\alpha\).
  3. Conversely, let \(\Phi\) be a twice continuously differentiable function with the properties (16.22). Then the field (16.19) satisfies equilibrium and the free lateral surface, and a warping function \(\psi\) exists (harmonic, with the boundary condition of theorem 16.10) that gives the same stresses.
Idea

The first claim is the compatibility condition (16.20), written with \(\Phi\). The second is the divergence theorem in the section, because the boundary term cancels owing to \(\Phi = 0\). The converse goes by the same theorem on a field from derivatives, this time for \(\psi\).

Proof
  1. From equation (16.19), \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/\partial y = -\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial z = \Phi_{\mathrm{zz}}\). The left side of equation (16.20) is therefore \(-\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nabla^2\Phi\) and equals \(2G\alpha\). The boundary condition is point 3 of lemma 16.15.
  2. The force in the direction \(y\): \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\,\mathrm{d}A\). By lemma 16.9 with the field \(\vek v = (0, \Phi)\) this is \(\oint\Phi n_{\mathrm{z}}\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\), because \(\Phi = 0\) on the boundary. Similarly with the field \((\Phi, 0)\) for the force in the direction \(z\): \(-\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}\,\mathrm{d}A = -\oint\Phi n_{\mathrm{y}}\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\). There are no normal stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), so there is no force in the direction \(x\). Since the shear resultants are zero too, the moments about \(y\) and \(z\) are zero as well (as in step 5 of the proof of theorem 16.10).
  3. The field \(\vek v = (y\,\Phi, z\,\Phi)\) has the divergence \(\Phi + y\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + \Phi + z\Phi_{\mathrm{z}} = 2\Phi + y\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + z\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\). By lemma 16.9, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}(2\Phi + y\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + z\Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint\Phi\,(y\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + z\,n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\), since \(\Phi = 0\) on the boundary.
  4. By equation (16.21), \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = -\int_{\mathrm{S}}(y\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + z\Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}A = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A\). The same moment for \(\psi\) equals \(GJ\alpha\) (theorem 16.10), whence \(J\).
  5. The converse. Let \(\Phi\) be as in point 3 of the theorem. The field \(\vek w = (0, -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}) = (0, \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\) is by construction the gradient of the function \(\Phi\), so equilibrium (16.17) is satisfied (mixed derivatives of \(\Phi\)). The derivative of \(\Phi\) along the boundary is zero, because \(\Phi = 0\) on the boundary. This derivative is \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{y}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{z}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}}\), so (16.18) holds.
  6. We look for \(\psi\) with \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}/(G\alpha) + z\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}/(G\alpha) - y\) (equations (16.16) rewritten). The mixed derivatives: \(\partial_{\mathrm{z}}\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{zz}}/(G\alpha) + 1\) and \(\partial_{\mathrm{y}}\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}}/(G\alpha) - 1\). They are equal exactly when \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}} + \Phi_{\mathrm{zz}} = -2G\alpha\), which holds. By theorem 4.114 (as in lemma 16.15) \(\psi\) therefore exists. For \(\psi\) we have \(\psi_{\mathrm{yy}} + \psi_{\mathrm{zz}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{zy}}/(G\alpha) - \Phi_{\mathrm{yz}}/(G\alpha) = 0\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \psi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}} = (\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{y}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{z}})/(G\alpha) + zn_{\mathrm{y}} - yn_{\mathrm{z}} = zn_{\mathrm{y}} - yn_{\mathrm{z}}\), since \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{y}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{z}}\) is the derivative along the boundary and is zero.

Source: SADD section 9.3.1, (9.3.9), (9.3.12), (9.3.15)-(9.3.18) (PDF p. 248-251). The converse and the use of the theorem on a field from derivatives are not from the source.

We proved the theorem when \(\Phi\) is twice continuously differentiable up to the boundary. For the circle, the ellipse and the triangle, which we compute in this section, the solutions are polynomials and the condition holds. The rectangle has corners. Along the side \(y = a\) we have \(\Phi = 0\), so there \(\Phi_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}} = -2G\alpha\), while along the side \(z = b\) we have \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\). The second derivative \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}}\) therefore has two different limits at the corner. The mixed derivative \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yz}}\) is not even bounded near the corner: the series of section 16.5 gives on the diagonal, at the distances \(0{,}1\), \(0{,}01\) and \(0{,}001\) mm from the corner, \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yz}}/(G\alpha) = 5{,}72\), \(8{,}65\) and \(11{,}58\), larger by \((4/\pi)\ln 10 = 2{,}93\) for each ten times smaller distance. So at the corner \(\Phi\) is not twice continuously differentiable, and the proof with the divergence theorem would need a cut-out near the corner and a limit. For sections with corners we do not prove it here. SADD (PDF p. 248-251) uses Green's theorem without this condition. The rectangle will be solved in section 16.5 with a series and with checked numbers.

Is the solution of equation (16.22) unique? If there were several, the same torsion would have several stress fields. We show that this is not so, by energy, as in chapter 11 we proved the uniqueness of the boundary value problem.

Lemma 16.17 Uniqueness of Prandtl's equation (enoličnost Prandtlove enačbe)

Let \(S\) be a section whose interior is connected and for which lemma 16.9 holds. Let \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) be functions, twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\), with \(\nabla^2f_1 = \nabla^2f_2 = -2G\alpha\) in \(S\) and \(f_1 = f_2 = 0\) on \(\partial S\). Then \(f_1 = f_2\).

Idea

The difference \(w = f_1 - f_2\) is harmonic and zero on the boundary. The energy \(\int|\nabla w|^2\) is then zero.

Proof
  1. Let \(w = f_1 - f_2\). Then \(\nabla^2w = 0\) in \(S\) and \(w = 0\) on the boundary.
  2. The field \(\vek v = w\,\nabla w = (w\,w_{\mathrm{y}}, w\,w_{\mathrm{z}})\) is continuously differentiable and has the divergence \(w_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + w\,\nabla^2w = |\nabla w|^2\) (product rule). By lemma 16.9, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint w\,(w_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + w_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\), since \(w = 0\) on the boundary.
  3. A continuous nonnegative function \(|\nabla w|^2\) with zero integral is zero everywhere (if it were positive at some point, it would be positive in a disc around it and the integral would be positive). So \(\nabla w = 0\).
  4. A function with zero gradient on a connected set is constant, and on the boundary \(w = 0\), so \(w = 0\).

Source: The same energy argument for the Laplace operator is in CM section 7.5.7 (PDF p. 340-342). The proof is not from the source.

The lemma means that for a given section there is at most one Prandtl function with zero on the boundary. If we find it by any means (by guessing, or by a series when it is twice continuously differentiable up to the boundary), it is the right one. For the rectangle, where this fails at the corners, see section 16.5. The stress field therefore does not depend on how we found \(\Phi\). The displacement field too is by theorem 11.4 unique with it, up to a rigid motion.

Let us try this on the ellipse, where \(\Phi\) can be guessed. Let the section have the semi-axis \(a\) along \(y\) and \(b\) along \(z\). The boundary is the curve \(y^2/a^2 + z^2/b^2 = 1\), and the function \(1 - y^2/a^2 - z^2/b^2\) is zero on it and positive in the interior. Take \(\Phi = c\,(1 - y^2/a^2 - z^2/b^2)\) with a constant \(c\). The boundary has the value zero for every \(c\), and we choose \(c\) so that \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2G\alpha\). Let us first draw this function [figure 16.9]. Above the boundary of the section we draw the profile along the axis \(y\), a parabola that falls from the top to zero at \(y = \pm a\), and the profile along the axis \(z\), which falls to zero at \(z = \pm b\). The height \(c\) is the top of the hill.

The volume under the hill is written in the theorem as \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A\). We can compute it by the change of variables theorem (theorem 4.59): we write a point of the section as \((y, z) = (a\,u,\ b\,v)\), where \((u, v)\) lies in the disc \(K\) of radius \(1\) centred at the origin. This linear mapping stretches the disc by the factor \(a\) along \(y\) and by the factor \(b\) along \(z\), so it maps it onto the ellipse, and it is injective on the whole plane. Its Jacobian determinant is constant, \(a\,b\): every piece of the disc is mapped into a piece of the ellipse with an \(ab\) times larger area.

Theorem 16.18 Torsion of an ellipse (torzija elipse)

Let the section be an ellipse with semi-axes \(a\) along the axis \(y\) and \(b\) along the axis \(z\), \(a \le b\), and let \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) be the moment.

  1. The Prandtl function of the ellipse with zero on the boundary is
    \[\Phi = G\alpha\,\frac{a^2b^2}{a^2 + b^2}\Big( 1 - \frac{y^2}{a^2} - \frac{z^2}{b^2} \Big) . \tag{16.24}\]
  2. The torsion constant is
    \[J = \frac{\pi\,a^3b^3}{a^2 + b^2} , \qquad \alpha = \frac{M_{\mathrm{x}}}{GJ} . \tag{16.25}\]
  3. The stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -2M_{\mathrm{x}} z/(\pi a b^3)\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2M_{\mathrm{x}} y/(\pi a^3 b)\), the largest is at the ends of the shorter axis and equals
    \[\tau_{\max} = \frac{2M_{\mathrm{x}}}{\pi\,a^2b} . \tag{16.26}\]
  4. The warping function is \(\psi = k\,yz\) with \(k = (b^2 - a^2)/(a^2 + b^2)\).
  5. For \(a = b = R\) this agrees with the circle: \(J = \pi R^4/2\) and \(\tau = M_{\mathrm{x}}r/I_{\mathrm{p}}\).
Idea

The function is a polynomial, so it has a constant Laplace operator and zero on the boundary. The constant \(c\) is chosen from the Laplace value, \(J\) from the moment, the stresses from the derivatives. By lemma 16.17 this is the only solution.

Proof
  1. Let \(\Phi = c\,(1 - y^2/a^2 - z^2/b^2)\). On the boundary \(\Phi = 0\). The second derivatives are \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}} = -2c/a^2\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{zz}} = -2c/b^2\), so \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2c\,(a^2 + b^2)/(a^2b^2)\). The condition \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2G\alpha\) gives \(c = G\alpha\,a^2b^2/(a^2 + b^2)\). This is equation (16.24). By lemma 16.17 this is the function of the ellipse, and by theorem 16.16 (point 3) it belongs to a torsion of the section.
  2. We compute the integrals over the ellipse with the mapping \((u, v) \mapsto (au, bv)\) of the introduction and with lemma 16.2 for the disc \(K\) of radius \(R = 1\). The area: \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\mathrm{d}A = ab\int_{\mathrm{K}}\mathrm{d}A = \pi ab\), since \(K\) has the area \(\pi\) (the proof of lemma 16.2 with the function \(1\) in place of \(r^2\), where \(\int_0^1 r\,\mathrm{d}r = 1/2\)). The term \(y^2 = a^2u^2\) gives \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}y^2\,\mathrm{d}A = a^3b\int_{\mathrm{K}}u^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \pi a^3b/4\) and similarly \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}z^2\,\mathrm{d}A = ab^3\int_{\mathrm{K}}v^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \pi ab^3/4\).
  3. Hence \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A = c\,(\pi ab - \pi ab/4 - \pi ab/4) = c\,\pi ab/2\) and by equation (16.23) \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = c\,\pi ab = G\alpha\,\pi a^3b^3/(a^2 + b^2)\). This is \(GJ\alpha\) with \(J\) from equation (16.25).
  4. From \(c = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(\pi ab)\) we get \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} = -2cz/b^2 = -2M_{\mathrm{x}}z/(\pi ab^3)\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} = 2cy/a^2 = 2M_{\mathrm{x}}y/(\pi a^3b)\). The magnitude: \(\tau^2 = (2M_{\mathrm{x}}/\pi ab)^2\,(y^2/a^4 + z^2/b^4)\).
  5. The maximum is on the boundary: with \(y = a\cos\theta\), \(z = b\sin\theta\) we have \(y^2/a^4 + z^2/b^4 = \cos^2\theta/a^2 + \sin^2\theta/b^2\), which for \(a \le b\) is largest at \(\cos^2\theta = 1\), at the point \((a, 0)\). There \(\tau = 2M_{\mathrm{x}}/(\pi ab)\cdot 1/a\), equation (16.26). An interior point has a smaller stress, since \(y^2/a^4 + z^2/b^4\) under the ellipse \(y^2/a^2 + z^2/b^2 = s^2 \le 1\) is at most \(s^2/a^2\).
  6. The warping function: from equations (16.16), \(G\alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z) = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} = -2G\alpha\,a^2z/(a^2 + b^2)\) and \(G\alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y) = -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} = 2G\alpha\,b^2y/(a^2 + b^2)\). With \(\psi = k\,yz\) we have \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z = (k - 1)z\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y = (k + 1)y\), so \(k - 1 = -2a^2/(a^2 + b^2)\) and \(k + 1 = 2b^2/(a^2 + b^2)\), both satisfied with \(k = (b^2 - a^2)/(a^2 + b^2)\). SymPy checked them.
  7. For \(a = b = R\) we have \(k = 0\), \(J = \pi R^6/(2R^2) = \pi R^4/2\) and \(\tau^2 = (2M_{\mathrm{x}}/\pi R^2)^2\,r^2/R^4\), so \(\tau = 2M_{\mathrm{x}}r/(\pi R^4) = M_{\mathrm{x}}r/I_{\mathrm{p}}\) (lemma 16.2). This is theorem 16.3.

Source: SADD example 9.1 (PDF p. 257-258) and ONATE2 figure 4.11 (PDF p. 201): \(J = \pi a^3b^3/(a^2 + b^2)\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{i}} = 2M/(\pi a b^2)\) for ONATE's larger semi-axis \(a\) and smaller \(b\), which are our \(b\) and \(a\). SADD has the semi-axes \(a\) along \(x\) and \(b\) along \(y\) and the validity \(a > b\). The proof with the uniqueness lemma and the linear mapping of the disc is not from the source.

Example 16.19 Ellipse 10 by 20 mm (elipsa 10 × 20 mm)

For an ellipse with \(a = 10\) mm along \(y\) and \(b = 20\) mm along \(z\) and a steel bar (\(G = 75\,385\) MPa) at \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m: \(J = 50\,265\) mm\(^4\), \(\alpha = 0{,}01320\) rad/m, \(G\alpha = 0{,}9947\) N/mm\(^3\), the top of the hill \(c = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(\pi ab) = 79{,}58\) N/mm. By equation (16.26) the largest stress is \(\tau_{\max} = 15{,}92\) MPa. The section bulges: the displacement along the bar's axis is \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha\psi = \alpha k\,yz\) with \(k = 0{,}600\) (point 4 of the theorem). On the boundary \(yz = \tfrac12 ab\sin 2t\) at the point \((a\cos t,\ b\sin t)\), so the displacement is largest at \(t = 45°\), at the point \((7{,}07;\ 14{,}14)\) mm, and there \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}792\ \mu\)m.

Let us look at where the stress flows in this ellipse [figure 16.10]. We draw the axes \(y\) and \(z\) and the boundary of the ellipse, where \(\Phi = 0\). Inside we draw the lines on which the function (16.24) has a constant value. Each is an ellipse similar to the boundary, with the equation \(y^2/a^2 + z^2/b^2 = s^2\), and on it \(\Phi = c\,(1 - s^2)\). They are drawn for \(s = 0{,}75\), \(0{,}5\) and \(0{,}25\), where \(\Phi\) equals \(7/16\), \(3/4\) and \(15/16\) of the value \(c\). In the center \(\Phi = c\). The stress \(\boldsymbol\tau = (\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}})\) by equation (16.19) we draw as an arrow, \(0{,}1\) cm per MPa. At the end of the shorter axis, at \((a, 0)\), it is \(15{,}92\) MPa long. At the end of the longer axis, at \((0, b)\), it is half as long, \(7{,}96\) MPa. At three interior points it is shorter, since \(y\) and \(z\) are smaller there. At one point we also draw the gradient \(\nabla\Phi = (\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\), the vector that points in the direction of steepest ascent of the function: toward the top, perpendicular to the stress, and of the same length.

The drawn lines show that the stress always runs along a line where \(\Phi\) is constant, and that the gradient is perpendicular to it. Such lines are called level lines (plastnice), like the lines of equal height on a map: they join points on the same layer of terrain (in Slovenian plast means layer), and the boundary of the section is the level line with the value zero. We saw the pattern on the ellipse, now we show that it holds everywhere.

Lemma 16.20 Stress along the level lines (napetost vzdolž plastnic)

Let \(\Phi\) be the Prandtl function of the section and \(P\) a point at which \(\nabla\Phi \ne \vek 0\). Then:

  1. The shear stress \(\boldsymbol\tau = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) at \(P\) is perpendicular to the gradient \(\nabla\Phi\).
  2. Its magnitude is \(|\boldsymbol\tau| = |\nabla\Phi|\).
  3. The stress is tangent to the level line \(\{\Phi = \text{constant}\}\) through \(P\).
Proof
  1. By equation (16.19), \(\boldsymbol\tau\cdot\nabla\Phi = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}\Phi_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\).
  2. \(|\boldsymbol\tau|^2 = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = |\nabla\Phi|^2\).
  3. Since \(\nabla\Phi \ne \vek 0\) and \(\Phi\) is continuously differentiable, near \(P\) the level line is by the implicit function theorem (theorem 8.34, with \(N = 2\) and \(m = 1\)) the graph of a continuously differentiable function of one coordinate, so a curve with a tangent. Let \(\vek t\) be the tangent vector of the level line at \(P\). The derivative of \(\Phi\) along the level line is zero, so \(\nabla\Phi\cdot\vek t = 0\). In the plane, for \(\nabla\Phi \ne \vek 0\) only vectors of one direction are perpendicular to it, so \(\boldsymbol\tau\) is parallel to \(\vek t\).

Source: SADD section 9.3.4 and figure 9.8 (PDF p. 254-258) use this property for the membrane and for the ellipse. The proof is not from the source.

Why is the stress at the end of the shorter axis twice as large as at the end of the longer? By the lemma the stress is the magnitude of the slope of the hill. The function falls from \(c\) to zero over the distance \(a\) along the axis \(y\) and over the distance \(b\) along the axis \(z\). The slope at the boundary is \(2c/a\) and \(2c/b\), the ratio is \(b/a = 2\), so the stress is larger where the boundary is nearer to the top. The stress is therefore not largest at the point farthest from the axis.

The ellipse is also a near miss for the conjecture of section 16.1: for the circle the stress is proportional to the distance from the axis, \(\tau = M_{\mathrm{x}}r/I_{\mathrm{p}}\) and is largest on the boundary. If we assumed the same for the ellipse, we would look for the stress at the farthest boundary, at the end of the longer axis, and obtain \(\tau = M_{\mathrm{x}} b/I_{\mathrm{p}}\) with \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = \pi ab\,(a^2 + b^2)/4 = 78\,540\) mm\(^4\), so \(50\,000 \cdot 20/78\,540 = 12{,}73\) MPa. The true stress there is \(7{,}96\) MPa, and at the end of the shorter axis \(15{,}92\) MPa: the conjecture is wrong at both points, at the end of the longer axis it is too large by 60 %, and it misses the largest stress by 20 %. The circle is a special case where \(\psi = 0\) and the sections stay plane. For the ellipse \(k = 0{,}600\) and the section bulges.

A function that is zero on the boundary is not yet a Prandtl function: by theorem 16.16 it must in addition satisfy the equation \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2G\alpha\). Let us take the simplest function that is zero on the boundary of a rectangle and check what it lacks. Let the rectangle have the half-sides \(a = 10\) mm along the axis \(y\) and \(b = 20\) mm along the axis \(z\), equal to the section 20 by 40 mm that we shall solve in section 16.5, and the function is

\[\Phi_{\mathrm{t}} = (a^2 - y^2)\,(b^2 - z^2) .\]
Example 16.21 A function that is zero on the boundary and is not the solution (funkcija, ki je na robu nič in ni rešitev)

The function \(\Phi_{\mathrm{t}}\) is zero on all four sides, \(y = \pm a\) and \(z = \pm b\). Its Laplace operator is \(\nabla^2\Phi_{\mathrm{t}} = -2\,(a^2 + b^2 - y^2 - z^2)\), which is not constant. The condition \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2G\alpha\) however demands the same number everywhere. We scale it so that it equals \(1\) at the center. Then the value of \(-\nabla^2\Phi_{\mathrm{t}}\) divided by the value at the center is \(1\) at the center, \(0{,}8\) at the middle of the longer side \((a, 0)\), \(0{,}2\) at the middle of the shorter \((0, b)\) and \(0\) at the corners. The lines of equal value are circles about the center with radii \(10\), \(20\) and \(\sqrt{500} = 22{,}36\) mm.

What would this mean? If we accepted \(\Phi_{\mathrm{t}}\), the left side of equation (16.20), which \(\psi\) must satisfy, would be zero at the corners instead of \(2G\alpha\), and at the middle of the longer side \(0{,}8\cdot 2G\alpha\). The warping function of step 6 in the proof of theorem 16.16 would demand different mixed derivatives, which for a function with continuous second derivatives are equal. So there is no warping function, and the pieces of material at a corner could not be put together into a whole without gaps and overlaps. Zero on the boundary is a necessary, not a sufficient condition. The function \(\Phi_{\mathrm{t}}\) returns in section 16.9 as a trial function for the lower bound of \(J\), with an error of \(-2{,}82\) %, since there it does not solve the equation but looks for the best function among such ones.

The ellipse and the circle are two sections where \(\Phi\) is guessed from the shape of the boundary. The same trick works for the equilateral triangle. The section is bounded by three lines, on each one of the three distances \(d_1\), \(d_2\), \(d_3\) to the sides has the value zero, and the product is zero on the boundary. Let us try it [figure 16.12]: we draw a triangle with side \(s\) and the distances \(d_{\mathrm{k}} = \rho - \vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot(y, z)\) from the \(k\)-th side, where \(\rho = s/(2\sqrt{3})\) is the radius of the inscribed circle and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\) the outward normal. The centroid is at the origin of coordinates, the side \(d_1 = 0\) is at the bottom, and

\[d_1 = \rho + z , \qquad d_2 = \rho - \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,y - \tfrac{1}{2}\,z , \qquad d_3 = \rho + \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,y - \tfrac{1}{2}\,z .\]
Example 16.22 Equilateral triangle (enakostranični trikotnik)

Let \(\Phi = c\,d_1d_2d_3\). After multiplying,

\[d_1d_2d_3 = \frac{\sqrt{3}\,s^3}{72} - \frac{\sqrt{3}\,s}{8}\,(y^2 + z^2) + \frac{z^3 - 3y^2z}{4} .\]

The term \(z^3 - 3y^2z\) is harmonic (\(6z - 6z = 0\)), the term with \(y^2 + z^2\) has the Laplace operator \(-\sqrt{3}\,s/2\), so \(\nabla^2(d_1d_2d_3) = -\sqrt{3}\,s/2\), constant. The condition \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2G\alpha\) gives \(c = 4G\alpha/(\sqrt{3}\,s)\). The function is zero on the boundary, because at every point of a side one of the distances is zero. By lemma 16.17 this is the Prandtl function of the triangle. The integral over the triangle (SymPy) gives \(J = \dfrac{2c}{G\alpha}\int_{\mathrm{S}} d_1d_2d_3\,\mathrm{d}A = \sqrt{3}\,s^4/80\), which agrees with ONATE2 (figure 4.11, PDF p. 201). The area is \(A = \sqrt{3}\,s^2/4\), so \(J/A^2 = \sqrt{3}/15 = 0{,}1155\). For \(A = 800\) mm\(^2\) we have \(s = 42{,}98\) mm, \(J = 73\,901\) mm\(^4\) and the largest stress at \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m is \(12{,}59\) MPa at the middle of a side. At the corners the stress is zero: there two distances in the product are zero, so both derivatives of \(\Phi\) are zero.

The level lines are not similar triangles, but become rounder toward the center. On the sides \(\Phi = 0\). By lemma 16.20 the stress is along the level lines, at the corners it is zero and it is largest at the middle of the sides (SADD, PDF p. 260). The corners therefore carry the least, as we shall also see for the rectangle (section 16.5).

Which section is stiffest in twisting, if all have the same area and the same material? We choose the area \(800\) mm\(^2\) (which the rectangle 20 by 40 mm has) and compare six sections [figure 16.13]. We draw a circle, a square, an ellipse 1 : 2, an equilateral triangle, a strip 1 : 2 and a strip 1 : 5, each with area \(800\) mm\(^2\). To the right of each we draw a horizontal line whose length is proportional to the torsion constant \(J\) of the section. A longer line means a smaller twist at the same moment, since \(\alpha = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(GJ)\).

Example 16.23 The same material, different stiffness (isti material, različna togost)

At \(A = 800\) mm\(^2\) the torsion constants are: circle \(101\,859\), square \(89\,969\), ellipse 1 : 2 \(81\,487\), equilateral triangle \(73\,901\), strip 1 : 2 \(73\,178\) and strip 1 : 5 \(37\,288\) mm\(^4\). The ratio to the circle is \(1\), \(0{,}883\), \(0{,}800\), \(0{,}726\), \(0{,}718\) and \(0{,}366\). The circle, the ellipse and the triangle are from this section. The square and the strips are from the series for the rectangle in section 16.5. The square agrees with ONATE2 (figure 4.11, PDF p. 201), which has the rounded \(J = 2{,}25\,a^4\) with half-side \(a\), so \(90\,000\) mm\(^4\).

Among these six the circle is stiffest, and the more stretched the section, the less stiff it is. That this holds for every section of the same area we neither prove nor claim here. Why is the strip 1 : 5 so soft? At the same twist \(\alpha\) the function \(\Phi\) is everywhere near the boundary, where it is zero, so the hill is low, and its volume is by equation (16.23) the moment \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\). In section 16.4 we shall see this on the membrane.

Prandtl's function is thus a second way to the same torsion. The warping function is the solution of an equation with a boundary condition on the derivative and gives displacements. Prandtl's function solves the Poisson equation with zero on the boundary and gives stresses. Both ways give the same torsion constant \(J\) (theorem 16.16, point 2).

16.4 The membrane analogy (membranska analogija)

Prandtl's function \(\Phi\) solves Poisson's equation with zero on the boundary (theorem 16.16), and the stresses follow by differentiation. That is a computation. Does anything we can see and hold solve the same equation? Such an object would give us a feeling for the solution before we compute it: where it is large, where small, how it behaves at the boundary. In this section we show that we have one: a thin stretched membrane under pressure.

Take a wire frame in the shape of the section, for example the ellipse with semi-axes \(a = 10\) mm along \(y\) and \(b = 20\) mm along \(z\) from example 16.19. Across it we stretch a membrane, for instance a soap film. If a uniform pressure \(p\) pushes on it from one side, it bulges, as a soap bubble does. We measure the bulge from the plane of the frame as the height \(\zeta\) above the point \((y, z)\) of the section, and its peak has the height \(h\). By construction the frame has height zero.

This membrane is the origin of the name. Prandtl, who at the time held the chair of engineering mechanics at Hannover, showed that a soap film gives all the information on the distribution of stress in torsion experimentally (TIMO PDF pp. 331-332, published in Physik. Z. 4, 1903). Griffith and Taylor used the soap-film method to determine stresses (TIMO PDF p. 332, report of 1917-1918), and the analogy proved very useful in the torsion problem (TIMO PDF p. 336). The reason lies in the difficulty of the computation: for most sections the solution is not easy to write down, and the film shows it by itself. We shall use the membrane differently. First we prove that the agreement is an exact mathematical fact, then we read from it what happens in the section, and every reading we check against an exact number, because the membrane is not completely identical with the equation.

To do that we must say what we demand of the membrane.

Definition 16.24 Membrane of small slope (opna z majhnim naklonom)

Let \(S\) be a section in the plane \(y, z\) (as in theorem 16.16) and let \(N > 0\) and \(p\) be numbers. A membrane of small slope (opna z majhnim naklonom) over \(S\) with tension \(N\) and pressure \(p\) is the graph \(x = \zeta(y, z)\) of a function \(\zeta\) over \(S\) for which:

  1. The membrane is stretched across the frame: \(\zeta = 0\) on the boundary \(\partial S\).
  2. The tension \(N\) (in N/mm) is the force per unit length of the edge of any piece of the membrane. It is the same at every point and in every direction and does not depend on the bulge. It acts along the tangent to the membrane, perpendicular to the edge of the piece.
  3. The pressure \(p\) (in N/mm\(^2\)) is uniform and acts perpendicular to the membrane.
  4. The slope is small: \(|\nabla\zeta| = \sqrt{\zeta_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + \zeta_{\mathrm{z}}^2} \le s\) with a small \(s\). The bound \(s\) and the error it brings are in lemma 16.28.
  5. The small-slope model: the vertical component of the force with which the rest of the membrane pulls the piece of the membrane over a rectangle \(D \subset S\) with sides parallel to the axes is taken as \(N\oint_{\partial \mathrm{D}}\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}s\). Here \(\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\) is the derivative of \(\zeta\) along the outward normal \(\vek n\) of the side in the plane of the frame. The exact component has under the integral the additional factor \(1/\sqrt{1 + |\nabla\zeta|^2}\) (point 3 of the proof of theorem 16.25), which at a slope of at most \(s\) lies between \(1/\sqrt{1 + s^2}\) and \(1\).
Explanation

The membrane is a model without bending stiffness: it carries only tension. Point 5 is the only approximation of the model. With it the equation of the membrane in theorem 16.25 is exact for the model, and only approximate for a real membrane. The tension \(N\) is a membrane force, a force per unit length of the edge (point 2), and is not the axial force of a bar. Chapter 18 will use the same kind of force. We draw the height \(\zeta\) in the direction of the bar axis \(x\), but the membrane is not a part of the bar, it is an auxiliary object above the section.

Source: SADD section 9.3.4 (PDF pp. 254-255): a membrane with uniform tension \(N\) and uniform pressure \(p\), which at small displacement does not change the tension. SADD uses the plane \(x, y\) and the height \(z\), we use the plane \(y, z\) and the height \(\zeta\). SADD's \(z(x, y)\) is our \(\zeta(y, z)\).

What follows from these demands for \(\zeta\)? We build it as it is drawn on a board, first in a cross-section. We draw the cross-section of the membrane along the axis \(y\) at constant \(z\), on the axis \(y\) that lies in the plane of the frame. From the membrane we cut out a piece between \(y_1\) and \(y_2\). The rest of the membrane pulls it at both ends with the tension \(N\) along the tangent to the membrane. The tangent makes the angle \(\theta_1\) or \(\theta_2\) with the horizontal. Each force \(N\) has a vertical component, \(N\sin\theta_1\) or \(N\sin\theta_2\), and both pull downward. Upward the piece is pushed by the pressure \(p\). The piece is at rest if the vertical forces balance.

This is not enough for a plate, because over a section the membrane occupies a surface. So we put the same picture into a plan. The membrane lies over the section \(S\), and the cross-section we drew is the cut along this line. The piece of the membrane we shall treat is not a strip but the piece over the rectangle \(D\) that lies inside \(S\), with sides parallel to the axes \(y\) and \(z\). On each side of the rectangle the outward normal \(\vek n\) points in the plane of the frame. The axes \(y\) and \(z\) are as before. Over the boundary \(\partial D\) the piece of the membrane has an edge where the rest of the membrane holds it.

We write the balance of the piece over \(D\) and prove it in a theorem. First let us say what we demand of the surface so that the computation works: \(\zeta\) is to be twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\). The reason is the same as for Prandtl's function (section 16.3): it too must have second derivatives up to the boundary.

Theorem 16.25 Equation of the membrane (enačba opne)

Let a membrane of small slope over \(S\) with tension \(N\) and pressure \(p\) (definition 16.24) be in equilibrium and let \(\zeta\) be twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\). Then

\[N\,\nabla^2\zeta = N\,(\zeta_{\mathrm{yy}} + \zeta_{\mathrm{zz}}) = -p \quad \text{in } S , \qquad \zeta = 0 \quad \text{on } \partial S . \tag{16.27}\]

The volume between the membrane and the plane of the frame is \(V = \int_{\mathrm{S}}\zeta\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Idea

We write the balance of every piece over a rectangle \(D\) as an integral over \(D\) and by the divergence theorem turn the boundary term into an integral over the interior. Since it holds for every \(D\), the integrand must be zero everywhere.

Proof
  1. Let \(D \subset S\) be a rectangle with sides parallel to the axes and \(\Sigma\) the piece of the membrane over it. The membrane is at rest, so the piece is at rest, and the sum of the vertical forces on it is zero.
  2. Pressure. The pressure acts perpendicular to the membrane, so the pressure force on the piece \(\Sigma\) is the integral of \(p\,\vek n\) over \(\Sigma\), where \(\vek n\) is the unit normal of the membrane. The piece \(\Sigma\) is the graph \(x = \zeta(y, z)\) over \(D\). By definition 4.36 (formula (4.18), with the axis \(x\) in the role of the height) it has the vector \(\vek N = (1, -\zeta_{\mathrm{y}}, -\zeta_{\mathrm{z}})\), the normal \(\vek n = \vek N/|\vek N|\) and the integral over it \(\int_\Sigma f\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{D}} f\,|\vek N|\,\mathrm{d}A\). The component \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\) is \(1/|\vek N|\), so \(\int_\Sigma n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{D}} 1\,\mathrm{d}A = |D|\) for every shape of the membrane. The vertical component of the pressure force on \(\Sigma\) is therefore exactly \(p\,|D|\). This is not an approximation.
  3. Tension. Over a side of the rectangle with outward normal \(\vek n\) the piece of the membrane has an edge, where the rest of the membrane pulls it with a force \(N\) per unit length of the edge of the membrane, in the direction of the tangent to the membrane perpendicular to the edge. Let \(\vek t\) be the unit vector along the side in the plane of the frame, \(\zeta_{\mathrm{n}} = \partial\zeta/\partial n\) the derivative along \(\vek n\) and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{s}}\) the derivative along \(\vek t\). The tangent plane of the membrane is spanned by the vectors \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} = \zeta_{\mathrm{s}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + \vek t\) along the edge of the membrane and \(\vek T_{\mathrm{n}} = \zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + \vek n\). The direction in this plane perpendicular to the edge is \(\vek m = \vek T_{\mathrm{n}} - \frac{\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\zeta_{\mathrm{s}}}{1 + \zeta_{\mathrm{s}}^2}\,\vek T_{\mathrm{s}}\), since \(\vek T_{\mathrm{n}}\cdot\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} = \zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\zeta_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}}\cdot\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} = 1 + \zeta_{\mathrm{s}}^2\). Its component along \(\vek n\) is \(1\), so it points outward. Its component \(x\) is \(\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}/(1 + \zeta_{\mathrm{s}}^2)\) and its length is \(|\vek m| = \sqrt{(1 + \zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^2 + \zeta_{\mathrm{s}}^2)/(1 + \zeta_{\mathrm{s}}^2)}\). Since \(\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^2 + \zeta_{\mathrm{s}}^2 = |\nabla\zeta|^2\), the unit vector \(\vek m/|\vek m|\) has the vertical component \(\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}/\sqrt{(1 + \zeta_{\mathrm{s}}^2)(1 + |\nabla\zeta|^2)}\). The length of the edge of the membrane over a part of the side is \(\int\sqrt{1 + \zeta_{\mathrm{s}}^2}\,\mathrm{d}s\) over this part (the arc-length formula). The vertical tension force over the side is therefore \(N\int\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}/\sqrt{1 + |\nabla\zeta|^2}\,\mathrm{d}s\). At \(|\nabla\zeta| \le s\) the factor \(1/\sqrt{1 + |\nabla\zeta|^2}\) lies between \(1/\sqrt{1 + s^2}\) and \(1\): at \(s = 0{,}1\) between \(0{,}9950\) and \(1\), at \(s = 0{,}2\) between \(0{,}9806\) and \(1\). The model (point 5 of definition 16.24) drops this factor, so in the model the vertical force over the side is \(N\int\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}s\). The price of this decision is measured in lemma 16.28.
  4. Balance. The edge of the piece pulls outward, so the vertical component of the tension force per unit length is \(+N\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\) (for a bulge upward \(\zeta_{\mathrm{n}} < 0\) and the force pulls down). Over the whole boundary \(\partial D\) the tension forces give \(N\oint_{\partial \mathrm{D}}\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}s\), the pressure gives \(+p\,|D|\), and the sum is zero: \(N\oint_{\partial \mathrm{D}}\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}s + p\,|D| = 0\).
  5. By lemma 16.9 with the field \(\nabla\zeta\) on the rectangle \(D\) we have \(\oint_{\partial \mathrm{D}}\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}s = \int_{\mathrm{D}}\nabla^2\zeta\,\mathrm{d}A\). So \(\int_{\mathrm{D}}(N\nabla^2\zeta + p)\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\) for every rectangle \(D \subset S\).
  6. Let \(f = N\nabla^2\zeta + p\). It is continuous. If it were positive at a point \(P\) inside \(S\), by continuity it would be positive on a small square around \(P\) and its integral over it would be positive, contradicting point 5. Likewise for negative. So \(f = 0\) at every interior point, and by continuity also on the boundary. This is the first equation.
  7. The boundary condition is point 1 of definition 16.24. The volume is a definition.

Source: SADD (9.3.33)-(9.3.35) (PDF p. 255): the equation of the membrane, the boundary condition and the volume. SADD derives the equation from the balance of a differential element of the membrane. Here it is derived from the balance of a finite piece with the divergence theorem, and the error of the small-slope model is written as a number.

The model of point 5 of definition 16.24 has a price: the equation of the membrane is not the exact equation of the film, the errors at a large slope are in lemma 16.28. But the solution \(\zeta\) of equation (16.27) is exactly determined, and that is what we shall need. Now we set the equation of the membrane beside Prandtl's.

Let us compare the equations \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2G\alpha\) and \(\nabla^2\zeta = -p/N\), both with zero on the boundary. They differ only in the right-hand side and in units (\(\Phi\) is in N/mm, \(\zeta\) in mm). If we multiply \(\zeta\) by a constant \(\kappa\), we get \(\nabla^2(\kappa\zeta) = -\kappa\,p/N\). If \(\kappa\,p/N = 2G\alpha\), the equations agree. Does it then follow that \(\Phi = \kappa\,\zeta\)? The answer is given by the uniqueness lemma that we proved for Prandtl's function (lemma 16.17).

Corollary 16.26 Membrane analogy (membranska analogija)

Let \(S\) be a section as in theorem 16.16, \(\Phi\) its Prandtl function with zero on the boundary at twist \(\alpha\), and let \(\zeta\) be the twice continuously differentiable function of theorem 16.25 for a membrane with tension \(N\) and pressure \(p\), chosen so that

\[\frac{p}{N} = \frac{2G\alpha}{\kappa} , \qquad \text{that is} \qquad \kappa = \frac{2G\alpha\,N}{p} . \tag{16.28}\]

Then:

  1. \(\Phi = \kappa\,\zeta\) in \(S\).
  2. The moment is \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\kappa\,V\) with the volume \(V = \int_{\mathrm{S}}\zeta\,\mathrm{d}A\), that is, twice the volume under the membrane, multiplied by \(\kappa\).
  3. The shear stress \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}) = \kappa\,(\zeta_{\mathrm{z}}, -\zeta_{\mathrm{y}})\) has the magnitude \(\tau = \kappa\,|\nabla\zeta|\), that is, \(\kappa\) times the slope of the membrane, and it is perpendicular to the slope, so it lies along a contour line of the membrane. A contour line is a curve on which \(\zeta\) is constant.
Idea

The function \(\kappa\zeta\) solves the same boundary problem as \(\Phi\), by the uniqueness lemma they are equal. The rest is a transcription of the equations of theorem 16.16 and definition 16.14.

Proof
  1. The function \(w = \kappa\zeta\) is twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\). By theorem 16.25 \(\nabla^2 w = -\kappa\,p/N = -2G\alpha\) in \(S\) and \(w = 0\) on \(\partial S\).
  2. By theorem 16.16 the same holds for \(\Phi\). By lemma 16.17 \(w\) and \(\Phi\) are equal.
  3. Moment: \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A = 2\kappa\int_{\mathrm{S}}\zeta\,\mathrm{d}A = 2\kappa\,V\) by equation (16.23).
  4. Stress: by equation (16.19) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} = \kappa\,\zeta_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} = -\kappa\,\zeta_{\mathrm{y}}\). The scalar product with the gradient is \(\zeta_{\mathrm{z}}\zeta_{\mathrm{y}} - \zeta_{\mathrm{y}}\zeta_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), so the stress is perpendicular to the gradient. The gradient is perpendicular to the contour line, so the stress is along it. The magnitude is \(\kappa\sqrt{\zeta_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + \zeta_{\mathrm{y}}^2} = \kappa\,|\nabla\zeta|\).

Source: SADD section 9.3.4 (PDF pp. 255-256): \(\phi = z\), \(p/N = 2\mu\alpha\), \(T = 2V\) and the properties of contour lines. SADD takes \(p/N = 2\mu\alpha\), so \(\Phi = \zeta\), and writes \(\mu\) for the shear modulus, we write \(G\). The converse by the uniqueness lemma and the constant \(\kappa\) are not from the source.

The corollary is a mathematical fact, not a statement about soap: we proved it by computation and not by experiment. SADD also limits its use: measuring the slope on a real membrane does not give sufficiently accurate stresses (PDF p. 256). Reading from the membrane is therefore a guide, and every reading below we confirm with an exact number.

Let us read first on the ellipse. The solution \(\Phi\) of the ellipse \(a = 10\) mm, \(b = 20\) mm is in theorem 16.18, so the membrane is \(\zeta = \Phi/\kappa\). As in example 16.19 take \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m: \(J = 50\,265\) mm\(^4\), \(\alpha = 0{,}01320\) rad/m and \(G\alpha = 0{,}99472\) N/mm\(^3\) (num-04.py). Let us choose the pressure with \(p/N = 0{,}0125\) mm\(^{-1}\). By equation (16.28) \(\kappa = 2G\alpha/(p/N) = 159{,}15\) N/mm\(^2\), that is, \(159{,}15\) MPa per unit of slope. By equation (16.24) the height of the peak is \(h = (p/N)\,a^2b^2/(2(a^2 + b^2)) = 0{,}5000\) mm and \(\zeta = h\,(1 - y^2/a^2 - z^2/b^2)\).

We draw this membrane in three views [figure 16.16]. The first is the profile along \(y\): a parabola with the peak \(h\) that reaches the boundary at \(y = a\) with the slope \(2h/a = 0{,}10\), drawn as a blue step. The second is the profile along \(z\), a flatter parabola that reaches the boundary at \(z = b\) with the slope \(2h/b = 0{,}05\). The ratio of the slopes is \(b/a = 2{,}000\). On the right is the plan: the boundary of the ellipse and three contour lines at \(\zeta = 0{,}75\,h\), \(0{,}50\,h\) and \(0{,}25\,h\), and the axes. By corollary 16.26 the stress is along the contour lines and equal to \(\kappa\) times the slope. At the point \(A\) at the end of the shorter axis the slope is \(0{,}10\) and the stress \(\tau_{\mathrm{A}} = 159{,}15 \cdot 0{,}10 = 15{,}92\) MPa, tangent to the boundary. At the point \(B\) at the end of the longer axis the slope is \(0{,}05\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{B}} = 7{,}96\) MPa. The intermediate point \(C\) is \((5, 10)\) mm. There \(\zeta = h\,(1 - 0{,}25 - 0{,}25) = 0{,}50\,h\), so it lies on the middle contour line. The derivatives are \(\zeta_{\mathrm{y}} = -2hy/a^2 = -0{,}050\) and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{z}} = -2hz/b^2 = -0{,}025\), the slope is \(|\nabla\zeta| = 0{,}0559\) and the stress \(\tau_{\mathrm{C}} = 159{,}15 \cdot 0{,}0559 = 8{,}90\) MPa, tangent to this contour line.

Example 16.27 Ellipse 10 by 20 mm on the membrane (elipsa 10 × 20 mm na opni)

The exact expression (theorem 16.18, equation (16.26)) gives \(\tau = 2M_{\mathrm{x}}/(\pi a^2 b) = 15{,}92\) MPa at \(A\) and \(2M_{\mathrm{x}}/(\pi a b^2) = 7{,}96\) MPa at \(B\), which are the numbers from the membrane. The volume is \(V = \pi a b h/2 = 157{,}080\) mm\(^3\) and \(2\kappa V = 50\,000\) N mm \(= 50{,}000\) N m, which is the \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) we started from. Balance of the piece over the rectangle \([-3, 5] \times [2, 9]\) mm (theorem 16.25): the sum of the boundary terms \(\sum\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\,l\) is \(-0{,}70000\) mm and \(-(p/N)\,|D| = -0{,}70000\) mm.

Source: Numbers: num-04.py, part A. The expressions for \(\tau\) are from theorem 16.18 (SADD example 9.1, PDF pp. 257-258).

What of this holds for every section? By the corollary the membrane says that the stress is along the contour lines and as large as the slope, so largest where the membrane is steepest. In the ellipse this is at the boundary, at the point nearest the centre. SADD says that this can be proved (exercise 9.5, PDF p. 256). We do not prove it here and use the statement only as a guide, confirmed on the ellipse and later on the rectangle. BARBER says the same in words: for rectangles, circles and ellipses the largest slope is at the boundary nearest the centre, and for a thin section where the section is thickest (BARBER section 16.2, PDF p. 256). At a sharp re-entrant corner of a section the stress, by the same source, is not bounded, we do not use this in the chapter.

The analogy says the same about stiffness. At the same twist \(\alpha\) the constant \(\kappa\) is the same for all sections, and \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\kappa V\) means that \(J = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(G\alpha)\) is proportional to the volume under the membrane. A section that has a low membrane has a small volume and a small stiffness. In example 16.23 the sections had the same area \(800\) mm\(^2\): the circle with \(J = 101\,859\) mm\(^4\) and the strip 1 : 5 with \(37\,288\) mm\(^4\). The ratio \(0{,}366\) means that the membrane over the strip 1 : 5 has \(0{,}366\) times the volume of the membrane over the circle. The membrane says this without computation: the strip is narrow, so everywhere it is near the boundary, where the height is zero.

The membrane says something more about narrow sections. Take a strip \(20 \times 40\) mm (\(a = 10\) mm along \(y\), \(b = 20\) mm along \(z\)) and draw it in two cross-sections [figure 16.17]. The section across the strip, along \(y\) at \(z = 0\), is close to the parabola \(a^2 - y^2\) (dashed). The section along the strip, along \(z\) at \(y = 0\), is flatter in the middle than the section across and falls only near the short edges. Vertically we measure the height \(\Phi/(G\alpha)\) in mm\(^2\), computed with the series that we prove for the rectangle in section 16.5 (num-04.py, part B).

The numbers confirm the guide, but not completely. At the centre \(\Phi(0, 0)/(G\alpha) = 91{,}097\) mm\(^2\), the parabola gives \(a^2 = 100\) mm\(^2\), the ratio is \(0{,}9110\). Along \(y\) at \(z = 0\) the value at \(y = 5\) mm is \(68{,}704\) against \(75\) mm\(^2\) for the parabola, and at \(y = 8\) mm it is \(33{,}248\) against \(36\). The slope at the middle of the longer edge is \(18{,}601\) mm, the parabola gives \(2a = 20\) mm, the ratio \(0{,}930\). Along \(z\) at \(y = 0\) the height towards the centre falls to the ratio \(0{,}8529\) at \(z = 10\) mm, \(0{,}5813\) at \(15\) mm and \(0{,}2837\) at \(18\) mm. At the side ratio \(1 : 2\) the middle is therefore not yet flat: already at \(z = 10\) mm the membrane is \(15\) % below the centre and the parabola overestimates the centre by \(9{,}8\) %. The flat middle will be longer for a longer strip, and how much exactly is told by section 16.6.

Now the near miss. Theorem 16.25 and its corollary hold exactly for the solution of equation (16.27). The real membrane, however, does not satisfy this equation everywhere: the model (point 5 of definition 16.24) dropped the factor \(1/\sqrt{1 + |\nabla\zeta|^2}\) of point 3 of the proof, which is far from 1 at a large slope. Let us see what this means on a strip.

Take a long strip \(|y| \le a = 10\) mm and a pressure \(p/N = k\) such that the real membrane has the slope \(\tan\theta = 0{,}5\) at the edge, that is, the angle \(\theta = 26{,}57°\). Then \(\sin\theta = 0{,}4472\) and \(k = 0{,}04472\) mm\(^{-1}\). We draw half of the strip [figure 16.18]: the axes \(y\) horizontal and \(\zeta\) vertical, in the same scale, without enlargement. We do not write the real membrane with equation (16.27) but with the exact balance of the free piece from \(y = 0\) to the edge. At \(y = 0\) it is pulled by the tension \(N\) horizontally, because there the slope is zero by symmetry. At the edge it is pulled by the tension \(N\) at the angle \(\theta\), with the vertical component \(N\sin\theta\) downward. Upward it is pushed by the pressure \(p\) over the length \(y\). The balance \(N\sin\theta = p\,y\) is exact for this membrane. The real membrane is a circular arc. The small-slope model (dashed) is the parabola that equation (16.27) gives.

Lemma 16.28 Error of the small-slope model (napaka modela majhnega naklona)

Let the membrane over a long strip \(|y| \le a\) (independent of \(z\), symmetric, the graph of a function \(\zeta_{\mathrm{t}}(y)\) with \(\zeta_{\mathrm{t}}(\pm a) = 0\) and horizontal tangent at \(y = 0\)) be exactly in equilibrium with the tension \(N\) along the tangent and the pressure \(p\). Let \(k = p/N\) and \(k a < 1\), let \(\theta(y)\) be the angle of the tangent with the axis \(y\), and let \(\zeta_{\mathrm{l}}\) be the solution of equation (16.27) at the same \(k\). Then:

  1. \(\sin\theta(y) = k\,|y|\) and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{t}}(y) = \big(\sqrt{1 - k^2y^2} - \sqrt{1 - k^2a^2}\big)/k\), a circular arc of radius \(1/k\).
  2. \(\zeta_{\mathrm{l}}(y) = k\,(a^2 - y^2)/2\).
  3. The slope of the model at the edge is \(k a = \sin\theta_{\mathrm{a}}\), the slope of the real membrane is \(s = \tan\theta_{\mathrm{a}}\). The ratio is \(\cos\theta_{\mathrm{a}} = 1/\sqrt{1 + s^2}\).
Idea

The balance of the piece from \(0\) to \(y\) gives \(\sin\theta\) exactly, the model puts \(\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta\), whence the parabola.

Proof
  1. For \(y > 0\) take the piece of the membrane between \(0\) and \(y\) (figure, free piece). At \(0\) the tangent is horizontal, so the vertical component of the tension forces there is zero. At \(y\) the vertical component is \(N\sin\theta(y)\) downward. Upward is the pressure force \(p\,y\) per unit length of the strip (point 2 of the proof of theorem 16.25 with a strip in place of \(D\)). The balance \(N\sin\theta(y) = p\,y\) gives \(\sin\theta = k\,y\).
  2. The slope is \(\zeta_{\mathrm{t}}' = -\tan\theta = -k\,y/\sqrt{1 - k^2y^2}\). The expression \(\big(\sqrt{1 - k^2y^2} - \sqrt{1 - k^2a^2}\big)/k\) has the same derivative and is zero at \(y = a\), so it equals \(\zeta_{\mathrm{t}}\) by the theorem on functions with equal derivatives (corollary 1.85). From it \(\big(\zeta_{\mathrm{t}} + \sqrt{1 - k^2a^2}/k\big)^2 + y^2 = 1/k^2\), the equation of a circle of radius \(1/k\).
  3. For the model equation (16.27) in this case is \(\zeta'' = -k\) and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{l}}(\pm a) = 0\), whence \(\zeta_{\mathrm{l}} = k\,(a^2 - y^2)/2\). Its slope at the edge is \(k a\), equal to \(\sin\theta_{\mathrm{a}}\) by point 1. The ratio to the real membrane is \(\sin\theta_{\mathrm{a}}/\tan\theta_{\mathrm{a}} = \cos\theta_{\mathrm{a}} = 1/\sqrt{1 + s^2}\).

Source: The real membrane as a circular arc and the comparison with the model are not from the source. The small-slope model is SADD section 9.3.4 (PDF pp. 254-255).

The numbers (num-04.py, part C). At \(s = 0{,}5\) the slope of the model at the edge is \(k a = 0{,}4472\) against the real \(0{,}5\), the ratio \(0{,}8944\), the model is \(10{,}56\) % too low. The height of the model is \(2{,}2361\) mm, the real membrane has \(2{,}3607\) mm, the model is \(5{,}28\) % too low. The area under the profile is \(29{,}814\) mm\(^2\) against \(31{,}824\) mm\(^2\), the model is \(6{,}31\) % too low. The factor \(1/\sqrt{1 + s^2}\) is \(0{,}9988\) at \(s = 0{,}05\) (error \(0{,}12\) %), \(0{,}9950\) at \(s = 0{,}1\) (\(0{,}50\) %), \(0{,}9806\) at \(s = 0{,}2\) (\(1{,}94\) %) and \(0{,}8944\) at \(s = 0{,}5\) (\(10{,}56\) %). The membrane of the ellipse in example 16.27 has the largest slope \(0{,}10\) and the factor \(0{,}9950\), so there the factor in the equation differs from \(1\) by at most \(0{,}5\) %. For the strip (lemma 16.28) at this slope the slope of the model at the edge is also \(0{,}5\) % too low. That the solution for a real membrane over the ellipse is as close to the model we expect, but do not prove. For a reading this is enough.

What follows for the analogy? Corollary 16.26 is mathematically exact: \(\Phi = \kappa\zeta\) for the solution of equation (16.27), whatever the slope. What is not exact is the link between this solution and a real soap membrane, and that is a fault of the choice of pressure, not of the analogy. For a given torsion \(\Phi\) and \(\alpha\) are fixed, and \(p/N\) is ours to choose. If we halve it, \(\kappa\) doubles, the slope and the height of the membrane halve (num-04.py), so the slope can be made as small as we like with the pressure, and the error of the model falls with it. At \(s = 0{,}5\) the pressure was chosen too large. The membrane is a guide for understanding, not a measuring instrument, as SADD warns (PDF p. 256).

The membrane gave us three guides: the stress is largest at the boundary where the membrane is steepest, it runs along the contour lines and is proportional to the slope, and the stiffness is proportional to the volume. The first two we confirmed on the ellipse, the third on the example of equal area. For narrow sections section 16.6 derives a formula from the flat middle of the membrane and measures it against the exact series.

16.5 The rectangular section (pravokotni prerez)

In chapter 12 we put the strip \(20 \times 40\) mm into the L-frame and took the torsion constant \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\) as given (equation (12.17)). With the ordinary polar moment \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 133\,333\) mm\(^4\) the displacement of the top of the frame would be \(26\) % too small (figure 12.16). Where does the number \(73\,178\) come from, and why is it nearly half of \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\)? This section answers both, for a rectangle, which the theory of the circular shaft does not cover.

The model is that of definition 16.1: a straight prism, isotropic linear elastic material (steel, \(G = 75{,}385\) GPa), free lateral surface, loaded only by the torque \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) about the axis \(x\). The section \(S\) is a rectangle with side \(2a\) along \(y\) and \(2b\) along \(z\), chosen so that \(a \le b\), with the origin at its centre. For the strip \(a = 10\) mm and \(b = 20\) mm. The twist per unit length is \(\alpha\). The centre of the rectangle is the centre of twist, because the section has two axes of symmetry, as we assumed already in chapter 12, and the reasons are in the section on the shear centre later in the chapter.

By theorem 16.16 the Prandtl function (Prandtlova funkcija) \(\Phi(y, z)\) (definition 16.14) must satisfy \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2G\alpha\) in the section and be zero on the boundary, and the stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \partial\Phi/\partial z\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\partial\Phi/\partial y\). By lemma 16.17 such a function is unique if it is twice continuously differentiable on an open set containing \(S\). The function of the rectangle will not be so at the corners, so we show its uniqueness in the proof of the theorem below with the same idea. So we do not have to derive the solution in its only possible form: it is enough to build one, check the conditions and appeal to uniqueness.

A polynomial that is zero on all four sides is the first try. The product \((a^2 - y^2)(b^2 - z^2)\) does that, but its Laplacian is not constant (section 16.3, where it returns as a trial function). So we go another way and build the solution in parts on figure 16.19.

We draw the section with the half width \(a\) along \(y\) and the half height \(b\) along \(z\). The same construction works for every \(a \le b\), the square included. First we look for a function that has the right Laplacian and is zero on the long sides \(y = \pm a\). A function of \(y\) alone does: \(\Phi_{\mathrm{p}} = G\alpha\,(a^2 - y^2)\) has \(\partial^2\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}/\partial y^2 = -2G\alpha\), so \(\nabla^2\Phi_{\mathrm{p}} = -2G\alpha\), and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}(\pm a, z) = 0\). This is exactly the parabola that appears for a long strip (the membrane of section 16.4 is curved across the narrow side like a parabola). For the rectangle it has an error on the short sides \(z = \pm b\): there \(\Phi_{\mathrm{p}} = G\alpha(a^2 - y^2)\), not zero.

We must cancel the error with a function \(\Phi_{\mathrm{h}}\) that has the value \(-G\alpha(a^2 - y^2)\) on the short sides, zero on the long ones, and \(\nabla^2\Phi_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\), so that the sum keeps the right Laplacian. A term of the form \(\cos(\lambda y)\cosh(\lambda z)\) is harmonic, because \(\partial^2_{\mathrm{y}}\cos(\lambda y) = -\lambda^2\cos(\lambda y)\) and \(\partial^2_{\mathrm{z}}\cosh(\lambda z) = +\lambda^2\cosh(\lambda z)\) (lemma 9.42, item 1). Zero on \(y = \pm a\) requires \(\cos(\lambda a) = 0\), so \(\lambda = \lambda_{\mathrm{n}} = n\pi/(2a)\) with odd \(n\). On the profile at the short side we must therefore expand the parabola \(a^2 - y^2\) in a series of cosines \(\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y)\). This is the sine series of lemma 13.10, shifted by \(a\): we take \(h(s) = s(2a - s)\) on \([0, 2a]\) and \(s = y + a\).

Lemma 16.29 The parabola as a cosine series (parabola kot vrsta kosinusov)

Let \(a > 0\), \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} = n\pi/(2a)\) and

\[c_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{32\,a^2}{\pi^3 n^3}\,(-1)^{(n-1)/2} \qquad (n = 1, 3, 5, \dots) . \tag{16.29}\]

The series \(\sum c_{\mathrm{n}}\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y)\) over odd \(n\) converges uniformly on \([-a, a]\) and has the sum \(a^2 - y^2\). Also \(\sum |c_{\mathrm{n}}|\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} = 2a\).

Proof

We must show that \(a^2 - y^2\) is a sine series by lemma 13.10 and that the coefficients are as stated. Only the odd ones are nonzero, and \(\sum|c_{\mathrm{n}}|\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\) is a known series of reciprocal squares.

  1. Let \(h(s) = s(2a - s)\) on \([0, 2a]\). It is a polynomial, hence continuously differentiable, and \(h(0) = h(2a) = 0\). By lemma 13.10 with \(L = 2a\), \(h(s) = \sum_{\mathrm{m} \ge 1}h_{\mathrm{m}}\sin(m\pi s/2a)\) uniformly, with sine coefficients \(h_{\mathrm{m}} = \frac1a\int_0^{2a}h(s)\sin\frac{m\pi s}{2a}\,\mathrm{d}s\) (equation (13.8)).
  2. Let \(\kappa = m\pi/(2a)\). Integrating by parts twice (lemma 1.81, product rule): \(\int_0^{2a}h\sin\kappa s\,\mathrm{d}s = \big[-h\cos\kappa s/\kappa\big]_0^{2a} + \frac1\kappa\int_0^{2a}h'\cos\kappa s\,\mathrm{d}s\). The first term is zero because \(h(0) = h(2a) = 0\). The second is \(\frac1{\kappa}\big(\big[h'\sin\kappa s/\kappa\big]_0^{2a} - \frac1\kappa\int_0^{2a}h''\sin\kappa s\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\). Its first term is again zero because \(\sin 0 = \sin m\pi = 0\), and \(h'' = -2\).
  3. What remains is \(\frac{2}{\kappa^2}\int_0^{2a}\sin\kappa s\,\mathrm{d}s = \frac{2}{\kappa^3}\big(1 - (-1)^m\big)\). This is zero for even \(m\) and \(4/\kappa^3 = 32a^3/(\pi^3m^3)\) for odd \(m\), so \(h_{\mathrm{m}} = 32a^2/(\pi^3 m^3)\) for odd \(m\) (SymPy: \(h_1/a^2 = 1{,}03205\)).
  4. With \(s = y + a\) and odd \(m\), \(\sin(m\pi s/2a) = \sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{m}} y + m\pi/2) = (-1)^{(m-1)/2}\cos\lambda_{\mathrm{m}} y\), since \(\cos(m\pi/2) = 0\) and \(\sin(m\pi/2) = (-1)^{(m-1)/2}\). So \(h_{\mathrm{m}}\sin(m\pi s/2a) = c_{\mathrm{m}}\cos\lambda_{\mathrm{m}} y\) and \(h(y + a) = a^2 - y^2\). This is the first claim.
  5. By lemma 9.83 (reciprocal squares) \(\sum_{\mathrm{n}\ \text{odd}}1/n^2\) converges, and \(|c_{\mathrm{n}}|\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} = 16a/(\pi^2 n^2)\). The sum is \(\frac{16a}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{\pi^2}{8} = 2a\) (the known sum of odd reciprocal squares, which follows from the pointwise convergence of the triangle wave in example 9.96, where \(\frac{4}{\pi^2}\sum_{\mathrm{n}\ \text{odd}}\frac1{n^2} = \frac12\)).

Source: BARBER section 16.4 (PDF p. 258-259, equations (16.45) to (16.49)) finds the coefficients by multiplying with a cosine and integrating, SADD (9.5.7) to (9.5.9) (PDF p. 264) with Fourier coefficients. The proof through the sine series lemma is not from the sources.

The lemma gives us the coefficients and the uniform convergence that we need for differentiation. One term is already close to the parabola: at \(y = 0\), \(c_1 = 103{,}2\) mm\(^2\) instead of \(a^2 = 100\) mm\(^2\), which is \(3{,}2\) %, and the largest deviation on \([-a, a]\) is \(4{,}3\) mm\(^2\). The first term is the blue curve on figure 16.19, the first two terms the orange dashed one, with \(c_1 + c_3 = 99{,}4\) mm\(^2\) at \(y = 0\) and a largest deviation of \(1{,}2\) mm\(^2\) (SymPy). Going from the side \(z = b\) inwards, term \(n\) shrinks by the factor \(\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} z)/\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b)\). For the strip at \(z = 0\) this factor is \(1/\cosh\pi = 0{,}0863\) for \(n = 1\) and \(1/\cosh 3\pi = 1{,}6\cdot10^{-4}\) for \(n = 3\). The higher terms nearly vanish in the interior.

Theorem 16.30 Torsion of the rectangular section (torzija pravokotnega prereza)

Let \(S = (-a, a) \times (-b, b)\) be a rectangle with \(0 < a \le b\) and let \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(c_{\mathrm{n}}\) be as in lemma 16.29. For the twist \(\alpha\) per unit length:

  1. The series
    \[\Phi(y, z) = G\alpha\Big[a^2 - y^2 - \sum_{\mathrm{n}\ \text{odd}}c_{\mathrm{n}}\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y)\,\frac{\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} z)}{\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b)}\Big] \tag{16.30}\]
    and the series of its first derivatives converge term by term uniformly on \(\bar S\). The function \(\Phi\) is continuous on \(\bar S\), zero on the boundary, has continuous second derivatives in the interior and \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2G\alpha\). The stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \partial\Phi/\partial z\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\partial\Phi/\partial y\) are in equilibrium in the interior, the lateral surface is free and the resultant force of the section is zero. The function \(\Phi\) is the only one that is continuously differentiable on \(\bar S\), twice continuously differentiable in the interior, zero on the boundary and has \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2G\alpha\), and it is the Prandtl function of the rectangle.
  2. The torque is \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = G J\alpha\) with
    \[J = \frac{16\,a^3 b}{3} - \frac{1024\,a^4}{\pi^5}\sum_{\mathrm{n}\ \text{odd}}\frac{1}{n^5}\tanh\frac{n\pi b}{2a} . \tag{16.31}\]
    This is the same equation as (12.17).
Proof

We must first show that the series satisfies Prandtl's equation (16.22), then compute the torque. The function is harmonic term by term, the boundary conditions come from lemma 16.29, differentiation term by term from the uniform convergence of the derivatives. Theorem 16.16 and lemma 16.17 do not hold at the corners, so we show their conclusions for the rectangle directly. The torque comes from integration by parts and then term by term.

  1. Let \(r_{\mathrm{n}}(z) = \cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} z)/\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b)\) for \(|z| \le b\). Because \(\cosh\) is even and increasing on \([0, b]\) (lemma 9.42, items 1 and 3, and the mean value theorem 1.84), \(0 < r_{\mathrm{n}} \le 1\) and \(r_{\mathrm{n}}(\pm b) = 1\). The term \(c_{\mathrm{n}}\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y)\,r_{\mathrm{n}}(z)\) has absolute value at most \(|c_{\mathrm{n}}|\), and \(\sum|c_{\mathrm{n}}| < \infty\) (lemma 16.29). By the Weierstrass criterion (theorem 9.85) the series converges uniformly on \(\bar S\) and its sum is continuous.
  2. The first derivatives of a term are \(-c_{\mathrm{n}}\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y)\,r_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(c_{\mathrm{n}}\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y)\,r_{\mathrm{n}}'/\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\) with \(|r_{\mathrm{n}}'/\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}| = |\sinh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} z)|/\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b) \le 1\). The absolute value is at most \(|c_{\mathrm{n}}|\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\), and \(\sum|c_{\mathrm{n}}|\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} = 2a\) (lemma 16.29). So both series of derivatives converge uniformly on \(\bar S\) (theorem 9.85).
  3. Let \(0 < \delta < b\) and \(|z| \le b - \delta\). Because \(\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} z) \le \mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}|z|}\) and \(\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b) \ge \mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b}/2\), \(r_{\mathrm{n}}(z) \le 2\,\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\delta} \le 2q^n\) with \(q = \mathrm{e}^{-\pi\delta/(2a)} < 1\), and the same holds for \(|\sinh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} z)|/\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b)\). For the strip and \(\delta = 4\) mm, \(q = 0{,}533\). Every second derivative of a term is \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) times \(c_{\mathrm{n}}\) times a sine or cosine times \(r_{\mathrm{n}}\) or \(\sinh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} z)/\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b)\), so its absolute value is at most \(2|c_{\mathrm{n}}|\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}^2q^n = \frac{16}{\pi n}\,q^n \le \frac{16}{\pi}q^n\), since \(|c_{\mathrm{n}}|\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = 8/(\pi n)\). The geometric series \(\sum q^n\) converges (lemma 9.83), so the series of second derivatives converge uniformly on the band \(|z| \le b - \delta\) (Weierstrass criterion).
  4. By the lemma on differentiating a uniformly convergent series (lemma 14.25, applied first in one variable and then in the other, chapter 14) \(\Phi\) has continuous second derivatives on the band, equal to the sums of the derivatives of the terms. As \(\delta\) is arbitrary, this holds at every interior point.
  5. Every term has \(\partial^2_{\mathrm{y}} + \partial^2_{\mathrm{z}} = (-\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}^2 + \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}^2)\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y)\,r_{\mathrm{n}}(z) = 0\) (lemma 9.42, item 1, and the theorem on derivatives of sine and cosine 8.12). So \(\nabla^2\Phi = G\alpha\,\nabla^2(a^2 - y^2) = -2G\alpha\).
  6. On \(y = \pm a\), \(\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} a) = \cos(n\pi/2) = 0\) for odd \(n\), so all terms of the series are zero, and \(a^2 - y^2 = 0\). On \(z = \pm b\), \(r_{\mathrm{n}} = 1\), so \(\Phi = G\alpha\big[a^2 - y^2 - \sum c_{\mathrm{n}}\cos\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y\big] = 0\) by lemma 16.29. The function \(\Phi\) is zero on the boundary.
  7. Theorem 16.16 and lemma 16.17 require the function to be twice continuously differentiable on an open set containing \(S\). Our \(\Phi\) is not so at the corners. If it were, then at the corner \((a, b)\) we would have \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\), because \(\Phi\) is zero along the side \(z = b\), and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\), because it is zero along the side \(y = a\), so \(\nabla^2\Phi = 0\) instead of \(-2G\alpha\). So we check the conclusions of both for the rectangle directly.
  8. Equilibrium and free lateral surface. In the interior \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial y + \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/\partial z = \Phi_{\mathrm{zy}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\), since by step 4 both mixed derivatives are sums of the same derivatives of the terms \(-c_{\mathrm{n}}\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y)\,r_{\mathrm{n}}'(z)\). On the side \(y = a\) we have \(\Phi(a, z) = 0\) for all \(z\), and by step 2 and lemma 14.25 \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(a, z)\) is the derivative of this function, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and with the normal \((1, 0)\) we get \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). The same holds on \(y = -a\), and on \(z = \pm b\) we have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\). At the corners both components are zero. The warping function \(\psi\) with \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = z + \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}/(G\alpha)\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = -y - \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}/(G\alpha)\), which gives these stresses by equation (16.12), is the series of lemma 16.32 below. The lemma uses only the series of derivatives of step 2, not this theorem. The stresses are therefore stresses of Saint-Venant torsion and \(\Phi\) is the Prandtl function (definition 16.14).
  9. Uniqueness. Let \(\tilde\Phi\) be another function, continuously differentiable on \(\bar S\), twice continuously differentiable in the interior, with \(\nabla^2\tilde\Phi = -2G\alpha\) in the interior and \(\tilde\Phi = 0\) on the boundary, and let \(w = \Phi - \tilde\Phi\). We use the idea of lemma 16.17 on the smaller rectangle \(S_\varepsilon = [-a + \varepsilon, a - \varepsilon] \times [-b + \varepsilon, b - \varepsilon]\), around which \(w\) is twice continuously differentiable: \(\int_{\mathrm{S}_\varepsilon}|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint_{\partial \mathrm{S}_\varepsilon}w\,\partial w/\partial n\,\mathrm{d}s\). By theorem 8.26, \(|\nabla w| \le K\) on \(\bar S\) for some number \(K\). A point of the boundary of \(S_\varepsilon\) lies at distance \(\varepsilon\) from the boundary of \(S\), where \(w = 0\), so by the mean value theorem 1.84 \(|w| \le \varepsilon K\) there. The right-hand side is therefore at most \(\varepsilon K^2(4a + 4b)\) in absolute value. The left-hand side differs from \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm{d}A\) by the integral over a frame of area less than \(\varepsilon(4a + 4b)\), so by at most \(\varepsilon K^2(4a + 4b)\). As \(\varepsilon \to 0\) we get \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), and then as in the lemma: \(\nabla w = 0\), \(w\) is constant and zero on the boundary, so \(w = 0\). This proves the first item.
  10. Torque and resultant. The moment of the stresses of the end section about the axis \(x\) is \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = \int_{\mathrm{S}}(y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} - z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\,\mathrm{d}A = -\int_{\mathrm{S}}(y\,\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + z\,\Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}A\) (theorem 16.10, step 5). We integrate by parts at fixed \(z\): \(\int_{-\mathrm{a}}^{a}y\,\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}\,\mathrm{d}y = \big[y\,\Phi\big]_{\mathrm{y}=-\mathrm{a}}^{a} - \int_{-\mathrm{a}}^{a}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}y = -\int_{-\mathrm{a}}^{a}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}y\), since \(\Phi(\pm a, z) = 0\), and the same in \(z\). By theorem 4.9, \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A\), which is equation (16.23), here without theorem 16.16. Likewise \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{-\mathrm{a}}^{a}\big[\Phi\big]_{\mathrm{z}=-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\,\mathrm{d}y = 0\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\). The series converges uniformly, so we integrate it term by term. \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}(a^2 - y^2)\,\mathrm{d}A = 2b\cdot\frac{4a^3}{3} = \frac{8a^3b}{3}\).
  11.
