For a term, \(\int_{-\mathrm{a}}^{a}\cos\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y\,\mathrm{d}y = \frac{2\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} a)}{\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}} = \frac{4a}{n\pi}(-1)^{(n-1)/2}\) and \(\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}r_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}z = \frac{2\tanh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b)}{\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}} = \frac{4a}{n\pi}\tanh\frac{n\pi b}{2a}\). The product with \(c_{\mathrm{n}}\) is \(\frac{32a^2}{\pi^3n^3}\cdot\frac{16a^2}{\pi^2n^2}\tanh\frac{n\pi b}{2a} = \frac{512\,a^4}{\pi^5n^5}\tanh\frac{n\pi b}{2a}\), because \((-1)^{(n-1)} = 1\).
  12. So \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2G\alpha\big[\frac{8a^3b}{3} - \frac{512a^4}{\pi^5}\sum\frac{1}{n^5}\tanh\frac{n\pi b}{2a}\big] = G\alpha J\) with \(J\) from equation (16.31).

Source: SADD example 9.4 (PDF p. 262-265, equations (9.5.10) to (9.5.12)) and BARBER section 16.4 (PDF p. 258-259) give the same series and the same \(J\), SADD with other letters: his \(\phi\) is our \(\Phi\), his \(T\) our \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), his axes \(x\), \(y\) are our \(y\), \(z\). The proof through the sine series lemma and uniqueness is not from the sources.

The proof showed four things. Every term of the series is harmonic, so the Laplacian stayed the right one that the parabola gave. The boundary condition on the short sides is just the cosine expansion of the parabola, and because the coefficients fall like \(1/n^3\) the series dies out quickly in the interior. And integration by parts moved the torque from the derivatives onto \(\Phi\) itself, and we obtained it with the integral of the series. Since \(\Phi\) has no second derivatives at the corners, we showed equilibrium, the free side and uniqueness for the rectangle directly, with the same idea as in section 16.3.

Let us compute for the strip \(20 \times 40\) mm (num-05.py). The first term of the series in \(J\) is \(1{,}00000\) times \(33\,337{,}2\) mm\(^4\), the second is \(0{,}00413\) and the third \(0{,}00032\) times as much, which gives

\[J = 106\,666{,}7 - 33\,488{,}5 = 73\,178{,}1 \text{ mm}^4 ,\]

and \(G J = 5516{,}5\) N m\(^2\). Direct numerical integration gives the same, \(2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A = 73\,178{,}137\) mm\(^4\), and \(\nabla^2\Phi/(G\alpha) = -2{,}0000\) at three points (finite difference check). At \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m, \(\alpha = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(GJ) = 0{,}00906\) rad/m. So the number that chapter 12 took as given is now computed.

Let us see where the stress is.

We draw the boundary of the section and on it the level lines of \(\Phi\), like the contour lines of a map of a hill: each line joins points with the same value, at the lines \(30\), \(60\) and \(90\) there is a number. The summit \(91{,}10\) mm\(^2\) is at the centre. By lemma 16.20 the stress is tangent to the level line and its magnitude is \(|\nabla\Phi|\), so the closer the level lines the larger the stress. At the middle of the long side the level lines are closest, the stress is largest there, and it points along the side. At the middle of the short side the level lines are farther apart and the stress is smaller. At the corner the two sides meet at a right angle. There \(\Phi\) is zero on both sides, so both tangential derivatives vanish and by equation (16.19) both stress components are zero.

Corollary 16.31 Stresses on the boundary of the rectangle (napetosti na robu pravokotnika)

Under the conditions of theorem 16.30 the magnitude of the stress \(\tau = \sqrt{\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}^2}\) at the middle of the long side \((\pm a, 0)\) is

\[\tau(a, 0) = 2a\,G\alpha\Big[1 - \frac{8}{\pi^2}\sum_{\mathrm{n}\ \text{odd}}\frac{1}{n^2\cosh(n\pi b/2a)}\Big] = k_\tau\,\frac{M_{\mathrm{x}}}{J} , \qquad k_\tau = 2a\Big[1 - \frac{8}{\pi^2}\sum_{\mathrm{n}\ \text{odd}}\frac{1}{n^2\cosh(n\pi b/2a)}\Big] , \tag{16.32}\]

and the stress there is along the axis \(z\). At the corners \(\tau = 0\).

Proof

We must show the value of the derivative at one point and at the corners. We get the values by differentiating the series term by term, which the uniform convergence of theorem 16.30, item 1, allows.

  1. At the point \((a, 0)\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \partial\Phi/\partial z = 0\), because \(\partial_{\mathrm{z}}\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} z) = \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\sinh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} z) = 0\) at \(z = 0\).
  2. The component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\partial\Phi/\partial y = G\alpha\big[2y - \sum c_{\mathrm{n}}\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y)\,r_{\mathrm{n}}(z)\big]\). At \(y = a\) and \(z = 0\), \(\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} a) = (-1)^{(n-1)/2}\), so \(c_{\mathrm{n}}\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} a) = \frac{16a}{\pi^2n^2}\) and \(r_{\mathrm{n}}(0) = 1/\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b)\). With the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{n}\ \text{odd}}1/n^2 = \pi^2/8\) (lemma 16.29, step 5), \(2a = \frac{16a}{\pi^2}\sum\frac1{n^2}\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}(a, 0) = G\alpha\cdot 2a\big[1 - \frac{8}{\pi^2}\sum\frac{1}{n^2\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b)}\big]\).
  3. By theorem 16.30, item 2, \(G\alpha = M_{\mathrm{x}}/J\), which gives the second form.
  4. At the corner \((a, b)\), \(\Phi\) has a zero on both sides that meet there. The tangential derivative along the side \(y = a\) is \(\partial\Phi/\partial z = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) and along the side \(z = b\) it is \(\partial\Phi/\partial y = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\), since \(\Phi\) is zero on the boundary (theorem 16.30, item 1, continuous first derivatives on \(\bar S\)). Both stress components are therefore zero.

Source: SADD (9.5.13) (PDF p. 264-265) for the largest stress at the middle of the long side, ONATE2 figure 4.11 (PDF p. 201) the same with a fitted formula. The proof is not from the sources.

For the strip \(k_\tau = 18{,}601\) mm, or \(0{,}9301\) of \(2a\). At \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m,

\[\tau(a, 0) = \frac{50\,000 \text{ N mm}}{73\,178 \text{ mm}^4}\cdot 18{,}601 \text{ mm} = 12{,}71 \text{ MPa} ,\]

and ONATE2 with a fitted formula (\(J = 73\,242\) mm\(^4\), \(+0{,}09\) %) gives \(12{,}74\) MPa. At the middle of the short side \(\tau(0, b)/(G\alpha) = 14{,}79\) mm, which is \(0{,}795\) of the largest, or \(10{,}10\) MPa (num-05.py). At \(500\) N m the stress would be ten times larger, \(127{,}1\) MPa, above the shear yield by the Tresca criterion (\(110\) MPa), which is why we took \(50\) N m. That this value is the largest over the whole section is not proved. We checked it on a grid of \(41 \times 81\) points of a quarter of the section (the largest value at the middle of the long side, num-05.py, item 15), and SADD (PDF p. 264) and the membrane analogy (corollary 16.26: the largest slope of the membrane is at the edge nearest the centre) predict it.

Let us also see what happens if we treat the rectangle like a circle. This is the last try that lemma 16.6 works out: plane sections, so \(\psi = 0\) and \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}}\). For the strip \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = I_{\mathrm{y}} + I_{\mathrm{z}} = 26\,667 + 106\,667 = 133\,333\) mm\(^4\) (lemma 5.27) and at \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m the twist is \(\alpha = 4{,}97\cdot10^{-3}\) rad/m instead of \(9{,}06\cdot10^{-3}\) rad/m, a twist \(45{,}1\) % too small (conversely \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) is \(82{,}2\) % larger than \(J\) and the true twist \(82{,}2\) % larger). By the circle formula \(\tau = G\alpha r\) the stress would be \(3{,}75\) MPa at the middle of the long side (\(r = a\)) instead of \(12{,}71\) MPa, and \(8{,}39\) MPa at the corners (\(r = 22{,}36\) mm), where the true value is zero. It is wrong in two directions at once: too small where the stress is largest, and a stress where there is none. This is the same number the L-frame shows in figure 12.16: the twisting of the column contributes \(4{,}97\) mm instead of \(9{,}06\) mm to the displacement of the top, because the ratio is \(J/I_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}5488\). Why is \(J\) smaller than \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\)? Lemma 16.12 gives \(I_{\mathrm{p}} - J = \int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla\psi|^2\,\mathrm{d}A\) for \(\psi\) twice continuously differentiable on an open set containing \(S\). The warping of the rectangle is not so at the corners, so here we check the equality numerically. With the warping function of the lemma below the integral is \(60\,155{,}2\) mm\(^4\) (\(60 \times 60\) point quadrature, num-05.py), \(45{,}1\) % of \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\), which is exactly \(1 - J/I_{\mathrm{p}}\). Warping thus lets the section twist under a smaller torque than a section that stays plane would need.

We already have the warping function (definition 16.7), because the Prandtl function carries it. By lemma 16.8, \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \alpha(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z)\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \alpha(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y)\), and by Hooke's law \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = G\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) (theorem 3.11).

Lemma 16.32 Warping of the rectangular section (zvitje pravokotnega prereza)

Under the conditions of theorem 16.30 the warping function, determined up to an additive constant that is a rigid axial shift, is

\[\psi(y, z) = y z - \sum_{\mathrm{n}\ \text{odd}}c_{\mathrm{n}}\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y)\,\frac{\sinh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} z)}{\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b)} . \tag{16.33}\]

It is odd in \(y\) and in \(z\) (so zero on the axis \(y\) and on the axis \(z\)), harmonic in the interior, and \(\psi(a, b) = ab - \frac{32a^2}{\pi^3}\sum_{\mathrm{n}\ \text{odd}}\frac{1}{n^3}\tanh\frac{n\pi b}{2a}\).

Proof

We must show that the series satisfies the relation of stresses and warping. We compute the derivatives of the series term by term and compare them with \(\Phi\).

  1. From \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = G\alpha(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z) = \partial\Phi/\partial z\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\alpha(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y) = -\partial\Phi/\partial y\) it follows that \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = z + \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}/(G\alpha)\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = -y - \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}/(G\alpha)\).
  2. With the expressions for \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) (step 2 of theorem 16.30), \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = z - \sum c_{\mathrm{n}}\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y)\,\sinh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} z)/\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b)\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = y - \sum c_{\mathrm{n}}\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y)\,r_{\mathrm{n}}(z)\). Both series converge uniformly (the same terms as in the theorem, the bound \(|c_{\mathrm{n}}|\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\)).
  3. The function (16.33) has these two derivatives (lemma 14.25), so \(\psi\) is the warping function sought, up to a constant. It is odd in \(y\) (sine, \(y\)) and in \(z\) (\(\sinh\), \(z\)), so it is zero on both axes.
  4. The term \(\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} y)\sinh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} z)\) is harmonic like \(\cos\cosh\), and so is \(y z\), because \(\partial^2_{\mathrm{y}}(yz) = \partial^2_{\mathrm{z}}(yz) = 0\). We replace the second derivatives by the sums of derivatives of the terms on the band \(|z| \le b - \delta\) as in step 3 of theorem 16.30, so \(\nabla^2\psi = 0\).
  5. At \((a, b)\), \(\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} a) = (-1)^{(n-1)/2}\) and \(\sinh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b)/\cosh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b) = \tanh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b)\), so \(c_{\mathrm{n}}\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} a)\tanh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b) = \frac{32a^2}{\pi^3n^3}\tanh(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} b)\).

Source: SADD (9.5.14) (PDF p. 265) gives the displacement after integrating (9.3.5), with figure 9.13 (PDF p. 265) of contour lines. The proof through the relation of \(\psi\) and \(\Phi\) is not from the sources.

For the strip \(\psi(a, b) = 91{,}83\) mm\(^2\) and at \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m the axial displacement of the corner is \(\alpha\psi(a, b) = 0{,}832\) µm. This is very little: \(4{,}2\cdot10^{-5}\) of the section width \(2a\). The displacement is largest not at the corners but on the long side at \(z = \pm 16{,}63\) mm, where \(\psi = 105{,}1\) mm\(^2\), which is \(0{,}953\) µm (fine division of the side, num-05.py). Figure 16.21 shows what it looks like when we enlarge the displacement strongly.

On the left we draw the section and on it the axes on which \(\psi = 0\) (lemma 16.32, oddness). The axes divide it into four quarters. In the quarters with \(y z > 0\), \(\psi > 0\), the quarters where the term \(y z\) wins, and we mark them with the signs, in the others it is negative. In every quarter we draw level lines of \(\psi\). On the right we take the end of the bar, seen obliquely, with the axis \(x\) along the oblique axis. The undeformed section is dashed. The edge of the warped section lies now above the dashed rectangle, now below it, as \(\alpha\psi\) carries it, and the arrow from corner to corner shows the displacement along the axis \(x\): the corners \((a, b)\) and \((-a, -b)\) are in front, the corners \((a, -b)\) and \((-a, b)\) behind. The sections therefore do not stay plane, as we guessed for the circle.

For comparison let us take other ratios of the sides \(b/a\) at \(a = 10\) mm (num-05.py). At \(b/a = 1\) it is the square, \(J = 0{,}1406\,(2a)^4 = 22\,492\) mm\(^4\).

\(b/a\) \(J\) (mm\(^4\)) \(J/(2b\,(2a)^3)\) \(J/I_{\mathrm{p}}\) \(\tau(a, 0)/(2a\,G\alpha)\) \(\tau(a, 0)\) at \(50\) N m (MPa)
1 22 492 0,1406 0,8435 0,6753 30,02
2 73 178 0,2287 0,5488 0,9301 12,71
5 233 053 0,2913 0,1345 0,9994 4,29
10 499 720 0,3123 0,0371 1,0000 2,00

With a longer rectangle \(J/(2b\,(2a)^3)\) approaches \(1/3\) and \(\tau(a, 0)\) approaches \(2a\,G\alpha\), because the series in \(\tanh\) and \(1/\cosh\) gets smaller and smaller. This is the long strip treated in the next section, there with the limit and its error. For the square the warping is least pronounced, \(J/I_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}84\) is closest to \(1\), because the square is closest to the circle, where \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}}\).

The rectangle is now solved. The findings:

  • The torsion constant of the strip is \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\), which is \(0{,}549\,I_{\mathrm{p}}\), and this very computation explains the number of chapter 12 (figure 12.16).
  • The stress is largest at the middle of the long side (\(12{,}71\) MPa at \(50\) N m) and zero at the corners.
  • The section warps, the axial displacement is \(0{,}832\) µm at the corners and \(0{,}953\) µm at most.
  • The circle formula with plane sections is therefore wrong: \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) is \(82{,}2\) % larger than \(J\), and the stress \(3{,}75\) against \(12{,}71\) MPa.

For thin strips of length \(h\) and thickness \(t\) the series in \(J\) reduces to its first term, which leads to \(J \approx h t^3/3\). This is the subject of the section on thin sections, where we return to \(b/a \to \infty\) with a quantitative error.

16.6 Thin strips and open sections (tanki trakovi in odprti prerezi)

The frame of chapter 12 had a section of \(20 \times 40\) mm, a rectangle, and for its torsion constant \(J\) we took the series of theorem 16.30. Structures, however, are often built from thin sheet profiles: an angle, a channel, an I-beam, a turbine blade. Their section is not a rectangle, so the series cannot be inserted, and a new boundary problem for every profile would be too much work. The question of this section is whether the theorem for one rectangle gives a simple calculation for a profile made of several rectangles. The answer is yes if the walls are thin enough, and the section says how thin, with a number.

We begin with one wall. The section is the rectangle \(S = \{(y, z) : |y| \le a,\ |z| \le b\}\) of theorem 16.30, and we now call it a strip (trak): the thickness is \(t = 2a\) along \(y\), the length is \(h = 2b \ge t\) along \(z\). The letter \(t\) is the thickness here, since time does not appear in this chapter, and \(h\) is the length of the strip, not the height of the beam of chapter 5. The model is the torsion of a prism of definition 16.1: an isotropic linear elastic material, the axis \(x\) through the middle, twist per unit length \(\alpha\), and the section warps freely.

We draw the section, a narrow rectangle. We write its thickness \(2a\) and length \(2b\) as two measures, because the ratio \(h/t = b/a\) will decide. In it we place the axes: \(y\) across the thickness and \(z\) along the length. By theorem 16.16 the Prandtl function \(\Phi\) is the height of the membrane above the section (corollary 16.26), which is zero on the boundary and has \(\nabla^2\Phi = \Phi_{\mathrm{yy}} + \Phi_{\mathrm{zz}} = -2G\alpha\). What does the membrane do across the thickness? Let us first see what we get if along most of the length it did not depend on \(z\). Then \(\Phi_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\), so \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}} = -2G\alpha\), the solution of this equation is \(\Phi = -G\alpha\,y^2 + c_1 y + c_0\), and \(\Phi(\pm a) = 0\) gives \(c_1 = 0\), \(c_0 = G\alpha a^2\):

\[\Phi(y) = G\alpha\,(a^2 - y^2) . \tag{16.34}\]

This is the parabola below the section, with the vertex \(G\alpha a^2\) in the middle and zeros on the faces \(y = \pm a\).

Is the membrane really independent of \(z\)? The answer is in the series for the rectangle. From it \(\Phi(0, z)\) is computed on the right: in the middle it is \(0{,}9992\) of the value \(G\alpha a^2\), at \(z = 0{,}6\,b\) it is \(0{,}955\), at the end it drops to zero. The reason for the plateau is the harmonic correction in the series: the terms \(\cosh(n\pi z/t)/\cosh(n\pi h/(2t))\) at the distance \(d\) from the end fall as \(\mathrm e^{-n\pi d/t}\), the first term has the ratio \(32/\pi^3 = 1{,}03\), so at \(d = t\) the deviation is \(1{,}03\,\mathrm e^{-\pi} \approx 4{,}5\,\%\) and at \(d = 1{,}5\,t\) only \(0{,}9\,\%\), which the computed series confirms (\(0{,}955\) and \(0{,}991\)). The end of the strip where the plateau does not hold is thus about \(t\) long. At \(h = 5t\) the two ends take \(2t\) out of \(5t\), at \(h = 20t\) only \(2t\) out of \(20t\), so the guess from the parabola is the better the larger \(h/t\) is.

The stress follows from the function \(\Phi\). By lemma 16.20 the stress is tangent to the level lines of \(\Phi\) and has the magnitude \(|\nabla\Phi|\). The level lines of the parabola (16.34) are parallel to the axis \(z\), so the stress is parallel to \(z\) with the magnitude \(|\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}| = 2G\alpha|y|\): zero in the middle and \(G\alpha t\) on the faces. The direction comes from equation (16.19): \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} = 2G\alpha y\), so the arrows point to \(+z\) at \(y > 0\) and to \(-z\) at \(y < 0\). By lemma 5.9 this stress along the faces gives the moment \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 2G\alpha\cdot 2b\int_{-\mathrm{a}}^{a}y^2\,\mathrm{d}y = G\alpha\,ht^3/6\), but this is only half. The other half is carried by the flow that turns at the ends of the strip, where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} \ne 0\) and the parabola does not hold. The whole moment is given by theorem 16.16, \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A\), which includes the ends too, hence

\[M_{\mathrm{x}} \approx 2\,G\alpha\cdot 2b\int_{-\mathrm{a}}^{a}(a^2 - y^2)\,\mathrm{d}y = 4\,G\alpha\,b\cdot\frac{4a^3}{3} = G\alpha\,\frac{h\,t^3}{3} . \tag{16.35}\]

Comparison with \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = GJ\alpha\) gives \(J \approx ht^3/3\) and \(\tau \approx G\alpha t = M_{\mathrm{x}} t/J\) on the faces. This is the guess from the picture. The theorem says how well it holds.

Theorem 16.33 Thin strip (tanek trak)

Let the section be the strip \(S = \{|y| \le a,\ |z| \le b\}\) with thickness \(t = 2a\), length \(h = 2b \ge t\), and let \(\alpha\) be the twist per unit length as in theorem 16.30. Then:

  1. The torsion constant is
    \[J = \frac{h\,t^3}{3} - \frac{64\,t^4}{\pi^5}\sum_{\mathrm{n} = 1, 3, 5, \dots}\frac{1}{n^5}\tanh\frac{n\pi h}{2t} , \tag{16.36}\]
    and \(\Big(1 - 0{,}631\,\dfrac{t}{h}\Big)\dfrac{h\,t^3}{3} \le J < \dfrac{h\,t^3}{3}\).
  2. The shear stress at the middle of the longer face \((\pm a, 0)\) is \(\tau(\pm a, 0) = f\,G\alpha\,t\) with
    \[1 - \frac{1}{\cosh\dfrac{\pi h}{2t}} \le f < 1 , \tag{16.37}\]
    and therefore \(\tau(\pm a, 0) < M_{\mathrm{x}} t/J\).
Proof

We must show the two estimates for \(J\) and \(f\). Both follow from the series for the rectangle with two facts: \(\tanh\) lies between \(0\) and \(1\), and we can bound the sums \(\sum 1/n^5\) and \(\sum 1/n^2\) over odd \(n\).

  1. The series for \(J\) of theorem 16.30 has \(16a^3b/3 = ht^3/3\) and \(1024\,a^4 = 64\,t^4\) at \(a = t/2\), \(b = h/2\), which is equation (16.36).
  2. For \(x > 0\) we have \(\sinh x = (\mathrm e^{x} - \mathrm e^{-x})/2 > 0\), because the exponential function increases, and by lemma 9.42 (item 4 with \(a = 0\), \(b = 1\)) \(\cosh x - \sinh x = \mathrm e^{-x} > 0\). So \(0 < \sinh x < \cosh x\) and \(0 < \tanh x < 1\). Every term of the sum in (16.36) is therefore positive and smaller than \(1/n^5\), which gives \(J < ht^3/3\).
  3. Let \(S_5 = \sum_{\mathrm{n}\ \mathrm{odd}} 1/n^5\). The first three terms are \(1 + 1/243 + 1/3125 = 1{,}004435\). We estimate the remainder for \(n \ge 7\) with the decrease of the function \(x \mapsto x^{-5}\). On the interval \([n-2, n]\) we have \(x^{-5} \ge n^{-5}\), so by lemma 6.10 (items 2 and 3, for the nonnegative difference \(x^{-5} - n^{-5}\)) \(2\,n^{-5} \le \int_{\mathrm{n}-2}^{n}x^{-5}\,\mathrm{d}x\). The intervals \([5, 7], [7, 9], \dots\) do not overlap, so the sum over odd \(n \ge 7\) is at most \(\tfrac12\int_5^\infty x^{-5}\,\mathrm{d}x = 1/(8\cdot 5^4) = 0{,}0002\). So \(S_5 \le 1{,}004635\).
  4. Hence the sum in (16.36) is smaller than \(S_5\), and the correction in (16.36) is smaller than \(\dfrac{64\,t^4 S_5}{\pi^5} = \dfrac{192\,S_5}{\pi^5}\,\dfrac{t}{h}\cdot\dfrac{h\,t^3}{3}\). Numerically \(192\,S_5/\pi^5 \le 192\cdot 1{,}004635/306{,}0197 = 0{,}6303 < 0{,}631\), which gives the lower bound for \(J\).
  5. By corollary 16.31 the stress at the middle of the longer face is \(\tau(\pm a, 0) = 2a\,G\alpha\Big[1 - \dfrac{8}{\pi^2}\sum_{\mathrm{n}\ \mathrm{odd}}\dfrac{1}{n^2\cosh(n\pi b/2a)}\Big]\). With \(2a = t\) and \(b/a = h/t\) this is \(f\,G\alpha\,t\), where \(f = 1 - \dfrac{8}{\pi^2}\sum_{\mathrm{n}\ \mathrm{odd}}\dfrac{1}{n^2\cosh(n\pi h/(2t))}\).
  6. Every term of the sum is positive, so \(f < 1\). The function \(\cosh\) increases on \([0, \infty)\), because its derivative is \(\sinh \ge 0\) (lemma 9.42, items 1 and 3), so \(\cosh(n\pi h/(2t)) \ge \cosh(\pi h/(2t))\). With the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{n}\ \mathrm{odd}}1/n^2 = \pi^2/8\) (lemma 16.29, step 5) the sum in \(f\) is at most \(\dfrac{\pi^2}{8\cosh(\pi h/(2t))}\), so \(f \ge 1 - 1/\cosh(\pi h/(2t))\), which is the estimate (16.37).
  7. From \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = GJ\alpha\) we have \(G\alpha t = M_{\mathrm{x}} t/J\), so \(\tau(\pm a, 0) = f\,M_{\mathrm{x}} t/J < M_{\mathrm{x}} t/J\).

Source: Series and upper bound: SADD section 9.5, equation (9.5.12) (PDF p. 264) and (9.5.15) (PDF p. 266), BARBER section 16.4, equation (16.41) (PDF p. 258). The lower bound \(1 - 0{,}631\,t/h\) and the stress estimate from the function \(1/\cosh\) are not from the sources, the computation is in num-06.py. That the stress at the middle of the longer face is the largest in the section is cited from SADD (9.5.13) (PDF p. 264-265) and visible from the membrane in section 16.4, it is not proved here.

How good is the bound? The table and figure 16.23 show that the ratio \(J/(ht^3/3)\) and the lower bound of theorem 16.33 nearly agree already at \(h/t = 5\).

We draw the axis \(h/t\) and on it the ratio \(J/(ht^3/3)\), which by theorem 16.33 is below \(1\). The curve is the ratio computed with the series. The bound \(1 - 0{,}631\,t/h\) lies below it, but only slightly, because at \(h/t \ge 5\) every \(\tanh(n\pi h/(2t))\) is larger than \(1 - 10^{-6}\) (the smallest is at \(n = 1\)) and the sum of equation (16.36) hardly differs from \(S_5\). The four points are examples: \(h/t = 1\), \(2\), \(5\), \(10\) with the ratios \(0{,}42\), \(0{,}69\), \(0{,}87\), \(0{,}94\). The constant \(J\) is certainly at least \(95\,\%\) of the thin value \(ht^3/3\) only for \(h/t \ge 12{,}7\) (the threshold): the bound \(1 - 0{,}631\,t/h = 0{,}95\) gives \(h/t = 12{,}62\), rounded up \(12{,}7\). The thin value is then at most \(1/0{,}95 = 1{,}053\) times \(J\), so at most \(5{,}3\,\%\) too large. For \(J\) to be at least \(99\,\%\) of the thin value we need \(h/t \ge 64\).

The thin value thus fails exactly for the sections we know. The square \(20 \times 20\) mm has by the series \(J = 22\,492\) mm\(^4\), while the formula \(ht^3/3\) gives \(53\,333\) mm\(^4\), \(2{,}4\) times too much. At \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m this means a twist of \(0{,}0124\) rad/m instead of \(0{,}0295\) rad/m. The strip \(20 \times 40\) mm of chapter 12 (\(h/t = 2\)) has \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\) against \(106\,667\) mm\(^4\), so \(0{,}69\): the twist would be \(0{,}00622\) rad/m instead of \(0{,}00906\) rad/m. The stress \(M_{\mathrm{x}} t/J\) at \(50\) N m is \(13{,}67\) MPa with the true \(J\) and \(9{,}38\) MPa with the thin value, the exact stress of the theorem is \(f\,G\alpha t = 0{,}930\cdot 13{,}67 = 12{,}71\) MPa. The thin value for \(J\) thus underestimates the stress by \(26\,\%\), while the formula \(M_{\mathrm{x}} t/J\) with the true \(J\) overestimates it by \(7{,}5\,\%\) (\(1/f = 1{,}075\)). The conclusion: for a strip with \(h/t < 12{,}7\) we use the series, and for \(h/t \ge 12{,}7\) the thin calculation, for which \(J\) is at least \(95\,\%\) of the value \(ht^3/3\).

Now a profile made of several strips.

Take a channel of sheet metal, measured along the mean lines: the web is \(h_1 = 40\) mm long, the flanges \(h_2 = h_3 = 20\) mm, the thickness is \(t = 2\) mm everywhere. The mean line of the section is a curve without a loop and the section has no hole: such a section is called open (odprt prerez). If we cut it into three strips \(h_{\mathrm{i}} \times t\), each has \(h_{\mathrm{i}}/t = 20\) or \(10\). By theorem 16.33 the ratio \(J_{\mathrm{i}}/(h_{\mathrm{i}}t^3/3)\) is at least \(0{,}968\) at \(h_{\mathrm{i}}/t = 20\) and at least \(0{,}936\) at \(h_{\mathrm{i}}/t = 10\). Let us therefore try to treat each strip as if it were alone. A slit tube with \(r_{\mathrm{m}} = 18\) mm and \(t = 4\) mm is likewise one strip, only bent: we unroll it into a strip of length \(\ell = 2\pi r_{\mathrm{m}}\), because BARBER (PDF p. 256) takes a mean line of arbitrary shape as long as the thickness varies slowly along it. At \(t/r_{\mathrm{m}} = 0{,}22\) the curvature is not negligible, so the calculation is poorer here.

Corollary 16.34 Open section of thin strips (odprt prerez iz tankih trakov)

Let the section consist of strips \(S_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(i = 1, \dots, N\), with thicknesses \(t_{\mathrm{i}}\) and mean-line lengths \(h_{\mathrm{i}} \ge t_{\mathrm{i}}\), each with \(h_{\mathrm{i}}/t_{\mathrm{i}}\) large enough for theorem 16.33. Let (H) be: on the whole strip \(S_{\mathrm{i}}\) the Prandtl function equals the parabola of the isolated strip, \(G\alpha(t_{\mathrm{i}}^2/4 - n_{\mathrm{i}}^2)\), where \(n_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the distance from the mean line of strip \(i\). (H) is an approximation that neglects the bands at the junctions of the strips and at the free ends, where the parabola does not hold. Then, approximately:

  1. \(J \approx \displaystyle\sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{N}\frac{h_{\mathrm{i}}\,t_{\mathrm{i}}^3}{3}\).
  2. All strips have the same \(\alpha\), strip \(i\) carries the share \(M_{\mathrm{i}}/M_{\mathrm{x}} = h_{\mathrm{i}}t_{\mathrm{i}}^3/\sum_{\mathrm{j}} h_{\mathrm{j}}t_{\mathrm{j}}^3\) of the moment, where \(M_{\mathrm{i}} = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{i}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A\) is its part of the integral of theorem 16.16, and has on its faces the stress \(\tau_{\mathrm{i}} \approx G\alpha\,t_{\mathrm{i}} = M_{\mathrm{x}} t_{\mathrm{i}}/J\). Away from the junctions and the free ends the stress is largest in the thickest strip. At a sharp re-entrant corner of a junction the stress is unbounded (source below).
  3. For a variable thickness \(t(s)\) along the mean line of length \(\ell\) we have \(J \approx \tfrac13\int_0^\ell t(s)^3\,\mathrm{d}s\) (without proof).
Proof

We must show that (H) and theorem 16.33 give items 1 and 2. Item 3 is quoted, not proved.

  1. By theorem 16.16 \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A\). The integral over \(S\) is the sum of the integrals over the strips (additivity of the integral), and by (H) the integral over strip \(i\) is the integral of the parabola of the isolated strip, which by equation (16.35) equals \(G\alpha\,h_{\mathrm{i}}t_{\mathrm{i}}^3/6\) (half of \(2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A\)), so \(M_{\mathrm{x}} \approx G\alpha\sum_{\mathrm{i}} h_{\mathrm{i}}t_{\mathrm{i}}^3/3\). Comparison with \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = GJ\alpha\) gives item 1.
  2. The section turns as a whole (definition 16.1), so \(\alpha\) is the same for all strips. The share of the strip \(M_{\mathrm{i}} = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{i}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A\) is by (H) and equation (16.35) equal to \(G\alpha\,h_{\mathrm{i}}t_{\mathrm{i}}^3/3\), which after division by \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) gives the share. By equation (16.34) the stress on the faces is \(G\alpha t_{\mathrm{i}}\), which is \(M_{\mathrm{x}} t_{\mathrm{i}}/J\) because \(G\alpha = M_{\mathrm{x}}/J\), and it is largest at the largest \(t_{\mathrm{i}}\).

Source: BARBER section 16.3, equations (16.33) to (16.39) (PDF p. 256-257): item 3 is there too, and the remark that the stresses at re-entrant corners are unbounded if the corner is sharp (PDF p. 256). SADD section 9.5, equations (9.5.15) and (9.5.16) (PDF p. 266). SADD says there that the largest stress is estimated with the narrowest rectangle, which is an error: \(\tau_{\mathrm{i}} = 2\mu\alpha a_{\mathrm{i}}\) by (9.5.15) grows with the thickness, so it is largest in the thickest strip, as BARBER says (PDF p. 257). The proof from (H) is not from the sources. ONATE2 section 4.10.7 (PDF p. 241-242) also treats the case of restrained warping, which we do not treat here.

We shall check the hypothesis (H) on an example, because we do not prove it here: the junctions of the strips and the free ends cannot be estimated with theorem 16.33.

Example 16.35 Steel channel and slit tube (jeklen U-profil in razrezana cev)

For the channel of figure 16.24 with \(G = 75{,}385\) GPa and \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 6{,}25\) N m:

  1. The sum over the three strips is \(J \approx (40 + 20 + 20)\cdot 2^3/3 = 213{,}3\) mm\(^4\) by item 1 of corollary 16.34, so \(GJ = 16{,}08\) N m\(^2\).
  2. \(\alpha = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(GJ) = 0{,}3886\) rad/m, which is \(22{,}3\,^\circ\)/m.
  3. The share of the web is \(40/80 = 50\,\%\), of each flange \(25\,\%\), so \(3{,}125\) N m and \(1{,}563\) N m each.
  4. The stress in all strips is \(M_{\mathrm{x}} t/J = 6250\cdot 2/213{,}3 = 58{,}6\) MPa, because \(t\) is the same everywhere. This is below the shear yield limit of steel, \(110\) MPa by the Tresca criterion.

Let us check (H). We solved the Prandtl equation for the channel with its outer outline (\(42 \times 21\) mm: the web \(2 \times 42\) mm, the flanges of thickness \(2\) mm reach from the outer face of the web to \(20\) mm from the mean line of the web) on a mesh (finite differences): at the step \(0{,}125\), \(0{,}1\) and \(0{,}0625\) mm we get \(J = 211{,}3\), \(211{,}6\) and \(212{,}0\) mm\(^4\). The value still grows, but slowly, and for the step going to zero we estimate \(J \approx 212{,}3\) mm\(^4\). The thin sum \(213{,}3\) mm\(^4\) is thus \(0{,}5\,\%\) larger than the exact value. This is the error of (H), which neglects the ends and the junctions. The stress at the junctions of the flanges and the web, however, the thin calculation does not capture: a sharp corner has by BARBER (PDF p. 256) an unbounded stress, in a real profile a fillet limits it, but by how much we do not compute here. The slit tube has by item 3 of corollary 16.34 with \(t = 4\) mm the constant \(J \approx \ell t^3/3 = 2412{,}7\) mm\(^4\). At \(50\) N m we get \(\alpha = 0{,}2749\) rad/m and \(\tau = M_{\mathrm{x}} t/J = 82{,}9\) MPa. At \(t/r_{\mathrm{m}} = 0{,}22\) this is an estimate that we do not trust to three digits.

Open sections are thus very soft in torsion: \(J\) is proportional to \(t^3\). Whether the same strip in a different shape, without the slit, would resist the twist more, we shall check in the section on hollow sections. For the channel, however, another question arises: through which point must the shear force pass so that the section does not twist. The answer is in the next section.

16.7 Shear centre (strižno središče)

The section on thin strips ended with a channel, where a question came up: through which point must a transverse force pass so that the section does not twist? Chapter 5 took the force to act in a plane of symmetry of the section for bending, and promised the shear centre for other sections. Chapter 12 claimed that for a section with two axes of symmetry the centroid is also the shear centre, and postponed the explanation to this chapter. The guess is natural: we bend a beam with a force through the centroid, so the centroid should be the right point. This section shows that the guess is right for the rectangle and wrong for the channel, and finds the right point with a number.

First let us say what we look for. The prism of definition 16.1 can also carry a transverse force \(V\) that is the same in every section, for example a force at the free end of a cantilever. Its line of action \(\ell\) can be put anywhere parallel to the axis \(y\) or \(z\). What happens to the section depends on the position of \(\ell\): when \(\ell\) passes by a certain point, the section twists as well as bends.

Definition 16.36 Shear centre (strižno središče)

Let a prism with the axis \(x\) through the centroids of the sections, as in chapter 5, be clamped at one end and loaded at the other with a transverse force \(V\) along the axis \(y\) or the axis \(z\) in the plane of the section. The shear centre of the section is the point \(S\) in the plane of the section with the property that a force whose line of action passes through \(S\) does not twist the section, for a force in the direction \(y\) and for a force in the direction \(z\). That the section at \(x\) does not twist means that the mean rotation of the section about the axis \(x\)

\[\bar\theta(x) = \frac1A\int_{\mathrm{A}} \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z}\Big)\mathrm{d}A = -\frac1A\int_{\mathrm{A}} \omega_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\mathrm{d}A \tag{16.38}\]

is zero, where \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}}\) is an element of the small rotation tensor of definition 1.116 and \(A\) the area of the section. In the torsion of a prism of definition 16.1 \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -\alpha xz\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = \alpha xy\), so \(\bar\theta(x) = \alpha x\), and the condition means \(\alpha = 0\).

Source: ONATE2 section 4.2.6, equations (4.17) and (4.18) (PDF p. 189) and section 4.2.7 (PDF p. 190-191), SADD section 9.8, equation (9.8.21) and the text after it, where SADD also calls the point the centre of flexure (PDF p. 277). The existence of the point \(S\) for a general section is taken from the sources and not proved. The letter \(S\) is a point in this section, not the section as a set, so the section is named in words. The point about which the section turns in torsion is, by ONATE2 (PDF p. 191), the elastic axis through \(S\), the equality of the two points is cited here and not proved.

The point \(S\) depends only on the shape of the section, not on the size of the force, and it can be computed from equilibrium without solving Prandtl's equation. How, the following consideration shows.

Let the section be thin and open, made of rectangular walls of thickness \(t\), like the channel of section 16.6. We split the transverse force \(V\) as in chapter 5: from the moment \(M(x)\) we have a longitudinal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) that changes along the axis, and a piece of the beam is in equilibrium only if a shear stress on the cut holds it. Jourawski's theorem 5.39 did this for a horizontal cut across a section with a plane of symmetry. Here we cut across a wall, which can be a flange, so the cut has another direction, and the section has no plane of symmetry \(x\)-\(y\). The theorem therefore does not cover our cut, and we must repeat the same consideration, which is the lemma on the shear flow. We take the second moment \(I\) about the axis \(z\) through the centroid of the section and require that the product moment \(\int yz\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), which for our profiles the symmetry about the axis \(z\) ensures. Then for bending in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) we still have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -My/I\) as in theorem 5.35, since the theorem needs only that \(y\) and \(z\) are principal axes. Chapter 5 proves this for a section with symmetry about the axis \(y\). For a section with the other axis of symmetry we take the statement from ONATE2 (equations (4.12) to (4.14), PDF p. 189) and do not prove it.

A cut across a wall is not unique, so first let us say what we measure. The mean line \(s\) of a wall is the straight or broken line along the middle of the walls, the beginning \(s = 0\) is at the free end of the wall. The cut is the plane that crosses the wall perpendicular to the mean line at \(s\) and separates from the section the part \(A^*(s)\) between the free end and the cut. We denote

\[Q(s) = \int_{\mathrm{A}^*(\mathrm{s})} y\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{16.39}\]

This is the first moment of a partial area of definition 5.38, only that we now measure it on the part bounded by a cut across a wall. The letter \(Q\) is used by SADD and EP, in this book the same thing is \(S\), but the letter \(S\) is the shear centre in this section. The shear flow (strižni tok) is the integral of the component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xs}}\) across the thickness of the wall, \(f(s) = \int \sigma_{\mathrm{xs}}\,\mathrm{d}n\), where \(\hat s\) is the tangent to the mean line in the direction of increasing \(s\) and \(n\) the distance from the mean line. On the cut, \(f\) is the force in the direction \(x\) per unit length of the axis with which the wall beyond the cut acts on the part \(A^*(s)\). Since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{sx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xs}}\) (theorem 2.36), the same \(f\) is, in the section, the force in the direction \(\hat s\) per unit length of the mean line.

Lemma 16.37 Shear flow in a thin wall (strižni tok v tanki steni)

Let a prism have the axis \(x\) through the centroids of the sections, let the section be made of walls whose lateral faces are free, let \(\int y\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\) and \(\int yz\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\) and \(I = \int y^2\,\mathrm{d}A\). Let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -My/I\) of theorem 5.35 hold, let the transverse force \(V\) be in the direction \(y\), the load without a component in the direction \(x\) (\(q_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), \(N = 0\)), and the stress continuous in \(x\). Then the shear flow in every wall at \(s\) is

\[f(s) = -\frac{V\,Q(s)}{I} . \tag{16.40}\]

The flow points toward the free end of the wall when \(V\,Q > 0\).

Idea

The part of the piece of the beam between two sections that lies beyond the cut across the wall is in equilibrium. What the longitudinal stresses on its faces do not balance, the shear flow on the cut must balance. The calculation is the same as for theorem 5.39, only that the cut is not horizontal.

Proof

We must show equation (16.40). We write the equilibrium of forces in the direction \(x\) for the part beyond the cut and divide by \(\Delta x\).

  1. Let \(P\) be the part of the slice between the sections \(x\) and \(x + \Delta x\) with the cross-section \(A^*(s)\). It is a part of a body in equilibrium, so by definition 2.3 the sum of forces on it is zero. The force on a face is the stress vector multiplied by the area, by Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.24).
  2. The faces of \(P\) are the right one at \(x + \Delta x\) with the normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), the left one at \(x\) with the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), the cut with the normal \(\hat s\) (it points from \(P\) into the wall toward larger \(s\)) and the free lateral faces of the wall, on which the stress vector is zero. The load has no component \(x\), so the remaining terms in the direction \(x\) vanish.
  3. The component \(x\) of the stress vector is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) on the right and left faces and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{sx}}\) on the cut. So
    \[N^*(x + \Delta x) - N^*(x) + \int_{\mathrm{x}}^{x + \Delta x}\! f(\xi, s)\,\mathrm{d}\xi = 0 , \qquad N^*(x) = \int_{\mathrm{A}^*(\mathrm{s})}\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}A ,\]
    where by the symmetry of stress (theorem 2.36) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{sx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xs}}\), and the inner integral across the thickness is \(f\).
  4. We divide by \(\Delta x\) and take \(\Delta x \to 0\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40, item 2) and the continuity of the stress, \(N^*\) is differentiable and \((N^*)'(x) = -f(x, s)\).
  5. We insert \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -My/I\). The section does not change along the axis, so \(N^*(x) = -M(x)\,Q(s)/I\) and \((N^*)' = -M'\,Q/I\).
  6. By corollary 5.11 \(M' = -V\), so \((N^*)' = V\,Q/I\). From steps 4 and 6, \(f = -V\,Q/I\).
Explanation

There is no assumption of uniformity across the thickness, since the flow \(f\) by definition already integrates across the thickness. In the torsion of a thin wall a stress appears that is odd across the thickness (equation (16.34), the stress \(2G\alpha|y|\) with the sign of \(y\)). Its integral across the thickness is zero, so torsion contributes nothing to the flow \(f\), and equation (16.40) holds for the whole stress field, also when the section twists at the same time, since there is no longitudinal stress in torsion. In the thin model we take that the field of flows alone does not twist the section and that the twist is caused only by the torsional part, which is odd across the thickness. This is an assumption (idealization) of this section, the lemma does not prove it.

Source: SADD (D.9) (PDF p. 579-580) for a horizontal cut, ONATE2 (PDF p. 190) says that the shear stresses for a general section are computed by the procedure of appendix D. The proof is an extension of the proof of theorem 5.39 to a cut across a wall and is not from a source. The sign follows from the convention for \(V\) of chapter 5.

We test the lemma on the channel of example 16.35, that is, on a profile with mean lines of height \(h = 40\) mm (the web) and length \(b = 20\) mm (the flanges), thickness \(t = 2\) mm and force \(V = 500\) N in the direction \(y\). Let us draw it.

We draw the section, the letter U made of three rectangles, and in it the axes: \(y\) up along the web, \(z\) to the right along the flanges, with the origin at the centroid \(C\). The centroid lies, by the centroid of a composite figure (definition 5.21), at the distance \(z_{\mathrm{C}} = 2\,(b\,t)(b/2)/\big(t\,(h + 2b)\big) = b^2/(h + 2b) = 5{,}00\) mm from the mean line of the web, because the two flanges together have the area \(2bt\) with the centroid at \(b/2\) and the section has the area \(t\,(h + 2b)\). The second moment is, by theorem 5.28 (only the Steiner term, the own moment of a flange \(bt^3/12\) is \(0{,}06\,\%\) of the contribution),

\[I = \frac{t\,h^3}{12} + 2\,b\,t\left(\frac h2\right)^2 = \frac{t\,h^2\,(h + 6b)}{12} = 42\,667\ \text{mm}^4 . \tag{16.41}\]

The thin model replaces the section with the mean lines and ignores the overlap in the corners. The real section with the same mean lines has the outline \(42 \times 21\) mm (web \(2 \times 42\) mm, flanges \(19 \times 2\) mm from the face of the web on the side of the flanges to \(z = 20\) mm from its mean line) and the area \(160\) mm\(^2\). Its second moment is \(I = 2\cdot 42^3/12 + 2\cdot 19\,(21^3 - 19^3)/3 = 42\,773\) mm\(^4\), so the thin value is \(0{,}25\,\%\) smaller.

For a cut in the upper flange at the distance \(s\) from the free end, by definition (16.39) the part \(A^*\) is the rectangle \(t \times s\) with the centroid at the height \(h/2\), so \(Q = t\,s\,h/2\) and by lemma 16.37

\[f(s) = -\frac{V\,t\,h}{2I}\,s .\]

The flow in the upper flange is linear: zero at the free end and \(9{,}38\) N/mm (\(4{,}69\) MPa) at the web, since \(V\,t\,h\,b/(2I) = 500\cdot 2\cdot 40\cdot 20/(2\cdot 42\,667)\). The sign is minus, so it points toward the free end, in the figure from the web outward (\(+z\)) at \(V > 0\). For the lower flange \(y = -h/2\) and \(Q\) has the opposite sign, so it is the same triangle, and the flow points toward the web (\(-z\)). At the web the part \(A^*(y_0)\) is the upper flange and the part of the web above \(y_0\), so \(Q = b\,t\,h/2 + t\,(h^2/4 - y_0^2)/2\), which is \(800\) mm\(^3\) at the junction and \(1200\) mm\(^3\) in the middle. The flow there is \(V\,Q/I = 9{,}38\) and \(14{,}06\) N/mm and points up, because in the web the tangent \(\hat s\) points down. The stress in the middle of the web is \(14{,}06/2 = 7{,}03\) MPa. At the junction the flow continues from the web into the flange with the same value \(9{,}38\) N/mm.

Where does the sum of the flows point? We draw from the profile only the mean lines, because they carry the flows, and put the resultant of a flow on each. In a flange it is \(F = \int_0^b |f|\,\mathrm{d}s = V\,t\,h\,b^2/(4I) = 93{,}75\) N on a line parallel to \(z\) (for a linear flow the point of application is at \(b/3\) from the web). In the web the resultant is

\[\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2}\frac{V}{I}\Big(\frac{b\,t\,h}{2} + \frac{t\,(h^2/4 - y^2)}{2}\Big)\mathrm{d}y = \frac{V}{I}\cdot\frac{t\,h^2\,(h + 6b)}{12} = V ,\]

which by equation (16.41) is indeed \(V = 500{,}000\) N: the flows give exactly the transverse force. The flanges point in opposite directions at the heights \(\pm h/2\), so they are a couple with the moment \(F\,h\) about the axis \(x\) through the mean line of the web, and the web with the arm zero contributes nothing. The total moment of the flows is \(93{,}75\cdot 40 = 3750\) N mm.

The flows are therefore statically equivalent to one force \(V\) in the direction \(y\) on a line at the distance \(e\) from the mean line of the web. The moment of a force \(V\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) about \(x\) on a line with the coordinate \(z_\ell\) is, by the definition of the moment (lemma 5.9, \(\int(y\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} - z\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\,\mathrm{d}A\)), equal to \(-V\,(z_\ell - z_{\mathrm{w}})\) with respect to the mean line of the web \(z = z_{\mathrm{w}}\), and this must be \(F\,h\). So \(z_\ell = z_{\mathrm{w}} - F\,h/V\): the line lies on the side of the web that is opposite to the flanges.

Theorem 16.38 Shear centre of a channel (strižno središče U-profila)

Let the section be a thin channel with mean lines: a web of height \(h\), flanges of length \(b\), thickness \(t\) everywhere, \(t \ll b\) and \(t \ll h\), symmetric about the axis \(z\) through the centroid. Let the section follow the thin model and lemma 16.37. Then a transverse force in the direction \(y\) does not twist the section if it acts on a line parallel to \(y\) at the distance

\[e = \frac{3\,b^2}{h + 6\,b} \tag{16.42}\]

from the mean line of the web, on the side opposite to the flanges, and the shear centre \(S\) lies on the axis of symmetry \(z\) through the centroid \(C\). The centroid is at the distance \(z_{\mathrm{C}} = b^2/(h + 2b)\) from the mean line of the web on the side of the flanges, so \(S \ne C\) and the distance is \(e + z_{\mathrm{C}}\). For \(h = 40\) mm, \(b = 20\) mm, \(t = 2\) mm, \(e = 7{,}50\) mm, \(z_{\mathrm{C}} = 5{,}00\) mm and the distance is \(12{,}50\) mm.

Idea

The flow in the flanges gives a couple that the web does not have. The line on which one force \(V\) with the same moment acts is where the resultant of the flows is.

Proof

We must show that the line of the resultant of the flows is at the distance \(e\) of equation (16.42) and that this is the line for which there is no twist.

  1. The second moment of equation (16.41) is \(I = t\,h^2\,(h + 6b)/12\).
  2. In a flange, by lemma 16.37, the flow is \(|f| = V\,t\,h\,s/(2I)\) and the force \(F = V\,t\,h\,b^2/(4I)\), and in the web \(\int f\,\mathrm{d}y = V\) by the calculation above.
  3. The moment of the flows about the mean line of the web is \(F\,h\) (the couple of the flanges), since the web contributes nothing.
  4. A force \(V\) on a line at the distance \(e\) from the mean line of the web has the same moment \(V\,e\), so \(e = F\,h/V = t\,h^2\,b^2/(4I) = 3b^2/(h + 6b)\) by step 1.
  5. The section is symmetric about the axis \(z\), so (lemma 16.40 below) \(S\) lies on the axis \(z\), that is at the height \(y = 0\).
  6. The centroid: \(z_{\mathrm{C}} = b^2/(h + 2b)\) by the calculation above. For the given numbers \(e = 1200/160 = 7{,}50\) mm and \(z_{\mathrm{C}} = 400/80 = 5{,}00\) mm.
  7. The moment of the load about the axis \(x\) is the sum of the moment of the flows and the moment of the torsional part of the field, which is odd across the thickness. By the thin model of the explanation after lemma 16.37 the flows alone do not twist the section, the twist is caused only by the torsional part. This part carries the moment of the load minus the moment of the flows. If the force acts on the line of step 4, this difference is zero, the torsional part has the moment zero and by theorem 16.10 (\(M_{\mathrm{x}} = G\,J\,\alpha\)) its \(\alpha = 0\). The mean rotation of the section (16.38) is therefore zero, and by definition 16.36 this is the line through \(S\).
Explanation

The shear centre lies outside the profile, on the side of the web opposite to the flanges, at \(e = 7{,}50\) mm from the mean line of the web and \(12{,}50\) mm from the centroid. The same position is given by ONATE2 in figure 4.6 (PDF p. 190), which for a profile with thin walls gives the distance \(CA = 3b^2/(h + 6b)\) from the centre to the mean line of the web and \(AO = b^2/(h + 2b)\) from it to the centroid, which is the same as equation (16.42) and \(z_{\mathrm{C}}\) (the difference is zero in SymPy).

Source: ONATE2 section 4.2.6 and figure 4.6 (PDF p. 189-190). SADD section 9.8 (PDF p. 277) says that the centre does not necessarily fall into the section. Steps 2 to 4 are a calculation by the lemma and not a source. The error of the thin model is estimated only for \(I\), as \(0{,}25\,\%\) from the real section. For \(e\) we do not compute it, since in the real section both \(I\) and the force \(F\) in a flange change.

In the figure the force \(V\) on the line through \(S\) is drawn on the right as a vertical line at the distance \(e\) from the mean line of the web and the dimensions \(e\) and \(h\) measure the distances. This force is statically equivalent to the sum of the resultants in the flanges and the resultant in the web: the same force, the same moment.

And a force that does not act on this line? The definition says only that there is no twist if it passes through \(S\), and not how large the twist is otherwise.

Lemma 16.39 An offset force twists the section (izmaknjena sila zasuka prerez)

Let the transverse force \(V\) be in the direction \(y\) and let the line of its action \(\ell\) be parallel to the line \(\ell_{\mathrm{S}}\) through \(S\) and at the distance \(d\) from it. Then the stress field is the sum of the field for the force through \(S\) and the field of the torsion of a prism (definition 16.1) with the moment \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = V\,d\) about the axis through \(S\). The twist per unit length is \(\alpha = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(GJ)\) with \(J\) from theorem 16.10.

Proof

We must show that the difference of the two loadings gives the torsion of a prism.

  1. The loadings differ statically only by a couple: the force \(V\) on \(\ell\) and the force \(V\) on \(\ell_{\mathrm{S}}\) have the same resultant, and their moments about the axis \(x\) differ by \(V\,d\).
  2. For the force on \(\ell_{\mathrm{S}}\) the mean rotation of the section (16.38) is zero by definition 16.36. Elasticity is linear, so the field for \(\ell\) is the sum of this field and the field for the difference of the loadings, which is a couple with the moment \(V\,d\) at the end and nothing elsewhere.
  3. The difference of the loadings at the end has the resultant zero and the moment \(V\,d\) about the axis \(x\), so it is a torsional loading of definition 16.1. The exact field differs from the field of torsion only near the ends by Saint-Venant's principle (section 11.11), so far from the ends the field of the difference is torsion with \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = V\,d\). For thin open sections the zone at the clamp is long, because the warping is restrained there and the twist rate varies along the axis (ONATE2 section 4.10, PDF p. 227). We do not compute its length here.
  4. By theorem 16.10 \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = G\,J\,\alpha\), which gives \(\alpha\).

Source: ONATE2 section 4.2.7 (PDF p. 190-191): external forces at an arbitrary point \(D\) are equivalent to forces through the shear centre and a torque about the elastic axis. Saint-Venant's principle is cited from chapter 11 and is not proved.

The lemma tells how large the twist is: \(\alpha = V\,d/(GJ)\), proportional to the force and to the distance \(d\) from \(S\).

A thin wall carries bending and torsion each in its own way. The lemma gives only the integral \(f\) of the flow across the thickness. In the thin model we take the stress from the flow to be uniform across the thickness and equal to \(f/t\), as it is uniform across the width in theorem 5.39. The torsional one is odd across the thickness and largest on the faces, \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\,t/J\) (theorem 16.33). Both are parallel to the wall, so on one face they add and on the other they subtract, and the largest total stress is their sum.

16.7.1 When the centroid is the shear centre

Where do the centroid and the shear centre coincide? A consideration of symmetry answers this without computing flows.

Lemma 16.40 Symmetry and the shear centre (simetrija in strižno središče)

Let the prism be isotropic, linearly elastic, clamped at one end and loaded at the other. Let the section be symmetric about the axis \(y\), that is about the reflection \(z \mapsto -z\), and let the transverse force \(V\) be in the direction \(y\) with such a distribution of forces at the end that it is symmetric about this reflection. Then the stress field is symmetric: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(y, -z) = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(y, z)\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}(y, -z) = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}(y, z)\). The moment of these stresses about the centroid is zero, the line of the force \(V\) is the axis \(y\) and the section does not twist. Therefore:

  1. For a section with the axis of symmetry \(y\) the line of the force in the direction \(y\) without twist lies on the axis \(y\). For a section with the axis of symmetry \(z\) the line of the force in the direction \(z\) without twist lies on the axis \(z\).
  2. For a section with both axes of symmetry both lines are the axes of symmetry and the shear centre is their intersection, that is the centroid of the section.
  3. For a section with one axis of symmetry \(S\) lies on this axis.
Proof

We must show that the solution is symmetric and that the moment about the centroid is zero.

  1. The reflection \(R: (x, y, z) \mapsto (x, y, -z)\) maps the body onto itself, because the section is symmetric. If \(\vek u\) is a solution, \(\vek u^R(\vek r) = R\,\vek u(R\vek r)\) is a solution for the reflected data, because Hooke's law of an isotropic material (theorem 3.11) does not choose a direction.
  2. The data are symmetric: the clamping is zero, the load is symmetric by assumption. So the reflected data equal the original ones.
  3. By uniqueness (theorem 11.4, item 1) \(\vek u\) and \(\vek u^R\) have the same stresses. The clamped end admits only the rigid displacement zero, so by item 3 of the same theorem the displacements are equal too, \(\vek u^R = \vek u\). The components of stress transform under \(R\) as \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^R(y, z) = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(y, -z)\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}^R(y, z) = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}(y, -z)\). The equality gives the symmetry of the lemma.
  4. The moment about the axis \(x\) through the centroid is \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = \int_{\mathrm{A}} (y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} - z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\,\mathrm{d}A\). With \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) odd in \(z\), \(y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) is odd in \(z\), with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) even in \(z\), \(z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is odd in \(z\). The section is symmetric in \(z\), so both integrals are zero (lemma 5.24 for the centroid, the integral of an odd function over a symmetric region). So \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\).
  5. A force \(V\) on a line with the coordinate \(z_\ell\) has the moment \(-z_\ell\,V\) about \(x\) by the formula in the section on flows (lemma 5.9). By equilibrium this equals \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), so \(z_\ell = 0\) and the line is the axis \(y\). From \(\vek u^R = \vek u\) we get \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, -z) = u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z)\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, -z) = -u_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, z)\), so \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial y\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial z\) are odd in \(z\). The integrand of the mean rotation (16.38) is therefore odd in \(z\), its integral over the symmetric section is zero, and by definition 16.36 the section does not twist.
  6. A reflection about the axis \(z\) gives the same for a force in the direction \(z\). With both axes \(S\) is the intersection of both axes, that is the centroid (lemma 5.24). With one axis, say \(z\), the line of the force in the direction \(z\) lies on this axis, and the line of the force in the direction \(y\) is somewhere parallel to \(y\). The intersection lies on the axis, so \(S\) lies on the axis.

Source: SADD section 9.8 (PDF p. 277): for a section with two perpendicular axes of symmetry \(S\) lies at the intersection and is the centroid, with one axis it lies on it. COOK (PDF p. 43) and ONATE2 figure 4.6 (PDF p. 190) for a section with one axis. The proof is ours and not from a source.

Let us look at an example with two axes of symmetry that is not a rectangle: the I profile.

We draw the section, the letter I, which is symmetric about both axes, and in the web the resultant \(V\). In both half-flanges above and below we put the resultants of the flow \(F = 53{,}57\) N, by lemma 16.37 \(F = V\,t\,h\,b^2/(4I)\) with \(I = 74\,667\) mm\(^4\). The two halves of the same flange pull from the web outward and balance on the same line, so the total force of the flange is zero, the moment about the web is zero and \(S\) is at the centroid, as lemma 16.40 says (item 2). This is also the claim of chapter 12 for the rectangle \(20 \times 40\) mm: two axes of symmetry, so the shear centre is at the centroid.

16.7.2 The centroid is not the shear centre: the channel under a force

Now we use theorem 16.38 and lemma 16.39 for the twist. First the natural but wrong choice: we put the force \(V = 500\) N at the free end of the cantilever through the centroid \(C\).

Corollary 16.41 Twist of a channel under a force through the centroid (zasuk U-profila pod silo skozi težišče)

Let the channel of theorem 16.38 be of steel (\(G = 75{,}385\) GPa) and let the force \(V = 500\) N act through the centroid \(C\). Then \(d = e + z_{\mathrm{C}} = 12{,}50\) mm, the torsional moment is \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = V\,d = 6{,}25\) N m, the torsion constant of the open section is \(J = (h + 2b)\,t^3/3 = 213{,}3\) mm\(^4\) by corollary 16.34, and

\[\alpha = \frac{V\,d}{G\,J} = \frac{6{,}25}{16{,}08}\ \mathrm{rad/m} = 0{,}3886\ \mathrm{rad/m} = 22{,}3\,^\circ/\mathrm{m} . \tag{16.43}\]

In uniform torsion, far from the clamp, the torsional stress in the walls is \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\,t/J = 58{,}6\) MPa, the shear stress from bending is at most \(7{,}03\) MPa, the ratio is \(8{,}3\), and the largest total shear stress is on the face of the web near the middle, \(65{,}6\) MPa. For a force through \(S\), \(\alpha = 0\) and the largest shear stress is \(7{,}03\) MPa.

Proof

We must show the numbers.

  1. The distance \(d\) between \(\ell\) (through \(C\)) and \(\ell_{\mathrm{S}}\) is \(e + z_{\mathrm{C}} = 7{,}50 + 5{,}00 = 12{,}50\) mm by theorem 16.38. So \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 500\cdot 0{,}0125 = 6{,}25\) N m by lemma 16.39.
  2. \(J = 80\cdot 8/3 = 213{,}3\) mm\(^4\) and \(GJ = 75\,385\cdot 213{,}3 = 1{,}608\cdot 10^{7}\) N mm\(^2\) \(= 16{,}08\) N m\(^2\).
  3. \(\alpha = 6{,}25/16{,}08 = 0{,}3886\) rad/m, so \(22{,}27\,^\circ\)/m.
  4. The stress from torsion by theorem 16.33: \(\tau_{\max} \approx M_{\mathrm{x}}\,t/J = 6250\cdot 2/213{,}3 = 58{,}6\) MPa. The stress from bending in the middle of the web is \(f/t = 14{,}06/2 = 7{,}03\) MPa, their sum \(65{,}6\) MPa, below the shear yield strength of steel \(110\) MPa by Tresca's criterion.

Source: The calculations are in outlines/ch-torzija/num-07.py. The model is uniform torsion with a freely warping section (definition 16.1), at the clamped end the warping is restrained and by ONATE2 (section 4.10, PDF p. 227) the twist rate there varies along the axis, which is not treated here (COOK, PDF p. 42-43, ONATE2 section 4.10, PDF p. 227-246 are only mentioned).

The twist is large because \(GJ\) of a thin open section is small: an offset of only \(12{,}5\) mm twists the profile by \(22{,}3\) degrees per metre. This is the twist rate of uniform torsion, far from the clamp. For a cantilever of length \(L = 0{,}25\) m the end would turn by \(\alpha L = 5{,}57^\circ\) if the section warped freely everywhere. At the clamp the warping is restrained and the twist rate varies along the axis (ONATE2 section 4.10, PDF p. 227), so \(5{,}57^\circ\) is not the true end rotation of this cantilever. We do not compute the true one here.

We draw first the section before loading as a grey dashed line, in it the centroid \(C\) and the shear centre \(S\) on the left, \(12{,}5\) mm from the centroid. In the left picture the force \(V\) acts through \(C\) upward. The section after loading (orange) is lifted and turned about \(S\), because the force is to the right of \(S\) and turns counterclockwise. The angle is \(\theta = \alpha L\) and is enlarged three times in the figure so that we can see it. In the right picture the force acts through \(S\) and the section after loading does not turn, it only moves up by the same distance \(\delta\). By equation (5.54) \(\delta = V L^3/(3EI) = 0{,}31\) mm at \(E = 196\) GPa, enlarged in the figure.

The guess that the centroid is the right point therefore does not pass the test for the channel: the largest shear stress for a force through \(S\) drops from \(65{,}6\) MPa to \(7{,}03\) MPa, and the twist to zero. An offset of \(12{,}5\) mm is already large for the channel, for the slit tube it will be larger.

Example 16.42 Shear centre of a slit tube (strižno središče razrezane cevi)

The tube of example 16.35 has the mean radius \(r = 18\) mm, thickness \(t = 4\) mm and is cut along a generator. Let the slit be at \(\theta = 0\) on the axis \(z\) (\(\theta\) is the polar angle in the plane of the section, measured from the axis \(z\) toward the axis \(y\), as in chapter 11). Let \(V = 500\) N in the direction \(y\).

  1. The ring has the radii \(R_{\mathrm{i}} = 16\) mm and \(R_{\mathrm{o}} = 20\) mm. In polar coordinates (theorem 4.59, \(y = \rho\sin\theta\)) the exact second moment is \(I = \pi\,(R_{\mathrm{o}}^4 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^4)/4 = 74\,191\) mm\(^4\) (lemma 16.2), and for a thin ring \(\pi\,r^3\,t = 73\,287\) mm\(^4\), which is \(1{,}2\,\%\) less.
  2. The first moment of the part from the slit to \(\theta\) is, by the same theorem, \(Q = \int_0^\theta\!\int_{\mathrm{R}_\mathrm{i}}^{R_{\mathrm{o}}}\rho\sin\theta'\,\rho\,\mathrm{d}\rho\,\mathrm{d}\theta' = \dfrac{R_{\mathrm{o}}^3 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^3}{3}\,(1 - \cos\theta)\), and for a thin ring \(r^2\,t\,(1 - \cos\theta)\), which is \(0{,}4\,\%\) smaller (\(1296\) against \(1301{,}3\) mm\(^3\)). The shear flow by lemma 16.37 in the thin model has the magnitude \(f = V\,(1 - \cos\theta)/(\pi\,r)\), largest \(17{,}68\) N/mm at the back (\(\theta = \pi\)). At \(t/r = 0{,}22\) the remaining steps are estimates that do not hold to three digits.
  3. The flow runs tangentially in the direction of decreasing \(\theta\), with the unit vector \((\sin\theta, -\cos\theta)\) in \((z, y)\). The force in the direction \(y\) is \(-r\int_0^{2\pi} f\cos\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = V\,\dfrac{1}{\pi}\,\pi = V\) and in the direction \(z\) zero.
  4. The moment of the flows about the axis of the tube, with the arm \(r\) of each piece of arc, is \(\int_0^{2\pi} f\,r^2\,\mathrm{d}\theta = V\,r\cdot 2 = 2Vr = 18\,000\) N mm. So the line of the force \(V\) is at the distance \(2r = 36\) mm from the axis of the tube on the side opposite to the slit. The outer radius is \(20\) mm, so the line is \(16\) mm outside the section.
  5. If the force passes through the axis of the tube: \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 18{,}0\) N m, \(J = 2\pi\,r\,t^3/3 = 2413\) mm\(^4\) (corollary 16.34), \(\alpha = 0{,}0990\) rad/m \(= 5{,}67\,^\circ\)/m and \(\tau = M_{\mathrm{x}}\,t/J = 29{,}8\) MPa, the stress from bending is \(17{,}68/4 = 4{,}42\) MPa.

We draw the ring with the slit on the right and in it the axis of the tube \(O\). Outside the ring the flow is a diagram that is zero at the slit and grows to the back. The force \(V\) is through \(S\), at the distance \(2r\) from \(O\) and outside the section. The shear centre therefore lies outside the material, which SADD explicitly allows (PDF p. 277: the centre does not necessarily lie in the section).

The slit tube is the opposite of the tube without a slit of example 16.35: for an unbroken tube the section has two axes of symmetry and by lemma 16.40 the centre is on the axis. The cut takes it away by \(2r = 36\) mm.

The section ends where it began: with the question whether the same strip, so soft in the open form, would resist twisting more if we closed it. The answer is in the next section on hollow sections.

16.8 Hollow sections and thin-walled tubes (votli prerezi in tankostenske cevi)

The slit tube of the previous section gave \(\alpha = 0{,}2749\) rad/m and a stress of \(82{,}9\) MPa at \(50\) N m. The same tube without the slit is what drive shafts, rotors and frames are built from, because it looks much stiffer. How much stiffer cannot be guessed from the section, and a section counts as a tube only because there is a hole in it: the calculation with Prandtl's function has to know about the hole. This section first says what the hole changes in the problem (theorem 16.45), then solves the tube and compares it with the circle of section 16.1, and finally derives from the same problem the simple formula for thin walls that engineers use for profiles of any shape, and measures its error as a number.

Prandtl's function of section 16.3 was made for a section without holes. Its existence was guaranteed by the theorem on a field from partial derivatives (theorem 4.114) because the region is simply connected. The ring of corollary 4.113 is not, and what holds for the ring holds for every section that has a hole. Let us see what this means for our problem.

Definition 16.43 Section with holes (prerez z luknjami)

Let \(\Gamma_0\) be a simple closed curve in the plane \(y, z\) with piecewise continuous tangent and \(D_0\) the region it bounds. Let \(\Gamma_1, \dots, \Gamma_{\mathrm{m}}\) be pairwise disjoint simple closed curves in \(D_0\) with the same property and \(H_{\mathrm{k}}\) the region bounded by \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\), with area \(A_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\). If the \(H_{\mathrm{k}}\) are pairwise disjoint regions, the section with \(m\) holes (prerez z \(m\) luknjami) is the set

\[S = \overline{D_0} \setminus (H_1 \cup \dots \cup H_{\mathrm{m}}) , \tag{16.44}\]

with boundary \(\partial S = \Gamma_0 \cup \Gamma_1 \cup \dots \cup \Gamma_{\mathrm{m}}\). Hole \(k\) is the region \(H_{\mathrm{k}}\), which is not part of the body, and the outer boundary \(\Gamma_0\) is one curve. Because \(m \ge 1\), a section with holes is by corollary 4.113 (proved for the ring, the same for other shapes, without proof) and definition 1.136 multiply connected, that is, not simply connected. The normal \(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\) of the curve \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) points out of the hole, that is, into the material, and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{S}}\) is the outer normal of the section \(S\), which on \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) points into the hole, so \(\vek n_{\mathrm{S}} = -\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\).

Explanation

The word is composed: multiply connected means that two points of the section can be joined by several essentially different paths, because a path can go round the hole on the left or on the right. A tube and a hollow shaft have \(m = 1\), a profile with two cells \(m = 2\).

Source: SADD section 9.3.3 (PDF pp. 252-253) for sections with several holes, and BARBER section 16.5 (PDF pp. 260-261). The definition is not from a source.

We draw a section with one hole, because the idea is the same for every number of holes. The grey surface is the material \(S\). Its outer boundary \(\Gamma_0\) is a curve on which the lateral surface is free, so by lemma 16.15 Prandtl's function is constant there, and we may choose the value zero, because the stresses contain only derivatives of the function. The novelty is the hole with its curve \(\Gamma_1\): this surface is free too, so \(\Phi\) is constant on it, but the curve \(\Gamma_1\) is not joined to \(\Gamma_0\) inside the material, so there is no reason for the constant to be the same, and we write \(\Phi = \Phi_1\) with an unknown number \(\Phi_1\) in N/mm. On \(\Gamma_1\) we draw the normal \(\vek n\), pointing out of the hole, and mark the area of the hole \(A_1\). For later we add the loop \(C\), a closed curve in the material that goes once round the hole, in the direction of positive rotation about \(x\) (axes: \(y\) to the right, \(z\) up, \(x\) towards the reader). With it we shall check what happens to the functions \(\Phi\) and \(\psi\) on a path round the hole.

First: does Prandtl's function exist on this section as a single function at all?

Lemma 16.44 Prandtl function of a section with holes (Prandtlova funkcija prereza z luknjami)

Let \(S\) be a section with holes (definition 16.43), let \(\psi\) be the warping function of theorem 16.10, twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\), as the theorem demands, let the lateral surface be free on all curves \(\Gamma_0, \dots, \Gamma_{\mathrm{m}}\), and let lemma 16.9 hold for \(S\), for every region \(H_{\mathrm{k}}\) and for every region between \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) and a closed curve in \(S\) that goes round \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) and no other hole. Then:

  1. There is exactly one function \(\Phi\) on the interior of the section, twice continuously differentiable, that satisfies equation (16.19). It is determined up to an added constant.
  2. On every curve \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) the function \(\Phi\) is constant. We choose \(\Phi = 0\) on \(\Gamma_0\) and \(\Phi = \Phi_{\mathrm{k}}\) on \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) for \(k \ge 1\).
  3. \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2G\alpha\) in \(S\).
Idea

We cut the section with arcs from the hole to the outer boundary so that it becomes simply connected, and use the theorem on a field from derivatives. The jump of the function \(\Phi\) across a cut is the flux of stress through a loop round the hole, and that is zero.

Proof

We must show that \(\Phi\), made on the cut section, does not break at the cuts.

  1. For every hole \(k\) choose an arc \(c_{\mathrm{k}}\) from \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) to \(\Gamma_0\), separate from the other arcs and holes. The set \(S^\circ \setminus (c_1 \cup \dots \cup c_{\mathrm{m}})\) is open, connected and simply connected (a topological fact that we state here without proof, as with the cut ring in lemma 4.120). By step 2 of lemma 16.15, which uses only equilibrium (16.17), there is a function \(\Phi\) on it with derivatives \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\).
  2. The jump \([\Phi]_{\mathrm{k}}\) of the function \(\Phi\) across the cut \(c_{\mathrm{k}}\) is the difference of its values on the two sides. We get it by going along a loop \(C_{\mathrm{k}}\) round hole \(k\) from one side of the cut to the other, since \(\Phi\) is the integral of its gradient. With the unit tangent \(\vek t = (t_{\mathrm{y}}, t_{\mathrm{z}})\) of the loop, pointing in the direction of positive rotation, and its outer normal \(\vek n_{\mathrm{C}} = (t_{\mathrm{z}}, -t_{\mathrm{y}})\) we have \([\Phi]_{\mathrm{k}} = \oint_{\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{k}}(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} t_{\mathrm{y}} + \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} t_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = \oint_{\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{k}}(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}t_{\mathrm{z}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}t_{\mathrm{y}})\,\mathrm{d}s = \oint_{\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{k}}(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{C},\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{C},\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s\). This is the flux of the shear vector \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) through \(C_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  3. Let \(R_{\mathrm{k}}\) be the part of the section between \(C_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\). By lemma 16.9 with the field \(\vek v = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) the integral of the divergence over \(R_{\mathrm{k}}\), which is zero by equation (16.17), equals the flux through the boundary of \(R_{\mathrm{k}}\). This is the sum of the flux through \(C_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the flux through \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\), where the normal is \(\vek n_{\mathrm{S}}\) and the flux is zero by equation (16.18). So the flux through \(C_{\mathrm{k}}\) is zero, hence \([\Phi]_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\).
  4. Since the jumps are zero, the values of \(\Phi\) on the two sides of the cuts agree and \(\Phi\) is a twice continuously differentiable function on the whole interior, with the same derivatives and so with the same stresses. If \(\tilde\Phi\) is another such function, the difference has both derivatives zero in a connected set and is constant. This is point 1.
  5. Point 2 follows as in step 5 of lemma 16.15 for each of the curves \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\): the derivative of \(\Phi\) along the tangent is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) by equation (16.18), and each \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) is one connected curve. Since the stresses contain only derivatives, we can choose the constant so that \(\Phi = 0\) on \(\Gamma_0\).
  6. Point 3 is the computation of step 1 of theorem 16.16: the left side of equation (16.20) is \(-\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nabla^2\Phi\) and it equals \(2G\alpha\).

Source: SADD section 9.3.3 (PDF pp. 252-253): constants \(\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}\) on every inner curve, one chosen zero. BARBER section 16.5 (PDF p. 260): the same, with the remark that \(\Phi_1 = \Phi_0\) does not follow because the curves do not connect. The proof with cuts and flux is not from the sources.

So the function \(\Phi\) is a single one, but on the hole it has an unknown value \(\Phi_1\). What fixes this number? For a section without holes, equation (16.22) with zero on the boundary was enough, and by lemma 16.17 it has exactly one solution. Now the boundary has several curves and \(\Phi_1\) is an additional unknown, so we need an additional equation. We get to it with a question that we did not have to ask for a section without holes: is the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha\,\psi\) a single-valued function of the point? The displacement of a body is one vector at every point. The warping function \(\psi\) must therefore come back to the same value after every closed loop round the hole, just as in lemma 4.120 the displacement on the cut must not have a jump. The function \(\Phi\) guaranteed this only for itself, and for \(\psi\) it is a new requirement.

We write the requirement on the loop \(C\) and move it to the edge of the hole, because there the function \(\Phi\) is best known. The path along the loop is closed, so \(\psi\) does not change along it: the integral of the derivative \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}t_{\mathrm{y}} + \psi_{\mathrm{z}}t_{\mathrm{z}}\) along \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) is zero. We express the derivatives \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}}\) by the stresses from equation (16.16), and the stresses by \(\Phi\). Two things must be computed: how large the flux of the shear vector through the edge of the hole is, and what \(\oint(z\,t_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,t_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s\) is. The first will be the derivative of \(\Phi\) in the direction of the normal \(\vek n\), the second the area \(A_1\).

Theorem 16.45 Hole condition and torque of a section with holes (pogoj luknje in moment prereza z luknjami)

Let \(S\) be a section with \(m\) holes (definition 16.43) and let \(\Phi\) be the Prandtl function of lemma 16.44 with \(\Phi = 0\) on \(\Gamma_0\) and \(\Phi = \Phi_{\mathrm{k}}\) on \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\), twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\) (as in theorem 16.16, because the proof uses lemma 16.9 with fields made of \(\Phi\) and its derivatives), with the other assumptions of the lemma. Let \(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\) be the normal of \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) out of hole \(k\). Then:

  1. For every hole \(k = 1, \dots, m\)
    \[\oint_{\Gamma_\mathrm{k}}\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial n_{\mathrm{k}}}\,\mathrm{d}s = -2G\alpha\,A_{\mathrm{k}} . \tag{16.45}\]
  2. The same holds for every closed curve \(C\) in the interior of the section that goes once round hole \(k\) and no other, with the area \(A_{\mathrm{C}}\) it encloses instead of \(A_{\mathrm{k}}\). The normal \(\vek n_{\mathrm{C}}\) is the outer normal of the curve \(C\).
  3. The resultant force of the section is zero, and its moment about the axis \(x\) is
    \[M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A + 2\sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m}\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}\,A_{\mathrm{k}} , \tag{16.46}\]
    so \(J = \dfrac{2}{G\alpha}\Big(\displaystyle\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A + \sum_{\mathrm{k}}\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}A_{\mathrm{k}}\Big)\) and \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = GJ\alpha\).
  4. Let \((\Phi, \Phi_1, \dots, \Phi_{\mathrm{m}})\) and \((\tilde\Phi, \tilde\Phi_1, \dots, \tilde\Phi_{\mathrm{m}})\) be twice continuously differentiable functions on an open set that contains \(S\), with \(\nabla^2 = -2G\alpha\) in \(S\), zero on \(\Gamma_0\), constant values on \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the conditions (16.45). Then they are equal.
Idea

The condition from the single-valued warping function is the flux of \(\Phi\) through the hole. The moment is the divergence theorem with the field \((y\Phi, z\Phi)\), where the term on \(\Gamma_0\) cancels because \(\Phi = 0\), and on the holes \(-2\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}A_{\mathrm{k}}\) remains. Uniqueness is an energy proof as in lemma 16.17.

Proof

We must show four claims. We turn the tangent \(\vek t\) of the curve \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) in the direction of positive rotation, so that \(\vek t = (-n_{\mathrm{z}}, n_{\mathrm{y}})\), as in lemma 16.15.

  1. The function \(\psi\) is a single-valued function of the point of the section, continuously differentiable up to the boundary, so its derivative along the closed curve \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) satisfies, by the fundamental theorem of calculus, \(\oint_{\Gamma_\mathrm{k}}(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}t_{\mathrm{y}} + \psi_{\mathrm{z}}t_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\).
  2. From equation (16.16), \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/(G\alpha) + z\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/(G\alpha) - y\). The stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}t_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}t_{\mathrm{z}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} = -\partial\Phi/\partial n_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  3.
