The term with \(z\,t_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,t_{\mathrm{z}} = -(y\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + z\,n_{\mathrm{z}})\) is, by lemma 16.9 with the field \(\vek v = (y, z)\) on the region \(H_{\mathrm{k}}\) (the divergence is \(2\)), equal to \(\oint_{\Gamma_\mathrm{k}}(y\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + z\,n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = 2A_{\mathrm{k}}\), so \(\oint(z\,t_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,t_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = -2A_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  4. Steps 1 to 3 together give \(0 = -\dfrac{1}{G\alpha}\oint_{\Gamma_\mathrm{k}}\dfrac{\partial\Phi}{\partial n_{\mathrm{k}}}\,\mathrm{d}s - 2A_{\mathrm{k}}\), which is equation (16.45).
  5. Point 2: by lemma 16.9 with \(\vek v = \nabla\Phi\) on the region between \(C\) and \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\oint_{\mathrm{C}}\partial\Phi/\partial n_{\mathrm{C}}\,\mathrm{d}s - \oint_{\Gamma_\mathrm{k}}\partial\Phi/\partial n_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}s = \int\nabla^2\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A = -2G\alpha(A_{\mathrm{C}} - A_{\mathrm{k}})\). With equation (16.45) it follows that \(\oint_{\mathrm{C}}\partial\Phi/\partial n_{\mathrm{C}}\,\mathrm{d}s = -2G\alpha A_{\mathrm{C}}\). The sign in front of the second integral is minus because the outer normal of the region on \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) is \(-\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  6. Point 3, force: \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint_{\partial \mathrm{S}}\Phi\,n_{\mathrm{S},\mathrm{z}}\,\mathrm{d}s\) by lemma 16.9 with \((0, \Phi)\). On \(\Gamma_0\) we have \(\Phi = 0\), and on \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) we get \(\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}\oint_{\Gamma_\mathrm{k}}n_{\mathrm{S},\mathrm{z}}\,\mathrm{d}s = -\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot 0\), because \(\oint_{\Gamma_\mathrm{k}}n_{\mathrm{z}}\,\mathrm{d}s\) is zero by the lemma with \(\vek v = (0, 1)\) on \(H_{\mathrm{k}}\). Likewise \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\) with \((\Phi, 0)\).
  7. Point 3, moment: by lemma 5.9, \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = \int_{\mathrm{S}}(y\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} - z\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\,\mathrm{d}A = -\int_{\mathrm{S}}(y\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + z\Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}A\). The field \(\vek v = (y\Phi, z\Phi)\) has divergence \(2\Phi + y\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + z\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\), so \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}(y\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + z\Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint_{\partial \mathrm{S}}\Phi\,(y\,n_{\mathrm{S},\mathrm{y}} + z\,n_{\mathrm{S},\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s - 2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A\). On \(\Gamma_0\) we have \(\Phi = 0\), on \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\) we have \(\Phi = \Phi_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{S}} = -\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\), which by step 3 gives \(-2\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}A_{\mathrm{k}}\). So \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A + 2\sum_{\mathrm{k}}\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}A_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  8. Point 4: the difference \(w = \Phi - \tilde\Phi\) is harmonic, zero on \(\Gamma_0\), constant \(c_{\mathrm{k}}\) on \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{k}}\), with \(\oint_{\Gamma_\mathrm{k}}\partial w/\partial n_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\) (the difference of equations (16.45)). By lemma 16.9 with \(\vek v = w\nabla w\) we have \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint_{\partial \mathrm{S}}w\,\partial w/\partial n_{\mathrm{S}}\,\mathrm{d}s = -\sum_{\mathrm{k}}c_{\mathrm{k}}\oint_{\Gamma_\mathrm{k}}\partial w/\partial n_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\). As in lemma 16.17, \(\nabla w = 0\), \(w\) is constant and zero on \(\Gamma_0\), so \(w = 0\) and \(c_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\).

Source: Condition (16.45): SADD section 9.3.3, equations (9.3.26) to (9.3.29) (PDF p. 253) and BARBER section 16.5, equations (16.53) and (16.54) (PDF p. 261), both with Green's theorem on a loop round the hole. Moment: BARBER equation (16.55) (PDF p. 261) with \(\Phi = \Phi_{\mathrm{k}}\) in the hole. The proof with flux and the energy uniqueness are not from the sources. We cite, and do not prove, the existence of a solution for a general section (SADD PDF pp. 246-250 for a section without holes), and for the tube theorem 16.3 gives it with \(\psi = 0\).

Let us read the theorem. The hole condition (16.45) is one number for every hole, and our constant \(\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}\) used it up: the flux of \(\Phi\) out of the hole is exactly \(-2G\alpha A_{\mathrm{k}}\). The moment (16.46) has two terms: the first is an integral over the material, the second is the contribution of the hole, which, although there is no material in it, can be large. Let us see this on the tube.

Corollary 16.46 Torsion of a tube (torzija cevi)

Let the section be an annulus with outer radius \(R_{\mathrm{o}}\) and inner radius \(R_{\mathrm{i}} < R_{\mathrm{o}}\) with centre \(O\), \(S = \{R_{\mathrm{i}} \le r \le R_{\mathrm{o}}\}\), \(r = \sqrt{y^2 + z^2}\), with one hole \(H_1 = \{r < R_{\mathrm{i}}\}\) and \(A_1 = \pi R_{\mathrm{i}}^2\). Then

\[\Phi = \frac{G\alpha}{2}\,(R_{\mathrm{o}}^2 - r^2) , \qquad \Phi_1 = \frac{G\alpha}{2}\,(R_{\mathrm{o}}^2 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^2) , \qquad J = \frac{\pi}{2}\,(R_{\mathrm{o}}^4 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^4) = I_{\mathrm{p}} . \tag{16.47}\]
Proof

We must show that the function (16.47) is the Prandtl function of the tube, that it satisfies the conditions of theorem 16.45, and compute \(J\) from equation (16.46).

  1. By theorem 16.3, \(\psi = 0\) is a solution for the annulus with the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -G\alpha z\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\alpha y\), so by lemma 16.44 its Prandtl function exists, with the derivatives \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -G\alpha y\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -G\alpha z\). The function (16.47) has the same derivatives. Two functions with the same derivatives on a connected set differ by a constant, and both are zero at \(r = R_{\mathrm{o}}\), so (16.47) is the Prandtl function of the tube. By point 4 of theorem 16.45 it is the only one that satisfies the conditions of the theorem, so every other way of solving gives it too.

  2. \(\nabla^2\Phi = \dfrac{G\alpha}{2}\,\nabla^2(R_{\mathrm{o}}^2 - y^2 - z^2) = \dfrac{G\alpha}{2}(-2 - 2) = -2G\alpha\) and \(\Phi = 0\) at \(r = R_{\mathrm{o}}\). On \(r = R_{\mathrm{i}}\) we have \(\Phi = \Phi_1\).

  3. The normal out of the hole is radial, \(\partial\Phi/\partial n_1 = \partial\Phi/\partial r = -G\alpha R_{\mathrm{i}}\) on \(r = R_{\mathrm{i}}\), which is constant, so \(\oint_{\Gamma_1}\partial\Phi/\partial n_1\,\mathrm{d}s = -G\alpha R_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot 2\pi R_{\mathrm{i}} = -2G\alpha\,\pi R_{\mathrm{i}}^2 = -2G\alpha A_1\). The condition (16.45) holds.

  4. The integral over \(S\) by theorem 4.59 in polar coordinates: \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A = 2\pi\int_{\mathrm{R}_\mathrm{i}}^{R_{\mathrm{o}}}\dfrac{G\alpha}{2}(R_{\mathrm{o}}^2 - r^2)\,r\,\mathrm{d}r = \pi G\alpha\Big[\dfrac{R_{\mathrm{o}}^2r^2}{2} - \dfrac{r^4}{4}\Big]_{\mathrm{R}_\mathrm{i}}^{R_{\mathrm{o}}} = \dfrac{\pi G\alpha}{4}\,(R_{\mathrm{o}}^2 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^2)^2\).

  5. So by equation (16.46) \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = \dfrac{\pi G\alpha}{2}(R_{\mathrm{o}}^2 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^2)^2 + \pi G\alpha\,R_{\mathrm{i}}^2(R_{\mathrm{o}}^2 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^2) = \dfrac{\pi G\alpha}{2}(R_{\mathrm{o}}^2 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^2)(R_{\mathrm{o}}^2 + R_{\mathrm{i}}^2) = G\alpha\,\dfrac{\pi}{2}(R_{\mathrm{o}}^4 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^4)\), which is \(GJ\alpha\) with \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}}\) from lemma 16.2.

Source: The result \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}}\) for the tube is theorem 16.3 with \(\psi = 0\): a second way to the same result. BARBER section 16.5 (PDF pp. 260-261) mentions the tube as an example, SADD section 9.6 (PDF pp. 267-269) treats a hollow bar. The representation with the function \(\Phi\) is not from the sources.

The tube agrees with the circular annulus of section 16.1, which is a double check of both theorems: the first used a displacement without warping, the second the function \(\Phi\) with the hole. On the tube \(40/32\) mm of the figure we have \(R_{\mathrm{o}} = 20\) mm, \(R_{\mathrm{i}} = 16\) mm, \(t = 4\) mm, \(r_{\mathrm{m}} = 18\) mm, \(A_1 = 804{,}2\) mm\(^2\). The first term of the moment (16.46) is \(2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A = 32\,572\,G\alpha\) mm\(^4\) (units mm\(^4\), like \(J\)), the second \(2\Phi_1A_1 = 115\,812\,G\alpha\) mm\(^4\), together \(J = 148\,384\) mm\(^4\). The hole therefore contributes \(78{,}0\,\%\) of the whole: leaving it out would lose almost four fifths of the stiffness. At \(50\) N m we have \(\alpha = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(GJ) = 0{,}00447\) rad/m, and the stress is by corollary 16.4 \(\tau = M_{\mathrm{x}}r/I_{\mathrm{p}}\), so \(6{,}74\) MPa on the outer edge and \(5{,}39\) MPa on the inner one, in the section with the same direction everywhere (the blue arrows point round the hole in the same direction, because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\alpha y\) is positive at \(y > 0\)).

And what if we forget the hole condition?

Example 16.47 A tube with a wrong boundary condition (cev z napačnim robnim pogojem)

The tube \(40/32\) mm would be solved with \(\Phi = 0\) on both circles instead of \(\Phi = \Phi_1\) on the inner circle, as if the section were simply connected.

  1. The rotationally symmetric solution of the equation \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2G\alpha\) is \(\Phi/(G\alpha) = -r^2/2 + c_1\ln r + c_2\) (SymPy, num-08.py). From \(\Phi(20) = \Phi(16) = 0\) we get \(c_1 = 72/\ln 1{,}25 = 322{,}66\) mm\(^2\) and \(c_2 = -766{,}61\) mm\(^2\).
  2. The function has its largest value \(4{,}006\,G\alpha\) mm\(^2\) at \(r = 17{,}96\) mm, so only \(5{,}6\,\%\) of the true \(\Phi_1 = 72\,G\alpha\) mm\(^2\).
  3. The flux through the inner circle is \(\oint\partial\Phi/\partial n_1\,\mathrm{d}s = +418{,}9\,G\alpha\) mm\(^2\), whereas condition (16.45) demands \(-2G\alpha A_1 = -1608{,}5\,G\alpha\) mm\(^2\). The wrong \(\Phi\) even has the wrong sign: it rises away from the hole, the true function falls.
  4. The moment (16.46) with \(\Phi_1 = 0\) gives \(J = \frac{2}{G\alpha}\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A = 2415\) mm\(^4\). This is \(1{,}6\,\%\) of the true value and \(0{,}1\,\%\) more than \(\ell t^3/3 = 2413\) mm\(^4\) for the slit tube of example 16.35.

The reason for the last result: \(\Phi = 0\) on both faces of the wall is the problem of a strip with zero on both sides, as in theorem 16.33, and the wall of the tube is a strip, only bent into a circle. The wrong problem therefore has the solution of a strip bent into a closed ring without ends. This is not exactly the slit tube. The two faces of the slit must be free, but there the wrong \(\Phi\) would give a shear vector with the component \(-\partial\Phi/\partial r\) across the face, which is not zero (its resultant over the face is zero). Moreover, the slit tube has two free ends of the strip at the slit, which lower \(J\): for a straight strip with the same \(\ell/t = 113{,}1/4 = 28{,}3\), by theorem 16.33 by at most \(2{,}2\,\%\). The formula \(\ell t^3/3\) neglects both, so it agrees with the wrong problem to \(0{,}1\,\%\). The hole condition (16.45) is what closes the tube in the problem, and without it the calculation gives almost the stiffness of the slit tube.

The hole can be shown on the membrane.

We stretch the membrane of section 16.4 (corollary 16.26) over the outer edge and fix it on the line \(y\) at \(-R_{\mathrm{o}}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{o}}\), where the height is zero. Over the wall the membrane rises, as the height of the function \(\Phi\) rises towards the hole. Over the hole there is no material, so there is no membrane: there we place a thin flat plate without weight, which can only rise and fall, and glue the membrane to its edge. The plate is flat because \(\Phi\) does not depend on the point on the hole, being the constant \(\Phi_1\) on \(\Gamma_1\). The pressure \(p\) acts from below on the membrane and on the plate, in the tube it is the ratio \(p/N = 2G\alpha\) of the corollary, and the plate rises to the height at which it is in equilibrium: the membrane pulls it down along its edge with the force \(N\) per unit length, the vertical component is \(N\,|\partial\Phi/\partial n|\) (for small slopes, at slope \(0{,}2\) the error is \(1{,}94\,\%\), section 16.4), and the sum along the edge must balance the \(p\,A_1\) of the pressure on the plate:

\[N\oint_{\Gamma_1}\Big(-\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial n_1}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}s = p\,A_1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \oint_{\Gamma_1}\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial n_1}\,\mathrm{d}s = -\frac{p}{N}\,A_1 = -2G\alpha\,A_1 . \tag{16.48}\]

This is the hole condition (16.45): the equilibrium of the plate and the single-valued displacement \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) give the same equation. The height \(\Phi_1\) of the plate, which is unknown, is the one at which the forces are in equilibrium. Likewise the moment (16.46) is the whole volume under the membrane, plate included: \(2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A\) is twice the volume under the membrane over the material, and \(2\Phi_1A_1\) twice the volume of the cylinder under the plate, with base \(A_1\) and height \(\Phi_1\).

For thin walls we need less than the solution. The figure shows three panels of the same kind of tube, a general section with one hole.

The section is a tube of any shape, and its wall is thin compared with the size of the hole. The mean line is the dashed curve halfway between the two edges of the wall, its length is \(\ell\), and the area it encloses is \(A_0\). How \(\Phi\) varies across the wall we know only for the circular tube, so we take the simplest guess: across the thickness \(t\) it is linear, from \(0\) on the outer edge to \(\Phi_1\) on the inner one. Then the slope across the wall is \(\Phi_1/t\) everywhere, and by lemma 16.20 the stress has the size \(\tau = \Phi_1/t\) and is tangent to the wall.

This stress must satisfy equilibrium and the moment. Equilibrium: take a piece of wall between two transverse cuts \(s_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(s_{\mathrm{b}}\) along the mean line, of length \(L\) along the axis \(x\). The lateral faces of the piece are free, and on the end faces at \(x\) there is no normal stress, so in the direction \(x\) only the shear stress on the cuts acts. Its integral across the thickness is \(q(s_{\mathrm{a}})\,L\) on one cut and \(q(s_{\mathrm{b}})\,L\) on the other, where \(q = \tau\,t\) is the shear force per unit length of the mean line, and they point in opposite directions. Equilibrium in the direction \(x\) demands \(q(s_{\mathrm{a}})L = q(s_{\mathrm{b}})L\), so the flow \(q\) is constant along the whole mean line, and where the wall is thinner the stress is larger. Moment: we put the origin of the axes \(y, z\) at the point \(O\). The flow \(q\) runs at a point \(P\) of the mean line along its tangent \(\vek t\) and has about \(O\) the lever arm \(p\), the distance from \(O\) to the tangent at \(P\). On a straight stretch \(PP'\) of length \(\delta\) the force would be \(q\,\delta\) with the moment \(q\,p\,\delta\), which is \(2q\) times the area \(\tfrac12\,p\,\delta\) of the triangle \(OPP'\) (base times height over two). The triangles over all stretches cover the area \(A_0\), so we expect \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2qA_0\). We get exactly this without stretches. With the outer normal of the mean line \(\vek n = (t_{\mathrm{z}}, -t_{\mathrm{y}})\) the lever arm at the point \((y, z)\) is \(p = y\,t_{\mathrm{z}} - z\,t_{\mathrm{y}} = y\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + z\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\), so the moment of the flow about the axis \(x\) is

\[M_{\mathrm{x}} = \oint q\,(y\,t_{\mathrm{z}} - z\,t_{\mathrm{y}})\,\mathrm{d}s = q\oint(y\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + z\,n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = 2qA_0 ,\]

the last equality by lemma 16.9 with the field \(\vek v = (y, z)\), whose divergence is \(2\), on the region inside the mean line, as in step 3 of theorem 16.45. So \(q = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(2A_0)\) and \(\tau = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(2A_0t)\), the well-known formula of mechanics of materials. Now the same from \(\Phi\), because that also gives \(J\) and the error.

Theorem 16.48 Thin-walled closed section (tankostenski zaprt prerez)

Let \(S\) be a section with one hole (definition 16.43), \(\ell\) the length of the mean line (the curve halfway between \(\Gamma_0\) and \(\Gamma_1\) along the normal), \(A_0\) the area it encloses, \(t(s)\) the wall thickness along the mean line (\(s\) is the arc length). Let the following hold:

(H1) on the mean line \(\partial\Phi/\partial n = -\Phi_1/t(s)\), where \(\vek n\) is the normal of the mean line out of the hole (the mean slope across the wall),

(H2) \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A + \Phi_1A_1 = \Phi_1A_0\).

Then:

  1. \(\Phi_1 = \dfrac{2G\alpha A_0}{\oint ds/t}\).
  2. The flow \(q = \Phi_1 = \dfrac{M_{\mathrm{x}}}{2A_0}\) and the mean stress across the wall \(\tau = \dfrac{M_{\mathrm{x}}}{2A_0\,t(s)}\).
  3. \(J = \dfrac{4A_0^2}{\oint ds/t}\), and for constant thickness
    \[J = \frac{4A_0^2\,t}{\ell} . \tag{16.49}\]
  4. For a tube with mean radius \(r_{\mathrm{m}}\) and thickness \(t\), (H1) holds exactly and \(J_{\text{exact}}/J = 1 + t^2/(4r_{\mathrm{m}}^2)\).
Idea

The hole condition on the mean line gives \(\Phi_1\), and the moment contains the hypothesis (H2). For the tube we check both on the exact solution.

Proof

We must show four claims, the first two with the hypotheses, the third by combining, the fourth by computation.

  1. By point 2 of theorem 16.45 on the mean line with area \(A_{\mathrm{C}} = A_0\) we have \(\oint\partial\Phi/\partial n\,\mathrm{d}s = -2G\alpha A_0\). By (H1) the left side is \(-\Phi_1\oint ds/t\), whence point 1.
  2. By equation (16.46) and (H2), \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\big(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A + \Phi_1A_1\big) = 2\Phi_1A_0\), so \(\Phi_1 = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(2A_0)\). The mean slope of \(\Phi\) across the wall is \(\Phi_1/t\) (a height difference \(\Phi_1\) over a length \(t\)), and by lemma 16.20 this is the size of the stress.
  3. From points 1 and 2: \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2A_0\Phi_1 = 4G\alpha A_0^2/\oint ds/t\), which is \(GJ\alpha\). For constant \(t\) we have \(\oint ds/t = \ell/t\).
  4. For the tube \(\Phi = \tfrac{G\alpha}{2}(R_{\mathrm{o}}^2 - r^2)\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial r = -G\alpha r\), at \(r = r_{\mathrm{m}}\) it is \(-G\alpha r_{\mathrm{m}}\). From \(\Phi_1 = \tfrac{G\alpha}{2}(R_{\mathrm{o}}^2 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^2) = G\alpha\,r_{\mathrm{m}}t\) we get \(\Phi_1/t = G\alpha r_{\mathrm{m}}\), so (H1) holds exactly. From \(R_{\mathrm{o},\mathrm{i}} = r_{\mathrm{m}} \pm t/2\) we have \(R_{\mathrm{o}}^4 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^4 = (R_{\mathrm{o}}^2 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^2)(R_{\mathrm{o}}^2 + R_{\mathrm{i}}^2) = 2r_{\mathrm{m}}t\,(2r_{\mathrm{m}}^2 + t^2/2)\), so \(J_{\text{exact}} = \pi r_{\mathrm{m}}t\,(2r_{\mathrm{m}}^2 + t^2/2) = 2\pi r_{\mathrm{m}}^3t\,(1 + t^2/(4r_{\mathrm{m}}^2))\). Equation (16.49) with \(A_0 = \pi r_{\mathrm{m}}^2\) and \(\ell = 2\pi r_{\mathrm{m}}\) gives \(4\pi^2r_{\mathrm{m}}^4t/(2\pi r_{\mathrm{m}}) = 2\pi r_{\mathrm{m}}^3t\). The quotient is \(1 + t^2/(4r_{\mathrm{m}}^2)\).

Source: BARBER section 16.5.1, equations (16.56) to (16.59) (PDF pp. 261-262): \(\Phi\) linear across the wall, \(\tau = \Phi_1/t\), \(\Phi_1\) from the hole condition, moment and rigidity. ONATE2 section 4.3.5 (PDF pp. 204-206) the same for thin walls. The route with equilibrium of a piece and the lever arm is not from the sources, we do not name an author of the formula because none is in our sources. Claim 4 is not from the sources, the computation is in num-08.py.

The hypotheses (H1) and (H2) are a guess, so we test the theorem: is the error really what claim 4 says, and when does the formula fail? We let the inner diameter grow while the outer diameter stays \(40\) mm.

Example 16.49 Error of the thin-wall formula on a tube (napaka tankostenske formule na cevi)

For tubes with \(d_{\mathrm{o}} = 40\) mm and growing wall thickness, by equation (16.49) (num-08.py, part 4):

  1. \(d_{\mathrm{i}} = 38\) mm: \(t = 1\) mm, \(t/r_{\mathrm{m}} = 0{,}051\), \(J = 46\,620\) mm\(^4\), formula \(46\,589\) mm\(^4\), error \(-0{,}07\,\%\).
  2. \(d_{\mathrm{i}} = 36\) mm: \(t = 2\) mm, \(J = 86\,431\) mm\(^4\), formula \(86\,193\) mm\(^4\), \(-0{,}28\,\%\).
  3. \(d_{\mathrm{i}} = 32\) mm: \(t = 4\) mm, \(J = 148\,384\) mm\(^4\), formula \(146\,574\) mm\(^4\), \(-1{,}22\,\%\).
  4. \(d_{\mathrm{i}} = 30\) mm: \(t = 5\) mm, \(J = 171\,806\) mm\(^4\), formula \(168\,370\) mm\(^4\), \(-2{,}00\,\%\).
  5. \(d_{\mathrm{i}} = 20\) mm: \(t = 10\) mm, \(t/r_{\mathrm{m}} = 0{,}667\), \(J = 235\,619\) mm\(^4\), formula \(212\,058\) mm\(^4\), \(-10{,}0\,\%\).

The exact value is always larger, in agreement with the quotient \(1 + t^2/(4r_{\mathrm{m}}^2)\), which is \(1{,}0007\), \(1{,}0028\), \(1{,}0123\), \(1{,}0204\) and \(1{,}111\). The error grows with the square of \(t/r_{\mathrm{m}}\), because (H2) is an approximation that neglects the curvature of the wall.

The last line is the case where the theorem fails: a wall of thickness \(10\) mm at mean radius \(15\) mm is no longer thin. Rule: at \(t/r_{\mathrm{m}} \le 0{,}1\) the formula is accurate to \(0{,}3\,\%\), at \(t/r_{\mathrm{m}} \le 0{,}28\) to \(2\,\%\) (at \(0{,}3\) the error is already \(2{,}2\,\%\)), at \(t/r_{\mathrm{m}} = 0{,}67\) it is not usable. For a section that is not circular we do not prove the same bound, so we use the same scale only as an estimate.

Now the same tube in both forms.

Example 16.50 Closed and slit tube (zaprta in razrezana cev)

Tube \(40/32\) mm, \(G = 75{,}385\) GPa, \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m, figure 16.30, \(t = 4\) mm, \(r_{\mathrm{m}} = 18\) mm, \(\ell = 113{,}1\) mm:

  1. Closed: \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}} = 148\,384\) mm\(^4\), \(GJ = 11\,186\) N m\(^2\), \(\alpha = 0{,}00447\) rad/m. Stress \(6{,}74\) MPa outside and \(5{,}39\) MPa inside. Thin formula: \(\tau = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(2A_0t) = 6{,}14\) MPa, between the two values.
  2. Slit: by corollary 16.34 \(J = \ell t^3/3 = 2413\) mm\(^4\), \(\alpha = 0{,}2749\) rad/m, \(\tau = M_{\mathrm{x}}t/J = 82{,}9\) MPa.
  3. The ratio of stiffnesses \(J_{\text{closed}}/J_{\text{slit}} = 61{,}5\) and the ratio of largest stresses \(82{,}9/6{,}74 = 12{,}3\).
  4. The reason for \(61{,}5\): from theorem 16.48 (point 4), \(J_{\text{closed}}/J_{\text{slit}} = \dfrac{2\pi r_{\mathrm{m}}^3t\,(1 + t^2/(4r_{\mathrm{m}}^2))}{2\pi r_{\mathrm{m}}t^3/3} = 3\,\dfrac{r_{\mathrm{m}}^2}{t^2}\Big(1 + \dfrac{t^2}{4r_{\mathrm{m}}^2}\Big) = 3\cdot 20{,}25\cdot 1{,}0123 = 61{,}5\), because \(r_{\mathrm{m}}^2/t^2 = 20{,}25\).

The flow of stress explains where this size comes from. In the closed wall the shear flow goes round the hole in the same direction through the whole thickness, the whole wall contributes to the moment with the same sign and with the lever arm \(r_{\mathrm{m}}\), which is \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2qA_0\) of the theorem. In the slit wall there is no flow round the hole, because the slit would interrupt it: the stress runs forward on one face and back on the other, the profile across the wall is antisymmetric with zero in the middle. The forces of the two halves cancel, and what remains is a couple whose arm is of size \(t\) instead of \(r_{\mathrm{m}}\). The ratio \(r_{\mathrm{m}}/t = 4{,}5\) enters squared (\(3\,r_{\mathrm{m}}^2/t^2\) in point 4 of the example). In the closed wall the profile has the same sign but not the same size: \(6{,}74\) outside and \(5{,}39\) inside, because \(\tau = G\alpha r\) is larger at the larger radius.

From this follows advice for design. The tube \(40/32\) has, by mass, \(0{,}360\) of the cross-section of the solid shaft \(\varnothing 40\) mm and \(0{,}590\) of its \(J\) (num-08.py, part 6), so it has \(1{,}64\) times more stiffness per unit mass. The slit tube has the same mass and \(61{,}5\) times less stiffness than the closed one.

With theorem 16.45 we have also covered sections with several holes (cells): for every hole its own condition (16.45) holds with \(\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}\) as the unknown, and the moment (16.46) has one term \(2\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}A_{\mathrm{k}}\) for each. For thin walls with several cells we get a system of equations for the flows in the walls, which we state without derivation (SADD section 9.3.3, PDF pp. 252-254, and ONATE2 section 4.3.5.1, PDF p. 206). Others that we do not treat here: restrained warping and nonuniform torsion of hollow sections (COOK PDF pp. 42-43, ONATE2 section 4.10, PDF pp. 227-246).

A question remains: how well can we bound \(J\) without solving the problem? For a section with a hole this is harder, because a trial function must also satisfy the hole condition (16.45) or take the hole as a constant value. Section 16.9 bounds \(J\) from both sides on a section without a hole, where theorem 16.16 is enough.

16.9 Bounds of the torsion constant and finite elements

We took the torsion constant \(J\) of the \(20 \times 40\) mm strip in section 16.5 from a series, because Prandtl's equation on a rectangle is solved by separation of variables. For an L-shaped section, a section with rounded corners or any other outline there is no such series. The engineer still has to know how far the shaft twists, and besides the number needs to know how much it may be off. In this section we show that the torsion constant allows such knowledge. Both boundary problems of sections 16.2 and 16.3 are the search for the smallest value of something. So every trial function, even a poor one, gives a bound for \(J\): the warping function from one side, Prandtl's function from the other. When we compute these two bounds on a mesh of triangles we obtain finite elements for torsion whose error we know.

16.9.1 Upper bound from the warping function

Take a prism in Saint-Venant torsion (definition 16.1) and try another function \(\tilde\psi\) in place of the true warping function \(\psi\), that is a trial displacement field \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha\tilde\psi\). By lemma 16.8 the two shear strains of this field are \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \alpha(\tilde\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z)\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \alpha(\tilde\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y)\). Write the pair \((\tilde\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z,\ \tilde\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y)\) as the vector \(\nabla\tilde\psi - \vek w\), where \(\vek w = (z, -y)\) is the field that every point of the section gets from the rotation of the section as a rigid body. The strain energy density is \(\tfrac12(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}) = \tfrac12 G\alpha^2\,|\nabla\tilde\psi - \vek w|^2\), and the energy per unit length of the prism is \(\tfrac12 G\alpha^2 F(\tilde\psi)\) with the integral

\[F(\tilde\psi) = \int_{\mathrm{S}} |\nabla\tilde\psi - \vek w|^2\,\mathrm{d}A , \qquad \vek w = (z, -y) . \tag{16.50}\]

The true warping function has energy \(\tfrac12 G J\alpha^2\) (by theorem 16.10 \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = GJ\alpha\), and the work of the moment over the twist \(\alpha\) is half the product). So we expect \(F(\psi) = J\) and \(F(\tilde\psi) \ge J\) for every other function. This is the principle of minimum total potential energy (theorem 4.91) for the twisting of a prism. We prove it directly, because a section is not a body of that theorem.

Lemma 16.51 Warping functional and an upper bound of \(J\) (funkcional zvitja in zgornja meja \(J\))

Let \(S\) be the section of a prism in Saint-Venant torsion with the warping function \(\psi\) of theorem 16.10, whose second derivatives are continuous in the interior and first derivatives continuous up to the boundary. Let \(S\) be cut into finitely many pieces \(S_1, \dots, S_{\mathrm{m}}\) for which lemma 16.9 holds also for fields continuously differentiable up to the boundary of the piece (for a triangle chapter 15 proves it), meeting along whole edges. Let \(\tilde\psi\) be continuous on \(S\) and continuously differentiable up to the boundary on every piece. Then:

  1. \(F(\psi) = J\).
  2. \(J \le F(\tilde\psi)\).
  3. Equality \(J = F(\tilde\psi)\) holds exactly when \(\tilde\psi - \psi\) is a constant.
Idea

The difference \(F(\tilde\psi) - F(\psi)\) is the energy of the difference of the fields, because the mixed term vanishes through equilibrium and the free lateral surface.

Proof
  1. Let \(\vek q = \nabla\psi - \vek w\) and \(g = \tilde\psi - \psi\). The field \(\vek q\) is continuous up to the boundary. Its divergence is \(\nabla^2\psi - (\partial z/\partial y + \partial(-y)/\partial z) = 0 - 0\), because \(\psi\) is harmonic and \(\partial z/\partial y = \partial y/\partial z = 0\). On the boundary \(\vek q\cdot\vek n = \partial\psi/\partial n - (z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,n_{\mathrm{z}}) = 0\) by the boundary condition of theorem 16.10.
  2. From \(\nabla\tilde\psi - \vek w = \vek q + \nabla g\) it follows that \(F(\tilde\psi) = \int_{\mathrm{S}}|\vek q|^2\,\mathrm{d}A + 2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\nabla g\cdot\vek q\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla g|^2\,\mathrm{d}A\), where the first term is \(F(\psi)\).
  3. On a piece \(S_{\mathrm{k}}\) the field \(g\,\vek q\) has divergence \(\nabla g\cdot\vek q + g\,\mathrm{div}\,\vek q = \nabla g\cdot\vek q\). By lemma 16.9, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{k}}\nabla g\cdot\vek q\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint_{\partial \mathrm{S}_\mathrm{k}}g\,\vek q\cdot\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  4. Add over the pieces. An edge that two pieces share has opposite normals for the two, while \(g\) and \(\vek q\) are continuous there, so the contributions cancel. On the boundary \(\partial S\) we have \(\vek q\cdot\vek n = 0\). So \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\nabla g\cdot\vek q\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\).
  5. From steps 2 and 4, \(F(\tilde\psi) = F(\psi) + \int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla g|^2\,\mathrm{d}A \ge F(\psi)\). Equality requires \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla g|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), so \(\nabla g = 0\) on every piece (a continuous nonnegative function with zero integral is zero everywhere, as in the proof of lemma 16.17). A continuous function with zero gradient on every piece is constant on a connected section.
  6. The function \(\tilde\psi = 0\) is one of the admissible ones (one piece). From step 5, \(F(0) = F(\psi) + \int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla\psi|^2\,\mathrm{d}A\), and \(F(0) = \int_{\mathrm{S}}(z^2 + y^2)\,\mathrm{d}A = I_{\mathrm{p}}\). By lemma 16.12, \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}} - \int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla\psi|^2\,\mathrm{d}A\), so \(F(\psi) = J\). This proves points 1 and 2, point 3 is in step 5.

Source: The idea is the principle of minimum energy from chapter 4, recast for twisting. The form of \(F\) and step 6 are ours, with the equations of section 16.2. SADD section 9.3.2 (PDF pp. 251-252) writes the same problem for the warping function with other letters (his \(z\) is the bar axis, the section has \(x\) and \(y\)).

The function \(\tilde\psi\) does not have to be chosen so that it satisfies the boundary condition \(\partial\tilde\psi/\partial n = z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\). That condition is natural, as zero force at a free end is for the bar (chapter 6), and the functional finds it itself. This is the whole strength of the lemma: it asks only for a continuous function.

We test the lemma on a circle of radius \(R = 20\) mm, where we know the answer. For the circle \(\psi = 0\) (theorem 16.3), \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}} = \pi R^4/2 = 251\,327\) mm\(^4\). Take \(\tilde\psi = c\,y z\) with an unknown number \(c\). Then \(\nabla\tilde\psi - \vek w = ((c - 1)z,\ (c + 1)y)\) and

\[F(c\,yz) = (c - 1)^2\int_{\mathrm{S}} z^2\,\mathrm{d}A + (c + 1)^2\int_{\mathrm{S}} y^2\,\mathrm{d}A = (c^2 + 1)\,I_{\mathrm{p}} , \tag{16.51}\]

because \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} y^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{S}} z^2\,\mathrm{d}A = I_{\mathrm{p}}/2\) (the circle is symmetric under swapping \(y\) and \(z\)) and the terms \(\mp 2c\) cancel. The smallest value is at \(c = 0\) and equals \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\), so it is exact. At \(c = 0{,}3\) we get \(F = 1{,}09\,I_{\mathrm{p}} = 273\,947\) mm\(^4\), which is \(9{,}00\) % above \(J\). So the bound holds, and it also says that the warping function of the circle really is zero: every \(c \ne 0\) adds energy.

16.9.2 Lower bound from Prandtl's function

With the warping we caught \(J\) from above. Now we need it from below. Divide Prandtl's function by \(G\alpha\) to get \(\hat\Phi = \Phi/(G\alpha)\). By theorem 16.16 we then have \(\nabla^2\hat\Phi = -2\) in \(S\), \(\hat\Phi = 0\) on \(\partial S\) and \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A = GJ\alpha\), so

\[J = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\hat\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{16.52}\]

The function \(\hat\Phi\) has units mm\(^2\), and we see it as Prandtl's function for \(G\alpha = 1\).

Lemma 16.52 Prandtl functional and a lower bound of \(J\) (funkcional Prandtlove funkcije in spodnja meja \(J\))

Let \(S\) be a section as in theorem 16.16 with \(\hat\Phi\) twice continuously differentiable up to the boundary, cut into pieces as in lemma 16.51. Let \(f\) be continuous on \(S\), continuously differentiable up to the boundary on every piece, \(f = 0\) on \(\partial S\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f|^2\,\mathrm{d}A > 0\). Then

\[J \ge \frac{4\Big(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\Big)^2}{\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f|^2\,\mathrm{d}A} , \tag{16.53}\]

and equality holds exactly when \(f = c\,\hat\Phi\) for some constant \(c\).

Idea

The square \(|\nabla f - t\nabla\hat\Phi|^2\) is nonnegative for every \(t\). We choose the best \(t\).

Proof
  1. The field \(f\,\nabla\hat\Phi\) has divergence \(\nabla f\cdot\nabla\hat\Phi + f\,\nabla^2\hat\Phi = \nabla f\cdot\nabla\hat\Phi - 2f\) on a piece. By lemma 16.9 on every piece the integral equals the flux through the boundary of the piece. When we add, the contributions of a shared edge cancel (the fields \(f\) and \(\nabla\hat\Phi\) are continuous, the normals are opposite), and on the boundary of the section \(f = 0\). So \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\nabla f\cdot\nabla\hat\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\).
  2. For \(f = \hat\Phi\), step 1 and equation (16.52) give \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla\hat\Phi|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\hat\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A = J\).
  3. For every real number \(t\), \(0 \le \int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f - t\nabla\hat\Phi|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f|^2\,\mathrm{d}A - 4t\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A + t^2J\) by steps 1 and 2.
  4. At \(t = \frac{2}{J}\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\) this is \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f|^2\,\mathrm{d}A - \frac{4}{J}\big(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\big)^2 \ge 0\). Multiply by \(J > 0\) and divide by \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f|^2\,\mathrm{d}A\).
  5. Equality requires \(\nabla f = t\nabla\hat\Phi\) everywhere, so \(f - t\hat\Phi\) is a constant that is zero on the boundary.

Source: The computation is ours, with the equations of section 16.3. The assumption of two derivatives up to the boundary carries the same reservation as lemma 16.15: for a rectangle the second derivatives jump at the corners and the cut near a corner is not proved, SADD cites it (PDF pp. 246-251). The lower bound for the rectangle in this section therefore rests on that cited step.

In the language of energy the lemma is the principle of minimum complementary energy (theorem 4.100). By section 16.3 the stresses from any \(f\) are in equilibrium and the free lateral surface is unloaded, and the complementary energy per unit length is \(\tfrac{1}{2G}\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f|^2\,\mathrm{d}A\) at the moment \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\). The true stress picture has the smallest complementary energy \(M_{\mathrm{x}}^2/(2GJ)\). The same inequality follows. The lemma also says what matters about \(f\): the function must be zero on the whole boundary, and its height plays no role, since it cancels in the quotient. We test this.

On a circle of radius \(R\) take \(f = R^2 - r^2\), which is the exact shape (section 16.1). The integrals over the circle by the polar change of variables of theorem 4.59 are \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = 2\pi\int_0^R(R^2 - r^2)\,r\,\mathrm{d}r = \pi R^4/2\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = 2\pi\int_0^R 4r^2\cdot r\,\mathrm{d}r = 2\pi R^4\), and the quotient \(4(\pi R^4/2)^2/(2\pi R^4) = \pi R^4/2 = I_{\mathrm{p}}\) equals the exact value. By contrast \(f = (R^2 - r^2)^2\) has a zero on the boundary but the wrong shape: \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = \pi R^6/3\), \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = 4\pi R^8/3\), and the lower bound is \(\pi R^4/3 = \tfrac23I_{\mathrm{p}}\), which is \(167\,552\) mm\(^4\) at \(R = 20\) mm, \(33{,}33\) % below \(J\). The bound holds but is poor.

16.9.3 Bounds on the \(20 \times 40\) mm strip

Now take the strip of section 16.5 with half sides \(a = 10\) mm along \(y\) and \(b = 20\) mm along \(z\), where we know the exact value \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\) from the series and use it only for comparison. For the lower bound we need a function that is zero on all four sides. Such a function is \(f = (a^2 - y^2)(b^2 - z^2)\), the function \(\Phi_{\mathrm{t}}\) of example 16.21, which was not a solution of the equation there. Here its accuracy does not matter, because we are only looking for the best function of this form.

We draw it together with the true function [figure 16.33]. Everywhere it is the same \(20 \times 40\) mm section, at the scale \(0{,}8\) cm per \(10\) mm, with the \(y\) axis across the width and the \(z\) axis along the length. In the left section are the level lines of the function \(f\) at \(0{,}2\), \(0{,}4\), \(0{,}6\) and \(0{,}8\) of the peak, with the peak \(100\) mm\(^2\) at the centre (\(f\) has been multiplied by the constant \(c = 0{,}0025\), which the quotient (16.53) does not feel). In the middle section are the same lines of the true function \(\hat\Phi\), computed with the series of section 16.5, with peak \(91{,}1\) mm\(^2\). Both families are rounded closed curves, but the true lines are flatter near the middle of the longer side, because there \(\hat\Phi\) changes more slowly with \(z\). On the axis \(y = 0\), \(\hat\Phi\) falls from \(z = 0\) to \(z = 5\) mm by \(3{,}2\) % (from \(91{,}10\) to \(88{,}21\) mm\(^2\)), the trial function by \(6{,}25\) %. In a very long strip \(\hat\Phi\) would be nearly independent of \(z\) in the middle (section 16.6), at the ratio \(2\) this is only beginning.

We compute the quotient (16.53) for \(f\). The integrals are \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{-\mathrm{a}}^{a}(a^2 - y^2)\,\mathrm{d}y\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}(b^2 - z^2)\,\mathrm{d}z = \tfrac{4a^3}{3}\cdot\tfrac{4b^3}{3} = 14\,222\,222\) mm\(^4\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \tfrac{128}{45}a^3b^3(a^2 + b^2) = 1{,}1378\cdot10^{10}\) mm\(^6\) (the term \(4y^2(b^2 - z^2)^2\) and the term \(4z^2(a^2 - y^2)^2\) give \(\tfrac{128}{45}a^3b^5\) and \(\tfrac{128}{45}a^5b^3\)). The quotient is \(\tfrac{40}{9}\,a^3b^3/(a^2 + b^2) = 71\,111\) mm\(^4\), which is \(-2{,}82\) % relative to \(J\). Since the trial function has only the form \(c\,(a^2 - y^2)(b^2 - z^2)\), we add a term in \(y^2\) with a second free constant: \(f = (a^2 - y^2)(b^2 - z^2)(c_1 + c_2y^2/a^2)\). The best choice (\(c_1 = 0{,}002476\), \(c_2 = 0{,}0001268\), from \(\partial/\partial c_1 = \partial/\partial c_2 = 0\) of the functional \(\tfrac12\int|\nabla f|^2 - 2\int f\)) gives \(71\,152\) mm\(^4\), \(-2{,}77\) %. The extra parameter improved the bound by barely \(0{,}05\) percentage points, because the error is not in the shape across the width (there the true function is nearly a parabola) but along the length, where the trial function has no flat part. For a thinner strip this gets worse: when \(b/a\) goes beyond all limits, \(\tfrac{40}{9}a^3b^3/(a^2 + b^2) \to \tfrac{40}{9}a^3b\), while the thin strip has by section 16.6 \(J \to \tfrac{16}{3}a^3b\), so the ratio is \(5/6\) and the error tends to \(-16{,}7\) %. The error \(-2{,}82\) % holds for the ratio \(2\), not for every strip.

Example 16.53 A function that is not zero on the whole boundary is no lower bound (funkcija, ki ni nič na vsem robu, ni spodnja meja)

Try \(f_2 = b^2 - z^2\) with peak \(b^2 = 400\) mm\(^2\). This function is zero on the shorter sides \(z = \pm b\), but on the long sides \(y = \pm a\) (the thick lines in the figure) it is not. The computation by equation (16.53) nevertheless gives \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f_2\,\mathrm{d}A = 2a\cdot\tfrac{4b^3}{3} = 213\,333\) mm\(^4\), \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f_2|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = 2a\cdot\tfrac{8b^3}{3} = 426\,667\) mm\(^6\) and the quotient \(426\,667\) mm\(^4\), which is \(5{,}83\,J\). That is more than \(J\), so it is not a bound. Step 1 of the proof of lemma 16.52 has failed: the boundary term \(\oint f_2\,\partial\hat\Phi/\partial n\,\mathrm{d}s\) on the long sides \(y = \pm a\) is not zero, because \(f_2\) is not zero there and \(\partial\hat\Phi/\partial n\) is largest in absolute value there (the shear stress is largest at the middle of the long side, section 16.5). The same failure happens for \(f = 1\): the gradient is zero and the quotient has no value, because the denominator vanishes, and at the same time \(f\) is not zero on the boundary. The lemma asks for both, zero on the whole boundary and nonzero energy.

For the upper bound we need trial warping functions. The rectangle is a single piece and lemma 16.9 holds for it. Try \(\tilde\psi = k\,yz\), where \(k\) is a number. As for the circle, \(\nabla\tilde\psi - \vek w = ((k - 1)z,\ (k + 1)y)\) and

\[F(k\,yz) = (k - 1)^2\int_{\mathrm{S}} z^2\,\mathrm{d}A + (k + 1)^2\int_{\mathrm{S}} y^2\,\mathrm{d}A , \qquad \int_{\mathrm{S}} y^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \tfrac{4a^3b}{3} = 26\,667 , \quad \int_{\mathrm{S}} z^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \tfrac{4ab^3}{3} = 106\,667 \ \text{mm}^4 . \tag{16.54}\]

At \(k = 0\) (no warping, the assumption of section 16.1) \(F = I_{\mathrm{p}} = 133\,333\) mm\(^4\), \(82{,}2\) % above \(J\). At \(k = 0{,}3\), \(F = 97\,333\) (\(+33{,}0\) %). The derivative with respect to \(k\) is zero at \(k^* = (\int_{\mathrm{S}} z^2 - \int_{\mathrm{S}} y^2)/I_{\mathrm{p}} = (b^2 - a^2)/(a^2 + b^2) = 0{,}600\), and then \(F = 4\int_{\mathrm{S}} y^2\int_{\mathrm{S}} z^2/I_{\mathrm{p}} = 85\,333\) mm\(^4\) (\(+16{,}6\) %). The same \(k^*\) is also the warping function of the ellipse with the same semi-axes (theorem 16.18). At \(k = 1\), \(F = 4\int_{\mathrm{S}} y^2 = \tfrac{16}{3}a^3b = 106\,667\) mm\(^4\). This is exactly the thin-strip value \(h\,t^3/3\) with \(h = 2b = 40\) mm and \(t = 2a = 20\) mm. So the function \(yz\) is the warping of the thin strip, and the upper estimate \(J < ht^3/3\) of theorem 16.33 is, for the rectangle, a consequence of lemma 16.51.

We put all the bounds on a number line [figure 16.34]. We draw the axis for \(J\) in units of \(10^3\) mm\(^4\) from \(60\) to \(140\), with marks every \(20\). On it sits the exact value \(J = 73{,}178\) from the series. To the left of it is the lower bound \(71{,}111\) from the function \(f\). To the right is the upper bound \(85{,}333\) from \(k = 0{,}6\), and also \(106{,}667\) (\(k = 1\)) and \(133{,}333\) (\(k = 0\)), which are worse.

The lower bound is \(2{,}82\) % from the exact value, the best upper bound \(16{,}6\) %. The difference is in the trial functions. The true warping function of the strip is by equation (16.33) \(yz\) minus a series that corrects \(yz\) near the shorter sides \(z = \pm b\). With one number \(k\) we cannot capture that correction. The trial function \(f\), on the other hand, has almost exactly the right shape across the width and lacks only the flat part.

Theorem 16.54 Bounds of the torsion constant (meji torzijske konstante)

Let \(S\) be a section of lemma 16.52 and lemma 16.51. Then for every trial function \(f\) of lemma 16.52 and every trial function \(\tilde\psi\) of lemma 16.51

\[\frac{4\Big(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\Big)^2}{\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f|^2\,\mathrm{d}A} \ \le\ J\ \le\ F(\tilde\psi) . \tag{16.55}\]

For the \(20 \times 40\) mm strip (\(a = 10\) mm, \(b = 20\) mm) it therefore holds that

\[71\,111\ \text{mm}^4 \ \le\ J\ \le\ 85\,333\ \text{mm}^4 , \tag{16.56}\]

with \(f = (a^2 - y^2)(b^2 - z^2)\) and \(\tilde\psi = 0{,}6\,yz\). At \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m and \(G = 75{,}385\) GPa the twist per unit length \(\alpha = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(GJ)\) is therefore between \(0{,}00777\) and \(0{,}00933\) rad/m.

Idea

The left inequality is lemma 16.52, the right one lemma 16.51. The numbers only have to be computed.

Proof
  1. The left inequality (16.55) is lemma 16.52, the right one lemma 16.51.
  2. For \(f\) on the strip: \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = 14\,222\,222\) mm\(^4\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = 1{,}1378\cdot10^{10}\) mm\(^6\) (above), the quotient is \(71\,111\) mm\(^4\).
  3. For \(\tilde\psi = 0{,}6\,yz\), by equation (16.54), \(F = 0{,}16\cdot106\,667 + 2{,}56\cdot26\,667 = 17\,067 + 68\,267 = 85\,333\) mm\(^4\).
  4. Twist: \(\alpha = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(GJ)\) with \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\,000\) N mm and \(G = 75\,385\) N/mm\(^2\) equals \(7{,}77\cdot10^{-6}\) rad/mm \(= 0{,}00777\) rad/m at \(J = 85\,333\) mm\(^4\), and \(0{,}00933\) rad/m at \(J = 71\,111\) mm\(^4\).

Source: Inequality (16.55) and the numbers are ours (num-09.py). SADD in Example 16.4 (PDF pp. 535-536) solves Prandtl's equation with linear triangular elements, but gives no bounds for the torsion constant.

The exact value \(0{,}00906\) rad/m lies in this range, which is \(19{,}4\) % of \(J\) wide. For an engineer this is already useful: the shaft has a stiffness of at least \(G\cdot71\,111\ \text{mm}^4 = 5361\) N m\(^2\) and at most \(6433\) N m\(^2\), and for the torsional twist we get a bound that depends on no series.

16.9.4 Mesh of triangles

Two bounds on a section raise a question: how to find better trial functions when we do not know by shape where the true one is flat? The answer is the same as for the bar in chapter 7. We cut the section into pieces and write the function on every piece as a straight line, in the plane as a linear function. The pieces are triangles, because three values at the corners determine a linear function \(c_0 + c_1y + c_2z\) exactly.

For the \(20 \times 40\) mm strip we take a mesh. We cut the section into \(n \times 2n\) squares and each of them with one diagonal into two right isosceles triangles. The figure shows \(n = 2\): squares of side \(10\) mm, \(2\) across the width and \(4\) along the length, \(16\) triangles in all. The corners of the triangles are nodes (vozlišča). In the figure there are \(15\) of them, of which 12 on the boundary (open circles) and 3 free (filled circles), inside the section on the line \(y = 0\) at \(z = -10\), \(0\), \(10\) mm.

Definition 16.55 Triangle mesh and piecewise linear function (mreža trikotnikov in odsekoma linearna funkcija)

A triangle mesh (mreža trikotnikov) of the section \(S\) is a cut of \(S\) into finitely many triangles that meet along whole edges or at corners, and whose edges cover \(\partial S\). A piecewise linear function (odsekoma linearna funkcija) \(f_{\mathrm{h}}\) is a continuous function on \(S\) that is linear on every triangle. It is determined by the values at the nodes, \(f_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}N_{\mathrm{i}}\), where \(N_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the piecewise linear function with value \(1\) at node \(i\) and \(0\) at the other nodes (shape function, oblikovna funkcija).

Explanation

It is continuous because the edge shared by two triangles carries on both a linear function of one variable with equal values at the end points, hence the same function. The shape functions are the same as for the bar in chapter 7 (definition 7.2), only we have pieces of a plane instead of pieces of a line.

Source: The definition is ours. The linear triangle in its general form will come in chapter 15.

First look at what one of the triangles does [figure 16.36]. The shaded triangle in the upper left corner has nodes 1, 2 and 3, node 1 at the right angle. Since the integral \(\int|\nabla f_{\mathrm{h}}|^2\) over it depends only on three values, we write it with a matrix that is a special case of the element matrix for heat conduction (chapter 14), because the operator is the same.

Lemma 16.56 Matrix of a right isosceles triangle (matrika enakokrakega pravokotnega trikotnika)

Let a triangle with legs of length \(s\) have node 1 at the right angle and nodes 2 and 3 on the legs. Let \(f_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^3\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}N_{\mathrm{i}}\) be linear on it. Then

\[\int|\nabla f_{\mathrm{h}}|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \vek\varphi^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\vek\varphi , \qquad \mat K_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac12\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} , \tag{16.57}\]

independent of \(s\), and \(\int N_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}A = s^2/6\) for all three nodes.

Idea

Gradients of linear functions are constant, so the integral is the area times the scalar product of the gradients.

Proof
  1. The scalar product \(\nabla N_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\nabla N_{\mathrm{j}}\) does not change under a rotation of the coordinates (a rotation preserves scalar products). So we may take coordinates \(\xi\), \(\eta\) along the legs with node 1 at the origin, node 2 at \((s, 0)\) and node 3 at \((0, s)\).
  2. The linear functions with value \(1\) at their own node and \(0\) at the others are \(N_1 = 1 - \xi/s - \eta/s\), \(N_2 = \xi/s\), \(N_3 = \eta/s\). Their gradients \((-1, -1)/s\), \((1, 0)/s\) and \((0, 1)/s\) are constant.
  3. The area is \(A = s^2/2\). The entry \((\mat K_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{ij}} = A\,\nabla N_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\nabla N_{\mathrm{j}}\) is for \(i = j = 1\) equal to \(\tfrac{s^2}{2}\cdot\tfrac{2}{s^2} = 1\), for \((1, 2)\) and \((1, 3)\) it is \(\tfrac{s^2}{2}\cdot\tfrac{-1}{s^2} = -\tfrac12\), for \((2, 2)\) and \((3, 3)\) it is \(\tfrac12\), for \((2, 3)\) it is \(0\). The length \(s\) cancels.
  4. The integral \(\int N_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}A = A/3\) for a linear shape function of a triangle is proved in chapter 15 (the formula for the integral of area coordinates). With \(A = s^2/2\) this is \(s^2/6\).

Source: The computation is ours. We checked the matrix with \(s = 20\), \(10\), \(5\) mm in NumPy (num-09.py): the difference from the tabulated matrix is zero. COOK (PDF p. 483) states that torsion, with the warping function or with Prandtl's stress function, is described by the same equation as plane steady heat conduction, for the warping function with \(k = 1\).

The row sum \(1 - \tfrac12 - \tfrac12 = 0\) says that a constant function costs nothing, as for a bar without supports (lemma 7.16): this property will matter at once. All triangles of the mesh have legs along \(y\) or \(z\) and differ only in which corner has the right angle. Each contributes its matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\) at the places of its three nodes in the global matrix \(\mat K\), as when assembling bars (theorem 7.13). The sum over all triangles gives \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f_{\mathrm{h}}|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \vek\varphi^\T\mat K\vek\varphi\).

Prandtl's function on the mesh

Take a piecewise linear \(f_{\mathrm{h}}\) with value zero at all boundary nodes. Since the boundary of the section consists of triangle edges, \(f_{\mathrm{h}}\) is zero on the whole boundary too (a linear function with zero values at the ends of an edge is zero there). So \(f_{\mathrm{h}}\) is admissible in lemma 16.52. With the vector \(\vek b\) whose entry \(b_{\mathrm{i}} = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}} N_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) is twice the integral of the shape function (from lemma 16.56), \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f_{\mathrm{h}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \tfrac12\vek b^\T\vek\varphi\) and the quotient of the lemma is \((\vek b^\T\vek\varphi)^2/(\vek\varphi^\T\mat K\vek\varphi)\). Its largest value among functions with a zero on the boundary is the solution of the system

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{pp}}\,\vek\varphi = \vek b_{\mathrm{p}} , \qquad J_{\mathrm{h}}^{\Phi} = \vek b_{\mathrm{p}}^\T\vek\varphi = \vek\varphi^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{pp}}\vek\varphi , \tag{16.58}\]

where the index \(p\) marks only the free nodes. The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{pp}}\) is positive definite: if \(\vek\varphi^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{pp}}\vek\varphi = \int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla f_{\mathrm{h}}|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), then \(f_{\mathrm{h}}\) is constant and hence zero, since it is zero on the boundary. The largest value of the quotient is indeed \(\vek b_{\mathrm{p}}^\T\vek\varphi\), because for every other \(\vek\varphi'\) we have \((\vek b_{\mathrm{p}}^\T\vek\varphi')^2 = (\vek\varphi'^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{pp}}\vek\varphi)^2 \le (\vek\varphi'^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{pp}}\vek\varphi')(\vek\varphi^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{pp}}\vek\varphi)\) (the same computation with a square as in the proof of lemma 16.52, with \(\int|\nabla\cdot|^2\) replaced by \(\vek\varphi^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{pp}}\vek\varphi\)). For a node in the interior, the six triangles around it (at the right angle in two of them, at an acute angle in four) add up to \(K_{\mathrm{ii}} = 2\cdot1 + 4\cdot\tfrac12 = 4\), each of the four neighbours on legs gives \(-1\), and the neighbours on the diagonal give \(0\). Let us look at \(n = 2\).

For \(n = 2\) every free node has six triangles of area \(50\) mm\(^2\), so \(b_{\mathrm{i}} = 2\cdot6\cdot50/3 = 200\) mm\(^2\). The neighbours to the left and right lie on the boundary, where the value is zero, so the equations at the three free nodes have the form

\[4\varphi_1 - \varphi_2 = 200 , \qquad -\varphi_1 + 4\varphi_2 - \varphi_3 = 200 , \qquad -\varphi_2 + 4\varphi_3 = 200 . \tag{16.59}\]

From the symmetry \(\varphi_1 = \varphi_3\) and from the first equation \(\varphi_2 = 4\varphi_1 - 200\), into the second: \(-2\varphi_1 + 16\varphi_1 - 800 = 200\), so \(\varphi_1 = 71{,}43\) and \(\varphi_2 = 85{,}71\) mm\(^2\) (these are the numbers beside the free nodes in the figure). The true value at the centre is \(91{,}1\) mm\(^2\). The lower bound is \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\Phi = 200\,(71{,}43 + 85{,}71 + 71{,}43) = 45\,714\) mm\(^4\), \(37{,}5\) % below \(J\).

Warping function on the mesh

For the upper bound take a piecewise linear \(\tilde\psi_{\mathrm{h}}\) with values \(\vek\psi\) at all nodes, since there is no condition on the boundary. By equation (16.50), \(F(\tilde\psi_{\mathrm{h}}) = \vek\psi^\T\mat K\vek\psi - 2\vek\psi^\T\vek b_{\mathrm{w}} + I_{\mathrm{p}}\), where \((b_{\mathrm{w}})_{\mathrm{i}} = \int_{\mathrm{S}}\nabla N_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek w\,\mathrm{d}A\). The field \(\vek w = (z, -y)\) is linear and \(\nabla N_{\mathrm{i}}\) is constant on a triangle, so the contribution of a triangle is the area times the value at the centroid (the integral of a linear function over a triangle, chapter 15). At \(\mat K\vek\psi = \vek b_{\mathrm{w}}\) the smallest value is \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\psi = I_{\mathrm{p}} - \vek\psi^\T\vek b_{\mathrm{w}} = I_{\mathrm{p}} - \vek\psi^\T\mat K\vek\psi\), because for any other vector \(\vek\psi + \vek d\) the value of \(F\) is larger by \(\vek d^\T\mat K\vek d = \int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla d_{\mathrm{h}}|^2\,\mathrm{d}A \ge 0\), where \(d_{\mathrm{h}}\) is the piecewise linear function with the values \(\vek d\).

Example 16.57 The warping matrix without a fixed node is singular (matrika zvitja brez pritrjenega vozlišča je singularna)

For \(n = 2\) take all \(15\) nodes as free. The row sums of \(\mat K\) are zero (step 3 of lemma 16.56), so \(\mat K\) has the eigenvector \((1, \dots, 1)\) with eigenvalue zero: NumPy gives the smallest eigenvalue \(2{,}2\cdot10^{-17}\) and the second \(0{,}250\). The matrix is singular, so the system \(\mat K\vek\psi = \vek b_{\mathrm{w}}\) has no unique solution. This is not an error of the mesh: the warping function is determined up to a constant, as in lemma 16.11, and \(\tilde\psi_{\mathrm{h}} + c\) has the same energy. At the same time \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}(b_{\mathrm{w}})_{\mathrm{i}} = \int_{\mathrm{S}}\nabla(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}})\cdot\vek w\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), because \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\) and the gradient of a constant is zero, so the system is solvable. We fix one node, the lower left one (the square in the right figure), \(\psi_1 = 0\), and the matrix becomes positive definite: from \(\vek\psi^\T\mat K\vek\psi = 0\) it follows that \(\nabla\tilde\psi_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\), so a constant function, zero at the fixed node. The result is \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\psi = 87\,619\) mm\(^4\). If we fix the node at the centre or at the opposite corner \((a, b)\) instead, \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\psi\) is the same (\(87\,619\)), and the two fields differ only by a constant (the largest difference after subtracting the mean is \(1{,}6\cdot10^{-13}\) mm\(^2\)). Without fixing, a program reports a singular matrix, with fixing the answer does not depend on the choice of node.

The example answers a question every program must have: which node do we fix? The answer is any, because \(F\) does not feel a constant. For Prandtl's function this question does not arise, because the boundary is already fixed by the zero.

Corollary 16.58 Bounds from a triangle mesh (meje iz mreže trikotnikov)

Let the section \(S\) be a polygon that meets the assumptions of lemmas 16.51 and 16.52, and \(\mathcal{T}\) a triangle mesh (definition 16.55). Then

\[J_{\mathrm{h}}^\Phi\ \le\ J\ \le\ J_{\mathrm{h}}^\psi , \tag{16.60}\]

where \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\Phi\) is the solution of equation (16.58) and \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\psi = I_{\mathrm{p}} - \vek\psi^\T\mat K\vek\psi\) for \(\mat K\vek\psi = \vek b_{\mathrm{w}}\). If \(\mathcal{T}'\) is obtained from \(\mathcal{T}\) so that every triangle is a union of triangles of \(\mathcal{T}'\), then \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\Phi(\mathcal{T}) \le J_{\mathrm{h}}^\Phi(\mathcal{T}')\) and \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\psi(\mathcal{T}') \le J_{\mathrm{h}}^\psi(\mathcal{T})\).

Idea

The bounds are lemma 16.52 and lemma 16.51 with piecewise linear functions. A finer mesh has more functions, so the maximum is larger and the minimum smaller.

Proof
  1. A piecewise linear function with zero values at the boundary nodes is zero on the boundary, continuous and continuously differentiable on every triangle, so admissible in lemma 16.52. By equation (16.58), \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\Phi\) is the largest value of the quotient over all such functions, so by the lemma \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\Phi \le J\).
  2. Every piecewise linear function is admissible in lemma 16.51, and \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\psi\) is the smallest \(F\) over all these functions, so \(J \le J_{\mathrm{h}}^\psi\).
  3. If every triangle of \(\mathcal{T}\) is a union of triangles of \(\mathcal{T}'\), every function linear on the triangles of \(\mathcal{T}\) is also linear on the smaller ones, and continuity is kept. The space of functions for \(\mathcal{T}\) is thus a part of the space for \(\mathcal{T}'\). A maximum over a larger set is not smaller, a minimum over a larger set is not larger.

Source: The inequality and the numbers are ours (num-09.py). The lower bound for a rectangle requires the step that lemma 16.52 cites at a corner (see there).

On the strip, for the mesh in which every square is divided into four (from \(n\) to \(2n\)) and every triangle becomes a union of four smaller ones, point 3 holds. We checked it: the function of the mesh \(n = 2\), drawn on the mesh \(n = 4\), has the same value of the quotient (\(45\,714\) mm\(^4\)), and likewise \(n = 4\) and \(n = 8\) (\(65\,284\) mm\(^4\)).

\(n\) triangles free nodes \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\Phi\) [mm\(^4\)] error \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\psi\) [mm\(^4\)] error gap \((J_{\mathrm{h}}^\psi - J_{\mathrm{h}}^\Phi)/J\)
1 4 0 0 \(-100\) % 106 667 \(+45{,}8\) % \(145{,}8\) %
2 16 3 45 714 \(-37{,}5\) % 87 619 \(+19{,}7\) % \(57{,}3\) %
4 64 21 65 284 \(-10{,}8\) % 77 610 \(+6{,}06\) % \(16{,}8\) %
8 256 105 71 113 \(-2{,}82\) % 74 366 \(+1{,}62\) % \(4{,}45\) %
16 1024 465 72 654 \(-0{,}72\) % 73 482 \(+0{,}41\) % \(1{,}13\) %

We draw the table [figure 16.35]. The axis \(n\) has equal spacing for each doubling (\(1, 2, 4, 8, 16\)), the vertical axis is \(J_{\mathrm{h}}\) in \(10^3\) mm\(^4\). The horizontal line at \(73{,}178\) is the exact value from the series. The lower curve shows the values \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\Phi\), which rise from below, the upper one the values \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\psi\), which fall from above. The grey band between them is the gap in which \(J\) lies and which narrows.

From the table we read four things. First, in every row the two values are on the right sides of \(J\): \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\Phi < 73\,178 < J_{\mathrm{h}}^\psi\). Second, the error falls about fourfold at each doubling of \(n\) (\(-37{,}5\), \(-10{,}8\), \(-2{,}82\), \(-0{,}72\) %, ratios \(3{,}5\), \(3{,}8\), \(3{,}9\), and for the warping \(3{,}3\), \(3{,}7\), \(3{,}9\)), which is an observation from the table, not a theorem of this chapter. Third, at \(n = 8\) the value \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\Phi = 71\,113\) is almost equal to \(71\,111\) from the one trial function \(f\), which needed one number instead of \(105\) unknowns: a good shape is worth more than a fine mesh. Fourth, the gap is something we get from no mesh without bounds: at \(n = 16\), \(J\) lies between \(72\,654\) and \(73\,482\), the midpoint \(73\,068\) is \(0{,}15\) % below \(J\) and the largest error of the midpoint that the two bounds guarantee is \(0{,}57\) %. This holds without knowing \(J\), and the series confirms it. At \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m the twist \(\alpha\) is between \(0{,}00903\) and \(0{,}00913\) rad/m, the exact value is \(0{,}00906\).

Example 16.59 A mesh with no free node (mreža brez prostega vozlišča)

For \(n = 1\) the mesh has \(6\) nodes, all on the boundary, and \(4\) triangles. No node is free, so \(\vek\varphi = 0\) and \(J_{\mathrm{h}}^\Phi = 0\). Lemma 16.52 is not applicable for \(f_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) (\(\int|\nabla f_{\mathrm{h}}|^2 = 0\)), and the bound \(0 \le J\) holds but says nothing, so the row \(-100\) % in the table is not a program error. The upper bound at \(n = 1\) is \(106\,667\) mm\(^4\), \(45{,}8\) % above \(J\). A mesh becomes useful only when it has free nodes, as at \(n = 2\) (three free nodes, gap \(57{,}3\) %).

The mesh \(n = 2\) is one picture of everything: the values of \(\hat\Phi_{\mathrm{h}}\) at the free nodes on the left and the mesh for the warping \(\psi_{\mathrm{h}}\) on the right, with the fixed node. Which of the two meshes gives the lower and which the upper bound is told by inequality (16.60): on the left \(\hat\Phi_{\mathrm{h}}\) (value zero on the whole boundary) gives \(45\,714\), on the right \(\psi_{\mathrm{h}}\) (no condition on the boundary) gives \(87\,619\) mm\(^4\).

From history

Chapter 6 said in section 6.7 that at a lecture in 1941 Courant divided the problem of torsion of a hollow shaft into triangles and interpolated the stress function on each by straight lines from the values at the nodes (COOK, PDF p. 24). The stress function of torsion is in section 16.3 Prandtl's function, so Courant's interpolation by straight lines on triangles is exactly the piecewise linear function \(f_{\mathrm{h}}\) of this section, and its value at the nodes is the unknown of system (16.58). Courant treated a hollow shaft, where on a hole there is one more condition (section 16.8), which this section does not include.

Let us sum up what we have seen, because this section leans on several chapters. The warping function gives an upper bound of \(J\) (lemma 16.51, the principle of minimum potential energy), Prandtl's function a lower one (lemma 16.52, the principle of minimum complementary energy), both from arbitrary continuous functions, with no boundary conditions for \(\tilde\psi\) and with a zero on the boundary for \(f\). On a mesh of triangles both bounds become linear systems with the same matrix \(\mat K\), as for heat conduction in chapter 14 with source \(2\) and zero temperature on the boundary: the operator is the same, the phenomenon is not. The upper bound needs one node fixed, the lower does not. The one step that remained unproved is for the rectangle at the corners (lemma 16.52), and the numbers of the series and of the meshes agree with the two bounds.

16.10 Connections

The course abbreviations are the same as in section 1.19.

Earlier chapters took three things as a model, because we did not yet have torsion: chapter 12 took the equation \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = G J\,\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}'\) (equation (12.16)) with the number \(J\) as data, chapter 13 took \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = G I_{\mathrm{p}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\) (equation (13.14)) for the round shaft, and chapter 9 took the stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{t}}\) of a shaft under a disc. This chapter derived all three for a shaft in uniform torsion (section 16.1), and for the vibrating round shaft we check equation (13.14) below. Now we put them on one shaft and test them on numbers: what happens to the vibration of a shaft when the circle is replaced by the \(20 \times 40\) mm strip of chapter 12. The question is concrete: by how much does the first natural frequency change, which part of the shaft model must we replace and which may we keep.

Take the shaft of section 13.3. It is fixed in a wall at \(x = 0\), has length \(L = 1\) m and a free end at \(x = L\), and is made of steel (\(G = 75{,}385\) GPa, \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m\(^3\)). In the figure, in the first mode of vibration given by theorem 13.18 (b), each cross section is turned by \(\varphi(x) = \varphi_0 \sin(\pi x/2L)\), and as the curve below the shaft shows, the rotation grows from zero at the wall to its largest value at the free end. The line on a section is the rotation we see, so the rotation \(\varphi_0\) in the figure is greatly enlarged.

Chapter 13 found for the round shaft the speed \(c_{\mathrm{T}} = \sqrt{G/\rho} = 3108{,}8\) m/s and the frequency \(f_1 = c_{\mathrm{T}}/(4L) = 777{,}2\) Hz (theorem 13.18). What changes for the strip? The proof of theorem 13.16 has two steps that we must repeat, and each has its reason. The first is the angular momentum of a piece of the shaft. The section still turns about the axis as a rigid body (besides that it warps, see below), so per unit length it has angular momentum \(\rho I_{\mathrm{p}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{t}}\) with the same polar second moment \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 133\,333\) mm\(^4\) of the \(20 \times 40\) mm section, because angular momentum depends only on how the mass is spread around the axis. The second is the moment with which the neighbouring part of the shaft acts on the piece. That is no longer \(G I_{\mathrm{p}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\). By theorem 16.10 it is \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = G J\,\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\) with the torsion constant \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\) of theorem 16.30, and \(J = 0{,}549\,I_{\mathrm{p}}\) by lemma 16.12. The law of angular momentum for a piece \([a, b]\) gives, with the same steps 3 to 6 as in theorem 13.16,

\[\rho I_{\mathrm{p}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{tt}} = G J\,\varphi_{\mathrm{xx}} , \qquad c = \sqrt{\frac{G J}{\rho I_{\mathrm{p}}}} = c_{\mathrm{T}}\sqrt{\frac{J}{I_{\mathrm{p}}}} = 0{,}7408\,c_{\mathrm{T}} . \tag{16.61}\]

Hence \(c = 2303{,}1\) m/s and \(f_1 = c/(4L) = 575{,}8\) Hz. In the figure the arrow from the circle to the strip shows this: the frequency is multiplied by \(\sqrt{J/I_{\mathrm{p}}}\). Below each section stand its \(J\) and its frequency. The circle is the fixed term of the comparison: for it \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}}\), because a circle does not warp (corollary 16.13).

What would we get if for the strip we stayed with the model of chapter 13, that is replaced \(J\) by \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\)? This is the near miss, which fails the test. Equation (16.61) would have \(c = c_{\mathrm{T}}\) and \(f_1 = 777{,}2\) Hz, that is \(35{,}0\) % too much. The reason is the same as for the frame in chapter 12, where \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) in place of \(J\) gave a displacement from the twisting of the column of \(4{,}97\) mm instead of \(9{,}06\) mm (\(45\) % too little) and a total displacement of point \(C\) of \(11{,}35\) mm instead of \(15{,}44\) mm (\(26\) % too little): the strip is softer in torsion than \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) says, because the section warps, while the mass stays. In vibration \(\omega^2\) is proportional to the ratio of stiffness to inertia, and only the stiffness falls, to \(0{,}549\) of its former value.

Equation (16.61) neglects two things and both must be named. First: theorem 16.10 gives \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = G J\,\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\) for a twist per unit length that is constant along the shaft (uniform torsion, enakomerna torzija, definition 16.1). In vibration \(\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\) varies with \(x\), in the first mode it falls from its largest value at the wall to zero at the free end, where the rotation curve is horizontal, so for the strip the model is an approximation. We do not estimate the size of this approximation here. For the round shaft there is none. The displacement field \(\vek u = \varphi(x, t)\,(0, -z, y)\) has \(\operatorname{div}\vek u = 0\) and \(\nabla^2\vek u = \varphi_{\mathrm{xx}}\,(0, -z, y)\), because \(-z\varphi\) and \(y\varphi\) are linear in \(y\) and \(z\). By theorem 13.24 without body force, where the Lamé constants are \(\lambda\) and \(\mu = G\), this is a motion of the body exactly when \(G\,\varphi_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho\,\varphi_{\mathrm{tt}}\), which is equation (13.15). The lateral surface is free: the only nonzero stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -G z\,\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G y\,\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\), so on the lateral surface with normal \(\vek n = (0, y, z)/R\) the traction is \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = G\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\,(-z y + y z)/R = 0\) and \(t_{\mathrm{y}} = t_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). The model of chapter 13 is therefore exact for the circle also in vibration. For the strip the same computation fails. The warping \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\psi\) with \(\nabla^2\psi = 0\) gives in the direction \(x\) the left side \((\lambda + 2G)\,\varphi_{\mathrm{xxx}}\,\psi\), while equation (16.61) gives the right side \(\rho\,\varphi_{\mathrm{xtt}}\,\psi = G\,(J/I_{\mathrm{p}})\,\varphi_{\mathrm{xxx}}\,\psi\), and since for steel (\(\nu = 0{,}3\)) \(\lambda + 2G = 3{,}5\,G\) while \(G J/I_{\mathrm{p}}\) is only \(0{,}549\,G\), they do not agree. Second: the warping of the section moves during vibration. With the warping function (funkcija zvitja) \(\psi\) (definition 16.7) the axial displacement is \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\,\psi\), and its velocity has kinetic energy per unit length \(\tfrac12\rho\,\varphi_{\mathrm{xt}}^2\int \psi^2\,\mathrm{d}A\), which the equation did not have. How large is it? Since \(\psi\) for the strip is the series of section 16.5, we computed the integral: \(\int\psi^2\,\mathrm{d}A = 1{,}30\cdot10^{6}\) mm\(^4\) and \(\frac{1}{I_{\mathrm{p}}}\int\psi^2\,\mathrm{d}A = 9{,}75\) mm\(^2\) (num-10.out, as a check the same \(\psi\) gave the corner displacement \(0{,}832\) \(\mu\)m at \(50\) N m, as section 16.5 states). With the first mode \(\varphi = \varphi_0\sin(\pi x/2L)\) the ratio of the kinetic energies of warping and of rotation is

\[r = \frac{\int\psi^2\,\mathrm{d}A}{I_{\mathrm{p}}}\,\Big(\frac{\pi}{2L}\Big)^2 = 9{,}75\ \mathrm{mm}^2\cdot\Big(\frac{\pi}{2000\ \mathrm{mm}}\Big)^2 = 2{,}4\cdot10^{-5} ,\]

because by theorem 4.9 the kinetic energy splits into an integral over the section and an integral over \(x\), and the integrals over \(x\) are \(\int_0^L \varphi_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x = (\pi/2L)^2\,\varphi_0^2 L/2\) and \(\int_0^L \varphi^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \varphi_0^2 L/2\). The Rayleigh quotient (Rayleighov količnik) of the shaft (definition 13.52, with numerator \(\int_0^L G J\,\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) and denominator \(\int_0^L \rho I_{\mathrm{p}}\,\varphi^2\,\mathrm{d}x\)) with the same mode has, with the added energy, a denominator larger by the factor \(1 + r\). Hence \(\omega^2\) is lowered by the factor \(1/(1 + r)\) and the frequency by about \(r/2 = 0{,}0012\) %. For a shaft of length \(L = 1\) m the neglect of this energy is therefore justified. The ratio \(r\) grows with \(1/L^2\) and reaches \(0{,}38\) % at \(L = 80\) mm, where the frequency is lower by about \(0{,}19\) %, but there the length is only twice the longer side of the section (\(40\) mm), so uniform torsion is a poor model near the ends (section 11.11). The neglect therefore depends on the shape of the section and on the length, it does not hold for every shaft.

Example 16.60 Disc on the strip instead of the round shaft (disk na traku namesto na okrogli gredi)

A shaft fixed at \(x = 0\) carries at \(x = L = 1\) m a disc with moment of inertia \(J_{\mathrm{d}} = 0{,}05\) kg m\(^2\), as in example 13.23, but its section is \(20 \times 40\) mm. As in the proof of theorem 13.21 the boundary condition at the disc, which the shaft turns with a moment, is \(G J\,U'(L) = J_{\mathrm{d}}\,\omega^2\,U(L)\), so \(U'(L) = \lambda\,J_{\mathrm{d}}/(\rho I_{\mathrm{p}})\,U(L)\) with \(\lambda = \omega^2/c^2\) from equation (16.61). Equation (13.20) therefore holds unchanged with \(\mu = \rho I_{\mathrm{p}} L/J_{\mathrm{d}}\) and \(f_{\mathrm{r}} = c\,s_{\mathrm{r}}/(2\pi L)\), where now \(c = 2303{,}1\) m/s.

  1. The stiffness of the shaft is \(k_{\mathrm{t}} = G J/L = 5516{,}5\) N m/rad (by lemma 13.17 with \(J\) in place of \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\)), \(3{,}43\) times less than \(18\,946{,}3\) N m/rad for the circle (\(18\,946{,}3/5516{,}5 = 3{,}434\)).
  2. The one degree of freedom model gives \(\omega_{\mathrm{1PS}} = \sqrt{k_{\mathrm{t}}/J_{\mathrm{d}}} = 332{,}16\) 1/s, so \(f = 52{,}87\) Hz (for the circle \(97{,}97\) Hz).
  3. The inertia of the strip is \(\rho I_{\mathrm{p}} L = 7800\cdot1{,}3333\cdot10^{-7}\cdot 1 = 1{,}040\cdot10^{-3}\) kg m\(^2\), hence \(\mu = 0{,}02080\). The first root of \(s\tan s = \mu\) is \(s_1 = 0{,}14372\) (bisection in num-10.py), so \(f_1 = c\,s_1/(2\pi L) = 52{,}68\) Hz.
  4. By corollary 13.22 (with \(c\) in place of \(c_{\mathrm{T}}\)) the one degree of freedom model lies above the exact value: \(52{,}87/52{,}68 - 1 = 0{,}35\) %. For the circle the error was \(0{,}65\) %, because \(\mu\) was larger (\(0{,}0392\)). A smaller moment of inertia of the shaft relative to the disc, that is a smaller \(\mu\), means a better one degree of freedom model.

Source: The example and its numbers are ours (num-10.out). The value of \(J\) is from theorem 16.30, the equations are from chapter 13.

  • Space frame (AK, MK, chapter 12): equation (12.16), which the element took as an assumption, is proved by theorem 16.10. The number \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\) for the strip, which the element took from a source, is the sum of the series of theorem 16.30. The ratio \(J/I_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}549\) is the reason why the frame of chapter 12 (figure 12.16) with \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) in place of \(J\) underestimates the displacement from twisting by \(45\) % and the total displacement of point \(C\) by \(26\) %. The assumption that the centroid is the shear centre (strižno središče) holds for the strip by lemma 16.40, because it has two axes of symmetry. For a channel it is not true: the shear centre lies \(12{,}5\) mm from the centroid (section 16.7), and a force of \(500\) N through the centroid twists the channel in uniform torsion, far from a clamp, by \(22{,}3\) \(^\circ\)/m (corollary 16.41), so the element must place such sections on an axis through the shear centre or add an offset.
  • Vibration of shafts and the disc (VD, DSK, chapters 9 and 13): the stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{t}} = G I_{\mathrm{p}}/L\) of lemma 13.17 is now proved by theorem 16.3 and corollary 16.4. Example 16.60 shows what changes for a non-circular section: \(J\) in place of \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) in the stiffness, \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) stays in the inertia. Limit (figure 16.37): equation (16.61) is an approximation for a non-circular section. The kinetic energy of warping is estimated by \(r\), nonuniform torsion and warping restrained at the wall we do not estimate. For the circle the equation is exact.
  • Hollow shafts and rotors (DSK, chapters 24 and 23): for a hollow round shaft \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}} = \pi(R^4 - R_{\mathrm{i}}^4)/2\) (corollary 16.46). A \(40/32\) mm tube has \(J = 148\,384\) mm\(^4\) and at equal mass is \(4{,}56\) times stiffer than a solid shaft of diameter \(24\) mm (\(J = 32\,572\) mm\(^4\)). In the crankshaft of an engine the journal piece is round and \(G I_{\mathrm{p}}/\ell\) holds for it. For crank webs and cheeks, which are not round and are also loaded in bending, this chapter has no result and we state them as not covered.
  • Restrained warping (zadržan zvitek) and nonuniform torsion (AK, chapter 12): everything we derived means that the section can warp freely at the end. When a support or a joint holds it, the twist per unit length varies along the shaft and axial stresses appear in the section as well. COOK (PDF p. 42 to 43) describes an I beam five times as long as it is deep, in which complete restraint of warping at one end reduces the rotation at the other by about half and introduces axial normal stresses much larger than the torsional shear stress. The element of chapter 12 assumes free warping (section 12.5.1) and so has no extra degrees of freedom. Restrained warping needs them (the rate of twist at a node, a \(14 \times 14\) matrix), and programs often do not offer them (COOK, PDF p. 43). ONATE2 (section 4.10, PDF p. 227) says the same for thin open sections. The proof of this is not in the book: the derivation is in the sources named.
  • Multi-cell sections (več celic) and variable diameter (MK): in a section with several cells each cell must carry its own shear flow and equilibrium fixes the relations between them (ONATE2 section 4.3.5.1, PDF p. 206), and for a round shaft of variable diameter the field \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), \(u_\theta = u_\theta(r, z)\) is again a solution of all the field equations and the stress function is constant on the boundary (SADD section 9.7, PDF p. 270 to 271). We derive neither.
  • Heat conduction and membranes (MK, AK, chapters 14, 18 and 22): the equation \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2G\alpha\) with zero on the boundary (theorem 16.16) is the equation of steady heat conduction with a uniform source and zero temperature on the boundary, so the uniqueness of the solution and the element matrix of chapter 14 hold for it, and section 16.9 uses them for torsion. The reason is the same operator, not the same phenomenon. The membrane of section 16.4, a thin film without bending stiffness that carries a pressure \(p\) with tension \(N\) per unit length (corollary 16.26), has the same equation. The word membrane in shells (chapter 22) means something else, a shell that carries the load by axial forces in its middle surface only, and plates (chapter 18) have a bending stiffness that the film does not.
  • Limits of the chapter: the existence of the functions \(\psi\) and \(\Phi\) for a general section and Saint-Venant's principle at the ends are stated from sources. Open sections made of several strips (junctions), multi-cell sections, restrained warping and nonuniform torsion, variable diameter and plastic torsion are named or left out. The example of this section neglects the kinetic energy of warping, which \(r = 2{,}4\cdot10^{-5}\) justifies only for \(L = 1\) m, and does not estimate nonuniform torsion.
